first.name: The first Cypriots
first.origin: Farmers arriving by sea from the Levant and Anatolia
first.desc: Hunters camped on the island around 10,000 BCE, but Cyprus was settled around 8800 BCE by cultivators who shipped in wheat, barley and dogs; wild boar had been introduced by earlier hunters, and cattle, sheep and goats followed by boat over the next few centuries. They built round stone houses in tight villages and made bowls from grey andesite rather than clay. There was no ruler above the village.

sotira.name: Sotira villagers
sotira.origin: Indigenous, after a gap of several centuries whose length is still debated
sotira.desc: After the Aceramic villages emptied, the island was quiet until new farming communities appeared around 4500 BCE. They made the first Cypriot pottery, painted in the north and combed in the south, and lived in scattered villages that rarely lasted more than a few generations.

erimi.name: Chalcolithic communities
erimi.seat: Villages of the south-west, from Lemba to Erimi
erimi.desc: The first copper appears, hammered native metal made into small ornaments and then into hooks and chisels, and a striking figurine tradition in blue-green picrolite stone. Villages grew larger and buildings more formal, but the island was still a world of villages.

philia.name: Early Bronze Age Cypriots
philia.origin: Indigenous, with settlers from southern Anatolia
philia.seat: Villages and cemeteries of the north and centre
philia.desc: Around 2400 BCE new arrivals from Anatolia brought the cattle-drawn plough, rectangular mudbrick houses, and the island's first real copper industry; tin bronze became common only later, in the Middle Bronze Age. Copper from the Troodos foothills began to be worked in quantity, and the Red Polished pottery of this age is among the most inventive the island ever made.

alashiya.name: Alashiya
alashiya.origin: A Cypriot kingdom, named Alashiya in Near Eastern texts from about 1600 BCE, that dealt with Egypt as an equal and was forced into Hittite vassalage around 1200 BCE
alashiya.seat: Unknown. Enkomi is the usual guess, but the clay of the Alashiya letters points to the south coast near Kalavasos and Alassa. Other great towns: Kition, Hala Sultan Tekke
alashiya.desc: By the Late Bronze Age Cyprus was Alashiya, a copper-exporting kingdom whose king addressed the pharaoh as 'my brother' in the Amarna letters. Towns had ashlar buildings, a script of their own (Cypro-Minoan) and warehouses of oxhide copper ingots. Mycenaean pottery arrived in quantity from the fourteenth century BCE, carried mostly by Cypriot and Levantine ships; Aegean settlers came only after 1200 BCE, and the collapse that ended the Bronze Age remade the island.

rulers.n: No king of Alashiya is known by name
rulers.t: The Alashiya letters never name their sender. Kinyras, the Cypriot king of the Iliad, is legend.

The only king of Alashiya whose name survives, from letters found at Ugarit; the kings who wrote to Egypt in the Amarna archive are all anonymous, and this attribution should be checked against a specialist edition before publication.

kingdoms.name: The Greek city-kingdoms
kingdoms.origin: Greek settlers over an indigenous population, Phoenicians at Kition
kingdoms.seat: Independent kingdoms: Salamis, Paphos, Kourion, Amathus and others, first listed by name in 673 BCE
kingdoms.desc: After 1050 BCE Greek-speakers founded new towns, and by the seventh century the island held about ten small kingdoms. They wrote Greek in the old Cypriot syllabary, and they shared the island with a Phoenician colony at Kition, settled from Tyre around 850 BCE. At the very end of this age the kings of Salamis began to be buried with horses and chariots. No one power ruled the whole island.

rulers.n: No Cypriot king is attested by name before 673 BCE
rulers.t: The earliest named kings are the ten of Esarhaddon's prism, listed under the Archaic era.
The Cypriot king of the Iliad, who gave Agamemnon a breastplate; a figure of myth attached to Paphos, not a historical ruler.

rulers.n: The ten kings of Esarhaddon's prism
rulers.t: Ekishtura of Idalion, Pilagura of Chytroi, Kisu of Salamis, Ituandar of Paphos, Erisu of Soloi, Damasu of Kourion, Admesu of Tamassos, Damusi of Qartihadasti, Unasagusu of Ledra and Bususu of Marion: the first roll-call of Cypriot kings, most of them Greek names in Assyrian spelling.
Struck the first Cypriot coins, silver with a recumbent ram and his name in the syllabary, and dedicated a censer at Delphi.
Shut out of his own city by his brother Onesilos, he fled to the Persians and was restored when the revolt collapsed.
Led the island into the Ionian Revolt, besieged loyalist Amathus, and was killed in battle; the Amathusians hung his head over their gate.
Deserted to the Persians during the decisive battle, taking his chariots with him, and handed them the war.
First of the Phoenician kings of Kition known from coins, with Herakles for Melqart on the obverse.
The last independent king of Idalion, named on the bronze tablet that hires a physician during the siege; his city fell to Kition around 450 BCE.
Struck the recumbent lion coinage of Amathus on a stubbornly local weight standard.
Seized his throne at twenty, extended his rule over most of the island, fought Persia for a decade and kept his crown as a king to a king; Isocrates wrote an encomium for him.
Set up a trophy to Baal Oz for a victory in his first year, probably over Evagoras, and struck the first gold at Kition.
Son of Evagoras; reformed the coinage on a new standard and abandoned the Cypriot syllabary on his money.
Ruled Kition, Idalion and, from 342/341 BCE, Tamassos, numbering his regnal years on his coins for more than forty-five years; Ptolemy I had him executed.
Driven out by his own people, he took service with the Persian king and tried to win the throne back with Persian help.
Sold his city and his royal title to Pumayyaton of Kition for fifty talents and grew old at Amathus on the proceeds.
Held Salamis through a Persian siege, then sent ships to Alexander at Tyre and was rewarded with Tamassos.
Alexander's man and then Ptolemy's, the last king of Salamis; his family killed themselves in the palace, and an empty mound in the necropolis is thought to be his memorial.
Moved his capital to the new harbour town of Nea Paphos and was forced by Ptolemy to take his own life.
The first Marion king to strike gold; Ptolemy arrested him for siding with Antigonus, razed his city and moved its people to Paphos.
Last king of Lapethos, deposed and arrested by Ptolemy I in the same sweep, along with the ruler of Kyrenia.
The last Amathusian king in the record; he dedicated a gold wreath to Apollo on Delos in 313 BCE.
Married Eirene, a daughter of Ptolemy I, and so outlived every other Cypriot dynasty; his gold shows Apollo and Aphrodite.
Brother of Ptolemy I, governor at Salamis and the first man to strike coin on Cyprus as an outsider rather than a king; the kingdoms were over.

overlords.name: City-kingdoms under Assyria, Egypt and Persia
overlords.seat: The kingdoms kept their kings, paying tribute to the empire of the day
overlords.desc: Seven Cypriot kings submitted to Sargon II of Assyria around 709–707 BCE, and Esarhaddon's scribes listed ten kings of the island in 673. Egypt made Cyprus tributary under Amasis around 560 BCE, and by about 545 the Persians had taken it into their empire. Cyprus lay within a Persian province, but the city-kingdoms kept their own dynasties, coinage and quarrels.

rulers.n: The ten kings of Esarhaddon's prism
rulers.t: Ekishtura of Idalion, Pilagura of Chytroi, Kisu of Salamis, Ituandar of Paphos, Eresu of Soli, Damasu of Kourion, Admesu of Tamassos, Damusi of Qart-hadasht (Kition), Unasagusu of Ledra and Bususu of Nure (Amathus?). Some identifications are debated.
Founder of the Salamis dynasty known to Herodotus; first Cypriot king to strike coins.
Son and grandson of Evelthon, known from Herodotus's genealogy.
Refused to join the Ionian Revolt, was ousted by his brother and restored by the Persians.
Seized Salamis, led the island's revolt against Persia and was killed in battle; Amathus displayed his skull.
Philokypros was praised by Solon; his son Aristokypros fell fighting for Onesilos.
Deserted to the Persians during the battle near Salamis, deciding it.

persia.name: Achaemenid Persia
persia.origin: Persian Empire; Cyprus grouped with Phoenicia and Syria in the province 'Beyond the River'
persia.seat: Local kings ruled; Persian garrisons and Phoenician allies at Kition and elsewhere
persia.desc: Cyprus lay within a Persian satrapy but the city-kingdoms retained local dynasties. Salamis under Evagoras I became a centre of Greek culture and a thorn in the Persian side, and Greek fleets came three times, in 478, around 460 and in 450, to pull the island into the Greek world. Persian control was real but never total.

rulers.t: Expelled the Phoenician usurper Abdemon, Hellenised Salamis, fought Persia from 391 to about 380; murdered in 374.
Son of Evagoras I; Isocrates addressed two speeches to him.
Pro-Persian; deposed by his nephew Pnytagoras, later Persian governor of Sidon.
Joined the anti-Persian revolt of the 340s, survived, then fought for Alexander at Tyre and received Tamassos.
Last king of Salamis; backed Ptolemy and became governor of the island.

rulers.n: Baalmilk I, Azbaal, Baalmilk II of Kition
rulers.t: Phoenician dynasty of Kition; Azbaal captured Idalion and ruled as 'king of Kition and Idalion'.
Fought Evagoras I; struck the first gold and bronze coins of Kition.
Last king of Kition; sold Tamassos to Pnytagoras; executed by Ptolemy.
Last king of Idalion, named on the bronze Idalion Tablet.
Last king of Paphos; refounded Nea Paphos; forced to suicide by Ptolemy.

rulers.n: Androkles of Amathus, Pasikrates of Kourion, Stasioikos II of Marion, Stasikrates and Eunostos of Soli
rulers.t: The last kings of their cities, most of whom sailed with the Cypriot fleet to Alexander's siege of Tyre in 332.

ptolemies.name: Ptolemaic Egypt
ptolemies.seat: Salamis, then Nea Paphos as capital of the strategos
ptolemies.desc: After Alexander the city-kingdoms were abolished by Ptolemy I, and for two and a half centuries Cyprus was Egypt's timber yard, copper mine, grain store and naval base. A Ptolemaic governor ruled from Nea Paphos. Greek koine became the language of government, and the old Cypriot syllabary faded out by the end of the third century BCE.

rulers.t: Last king of Salamis, made Ptolemy's governor of the whole island; died by suicide or murder.
Ptolemy I's brother; governed Cyprus until Demetrius took Salamis in 306.
Earliest governor (strategos) attested by inscriptions, under Ptolemy IV; based at Salamis.
Strategos under the boy-king Ptolemy V; later chancellor in Alexandria.
Strategos who handed Cyprus to Antiochus IV in 168 and defected to the Seleucids.
Strategos and high priest of the island under Ptolemy VIII.
Younger brother of Ptolemy XII of Egypt, king of Cyprus as a separate kingdom; killed himself when Cato arrived.

rome.name: Roman Empire
rome.origin: Rome; from 22 BCE a senatorial province under a proconsul
rome.desc: Annexed in 58 BCE, Cyprus was a quiet, wealthy province of theatres, baths and villas. Paul and Barnabas preached here around 45 CE and the island claims the first Christian governor. Salamis was ruined in the Jewish revolt of 115–117, and a Christian island was already taking shape when the earthquakes of the 340s brought the ancient cities down.

rulers.t: Special commissioner who carried out the annexation; not a governor.
Governed Cilicia with Cyprus attached and wrote about the island's debts.
Twice proconsul of Cyprus, known from his tomb inscription at Histonium.
The proconsul who heard Paul at Paphos according to Acts 13.
Proconsul who rebuilt the Kourion theatre after an earthquake.
Proconsul named on a Kourion inscription for a statue of Nero.

byzantium.name: Byzantine Empire
byzantium.origin: Eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople
byzantium.seat: Salamis-Constantia, then Nicosia (capital of the theme from 965)
byzantium.desc: Cyprus was a Christian island with an independent church from 431 CE. Arab fleets raided from 649, and from 688 to 965 the island was a strange shared possession, paying tax to both the Caliphate and Constantinople. In 965 Nikephoros II Phokas's general Niketas Chalkoutzes recovered it, Cyprus became a Byzantine theme, and inland Nicosia became the capital.

rulers.t: Bishop of Salamis-Constantia and metropolitan of Cyprus; heresy-hunter and author of the Panarion.
Led the Cypriot bishops at Ephesus and won canon 8, the charter of the Church's independence.
Found the relics of Barnabas and secured Zeno's confirmation of autocephaly.
Archbishop deported with his flock to Nea Justinianoupolis; source of the title the Church of Cyprus still uses.
Archbishop who resigned in protest at official abuses; later Patriarch of Constantinople.
Usurper who ruled the island as a self-styled emperor until Richard I deposed him.
Rebuilt earthquake-ruined Salamis as Constantia, remitted its taxes and made it the capital of the island.
Paid for the basilica over Barnabas's tomb and gave the archbishop the sceptre, the purple and the red ink.
Reign of the great mosaic floors and the last generation of five-aisled basilicas; Archbishop Philoxenos enlarged the Barnabas shrine under him.
Agreed the condominium with Abd al-Malik in 688, then moved much of the population to Nea Justinianoupolis near Cyzicus in 691.
Bishop who is said to have followed his captured flock to the caliph's court and brought them home.
Patrician who recovered the island for Nikephoros II Phokas with a small force and made it a theme.
Governor who rebelled, was captured and was paraded through the Hippodrome dressed as a woman.
Rebel governor put down by John Doukas and Manuel Boutoumites for Alexios I.
The island's most effective Byzantine governor, patron of the paintings at Koutsovendis and scourge of Levantine pirates.
Governor captured when Raynald of Chatillon raided the island; his defeat let the Franks plunder it for three weeks.

lusignan.name: Kingdom of Cyprus, House of Lusignan
lusignan.seat: Nicosia; after 1291 the kings were also crowned Kings of Jerusalem at Famagusta, until the riot of 1372
lusignan.desc: Richard the Lionheart took the island in 1191 and it passed to Guy de Lusignan. His dynasty ruled for three centuries, building Gothic cathedrals and castles and putting the Greek Church under a Latin archbishop. It grew rich on Famagusta's trade after Acre fell, then slowly bled to Genoese and Mamluk pressure. Cyprus was the last crusader kingdom.

rulers.t: Lord of Cyprus, never crowned king; former King of Jerusalem.
Guy's brother; crowned first King of Cyprus in 1197; also King of Jerusalem 1197–1205.
Son of Aimery; child king under regency.
Long minority; Ibelin regents fight Frederick II's supporters 1228–1233.
Died aged about fourteen; end of the direct male line.
Of Antioch-Lusignan; also King of Jerusalem from 1268.
Reigned one year.
Lost Acre in 1291; deposed 1306–1310 by his brother Amalric of Tyre.
Peak of prosperity; patron of Bellapais.
Crusader king; sacked Alexandria in 1365; murdered by his knights in 1369.
Coronation riot 1372; Genoese invasion 1373–1374.
Held hostage in Genoa until 1385; titular King of Armenia from 1393.
Defeated and captured by the Mamluks at Khirokitia in 1426.
Married Helena Palaiologina.
Queen regnant, driven out by her half-brother; died in Rome in 1487.
Seized the crown with Mamluk backing; recovered Famagusta from Genoa; married Caterina Cornaro.
Infant king, died aged one.
Venetian-born last queen; forced to abdicate in 1489.

venice.name: Republic of Venice
venice.origin: Venetian Republic, governed by a Luogotenente and Provveditore
venice.seat: Nicosia, with Famagusta as the fortress port
venice.desc: Venice acquired the island through Queen Caterina Cornaro and ran it as a heavily taxed colony and a forward base against the Ottomans. Its lasting legacy is stone: the star-shaped walls of Nicosia and the vast ramparts of Famagusta. Famagusta's were complete by 1562; Nicosia's were still unfinished when the Ottomans landed in 1570.

rulers.t: Cyprus was governed from Nicosia by a lieutenant sent out from Venice, normally for two years, advised by two counsellors, with a Capitano commanding Famagusta, rectors in the lesser towns and a Provveditore Generale sent out in emergencies.
First lieutenant of Cyprus, appointed in the year Caterina Cornaro abdicated.
Lieutenant of Cyprus, later Doge of Venice from 1553 to 1554.
Lieutenant of Cyprus, later second in command of the Christian fleet and mortally wounded at Lepanto in 1571.
Lieutenant during the invasion; blamed by contemporaries for a timid defence and killed when Nicosia was stormed on 9 September 1570.
Lieutenant of Cyprus, then Capitano Generale da Mar who commanded the Venetian fleet at Lepanto, and Doge from 1577 to 1578.
Last lieutenant appointed; never reached the island.
Capitano of Famagusta, who held the fortress for ten and a half months and was flayed alive on 17 August 1571 after the surrender terms were broken.
Umbrian condottiere and governor of the island's troops, who ran the fighting defence of Famagusta and was killed at the surrender.

ottoman.name: Ottoman Empire
ottoman.origin: Ottoman Sultanate, Cyprus as an eyalet, later a sanjak
ottoman.desc: After the sieges of 1570 and 1571 Cyprus became an Ottoman province for three centuries. Latin rule ended and the Orthodox Church was restored, its archbishop becoming the leader of the Greek community. Turkish settlers formed the island's Muslim population. Neglect, locusts and heavy taxation marked much of the period.

rulers.t: Commander of the conquest and the island's first governor; he had Bragadin flayed at Famagusta and gave his name to its cathedral-mosque.
First beylerbeyi of the new province of Cyprus, credited with building the Buyuk Han in Nicosia; some scholars give the han to his successor Sinan Pasha.
Cyprus was a full eyalet under a governor of pasha rank with sanjaks on the mainland; some seventy governors came and went, few staying more than two years.
The island was downgraded to a sanjak assigned to the Ottoman admiral, who sent a deputy; real power passed to local aghas and tax farmers, and revolts followed.

rulers.n: The muhassils of the Grand Vizier
rulers.t: Cyprus was granted to the Grand Vizier as a source of income and run by a muhassil who bought the right to collect its taxes, the arrangement that made both extortion and the Church's power possible.
Governor of the brief restored eyalet, remembered for good order and for beginning the aqueduct to Larnaca in 1747.
Muhassil who doubled the tax demand; Greeks and Turks together stormed the palace in Nicosia and killed him, one of the few joint risings of the period.
Muhassil who ordered the hanging of Archbishop Kyprianos and the beheading of the three bishops on 9 July 1821 and the executions and confiscations that followed.

After the Tanzimat reforms Cyprus was governed by a mutasarrif under the Archipelago province and then, from 1861 and again from 1870, as a separate mutasarrifate until the British took over the administration.
Archbishop under whom the Porte came to treat the prelates as spokesmen of the Orthodox flock, the step conventionally dated to 1660.
Consolidated the archbishop's standing as head of the Greek community, with the right to petition Constantinople over the governor's head.
Presided over the years when the archbishop and the four bishops collected the Christians' taxes and were, in practice, the island's civil government.
Interpreter to the governor and tax intermediary, the richest man on the island; executed at Constantinople in 1809 after complaints from both communities.
Founder of the Hellenic School of Nicosia in 1812; hanged from a tree outside the palace on 9 July 1821 in the reprisals for the Greek revolt.

britain.name: British Cyprus
britain.origin: British Empire: occupied and administered from 1878, annexed 1914, Crown Colony 1925
britain.seat: Nicosia; the High Commissioner, later Governor, at Government House
britain.desc: Britain took over the administration in 1878 under the Cyprus Convention, keeping the island as a base on the road to India and Suez. It annexed Cyprus in 1914 and made it a Crown Colony in 1925. Roads, schools and courts were built and the population doubled, but the Greek majority's demand for union with Greece grew louder, exploding in the riots of 1931 and the armed EOKA campaign of 1955–59, which ended in independence rather than union.

rulers.t: First High Commissioner, who landed at Larnaca in July 1878 and set up the administration.
Governor whose Government House was burned in the October 1931 riots.
Governor of the authoritarian 'Palmerocracy' after 1931, with the legislature abolished.
Governor during the EOKA emergency; exiled Archbishop Makarios to the Seychelles in 1956.
Last Governor, who handed over power at independence on 16 August 1960.
Raised the British flag at Nicosia on 12 July 1878 and held the administration for ten days.
Built the first roads, courts and schools and the summer residence on the Troodos; the longest-serving of the early administrators.
Presided over the first stirrings of organised enosis politics in the Legislative Council.
High Commissioner during years of locust campaigns, agricultural debt and emigration.
Faced deadlock in the Legislative Council between Greek and Turkish members and the British bloc.
Opened the Cyprus Government Railway in 1905 and the rebuilt harbour at Famagusta.
In office when Britain annexed Cyprus in November 1914 after the Ottoman entry into the war.
Administered the island through the war, when Britain offered Cyprus to Greece and Athens declined.
Last High Commissioner and first Governor when Cyprus became a Crown Colony in 1925.
Held the governorship for a year in the immediate repression after the riots.
Relaxed some of Palmer's restrictions as war began and raised the Cyprus Regiment.
Governor through the war years, when trade unions and communal politics revived.
Offered a Consultative Assembly and a constitution which the Greek Cypriot leadership boycotted; resigned when the offer failed.
In office for the 1950 enosis plebiscite and the election of Makarios III as archbishop.
Governor when the constitution was again refused and EOKA opened its campaign on 1 April 1955.

republic.name: Republic of Cyprus
republic.origin: Independent republic under the Zurich and London agreements of 1959; member of the European Union since 2004
republic.desc: Cyprus became independent on 16 August 1960 with Archbishop Makarios III as president and a power-sharing constitution guaranteed by Greece, Turkey and Britain, which kept two Sovereign Base Areas. The constitution broke down in 1963, United Nations peacekeepers arrived in 1964, and in 1974 a coup backed by the Greek junta was answered by a Turkish invasion that has divided the island since. The Republic joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2008; talks on reunification continue.

rulers.t: Archbishop and first president; survived the 1974 coup and returned to office until his death.
President through the aftermath of division and the 1983 declaration in the north.
Businessman-president who applied for European Community membership in 1990.
Veteran negotiator who led accession talks with the European Union.
President when Cyprus joined the EU; opposed the Annan reunification plan in the 2004 referendum.
Communist-party president; the euro was adopted and the 2012–13 banking crisis struck.
Steered the bailout and recovery; the Crans-Montana talks of 2017 ended without agreement.
Former foreign minister, elected president in February 2023.

ERAS.name: Epipalaeolithic and Aceramic Neolithic
events: Hunters camp at Akrotiri-Aetokremnos, the earliest trace of people on Cyprus
Hunters quarry and grind red ochre at Ayia Varvara-Asprokremnos and carve the oldest human figurine known from Cyprus
Klimonas, near Amathus, is the oldest known village on Cyprus, with a ten-metre communal round building
A well eight metres deep is cut into bedrock at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia, among the oldest water wells known anywhere
Cattle, goats and Mesopotamian fallow deer are ferried across from the mainland; sheep follow within a few centuries
Cappadocian obsidian comes ashore at Akanthou-Arkosykos on the north coast, which handles more of it than every other Cypriot site put together
At Shillourokambos a man is buried beside a cat, the world's oldest evidence of cat taming; villagers at Kalavasos-Tenta ring their hilltop with a wall and ditch
Khirokitia founded, a walled village of round stone houses
Cattle vanish from the island and are not seen again until the Bronze Age; fallow deer become the mainstay of the meat supply
Fishermen at Cape Andreas-Kastros, at the tip of the Karpas, take tuna and grouper from deep water
The Aceramic villages are abandoned and the island falls quiet
ERAS.region: Farming spreads through the Fertile Crescent. Jericho and Çatalhöyük are large towns. There is no pottery yet anywhere in the Near East when the first Cypriots arrive.

life.economy: Almost everything the first farmers lived on came by boat: emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils and pulses as seed grain, and sheep, goats, cattle and dogs as breeding stock, with Mesopotamian fallow deer released to be hunted rather than herded. Cattle failed and died out during the period and were not seen on the island again for some three thousand years, so meat came from deer, sheep, goats and pigs, while olives, figs, pistachios, plums and pears were gathered wild. There was no metal and no pottery; the only imports that survive are blades of Anatolian obsidian, about three hundred of them at Shillourokambos alone, and vessels were carved instead from hard grey andesite.
life.language: The language of these people is unrecoverable. Writing would not be invented anywhere for another five thousand years and no later text preserves a word of what was spoken here, so the most that can be said is that the settlers came from the Levant and Anatolia and are likely to have spoken something related to the pre-Semitic and pre-Indo-European languages of the Near East. It has occasionally been suggested that the non-Greek Eteocypriot still spoken at Amathus in the fourth century BCE descends from this earliest layer, but the suggestion is untestable and most scholars will not press it back beyond the Bronze Age.
life.religion: There are no temples, no shrines and no unambiguous cult buildings; ritual, so far as it can be seen at all, happened in and under the house. At Khirokitia the dead were laid in shallow pits beneath the plastered floors with the knees drawn up, and a quern or another heavy stone was often placed on the body, adults and children alike, before a new floor was laid over them. Schematic stone heads and figurines were carved, and at Shillourokambos a man was buried with a cat laid beside him, but what any of it meant is guesswork.
life.people: Villages were small and tightly packed: Khirokitia, the largest known, is thought never to have held more than three hundred to six hundred people at a time in round stone houses inside a perimeter wall, and Klimonas, almost two thousand years older, had a communal round building ten metres across. The Khirokitia skeletons give a mean age at death of about thirty-five for men and thirty-three for women among those who survived childhood, with very high infant mortality, and men stood around 160 centimetres, women around 150. Diet was overwhelmingly terrestrial, with little or no marine food in the isotope record even at coastal sites, and the whole population descends from a deliberate seaborne migration that must have moved people, seed and livestock in organised boatloads.

pop.n: No island-wide figure can be recovered. Khirokitia, the largest village known, may have held a few hundred people at any one time.

reading.t: The Archaeology of Cyprus: From Earliest Prehistory through the Bronze Age
reading.n: The standard synthesis of the island's prehistory, from the first hunters to the end of the Bronze Age.

reading.t: Cyprus Before History: From the Earliest Settlers to the End of the Bronze Age
reading.n: A readable single-volume account of prehistoric Cyprus for the general reader.

reading.t: Faunal Extinction in an Island Society: Pygmy Hippopotamus Hunters of Cyprus
reading.n: The Aetokremnos excavation report, and the argument that the first Cypriots hunted the island's dwarf hippos to extinction.

reading.t: First wave of cultivators spread to Cyprus at least 10,600 y ago
reading.n: The PNAS paper on Klimonas that pushed the first Cypriot village back two millennia.

reading.t: Fouilles récentes à Khirokitia (Chypre)
reading.n: The French mission's reports on the walled Neolithic village, the best-preserved of its age in the eastern Mediterranean.

reading.t: Khirokitia: Final Report on the Excavation of a Neolithic Settlement in Cyprus
reading.n: The original excavation of Khirokitia, still the foundation of everything written about it since.

ERAS.name: Ceramic Neolithic
events: The last Aceramic villages fall silent; whether the island emptied or its people simply became harder to see is still argued
Pottery appears already fully formed, brought from the mainland rather than invented on the island
New villages appear: Sotira-Teppes on a hilltop above the Kouris valley and Ayios Epiktitos-Vrysi on the north coast
At Paralimni-Nissia on the east coast some forty houses are ringed with a horseshoe-shaped wall beside a natural harbour
Villagers at Kalavasos-Kokkinoyia cut chambers into the soft bedrock instead of building houses, and leave triton shells in two of them
Combed Ware is the signature pottery of the southern villages, Red-on-White of the northern ones
The dead move out of the houses: twelve graves are dug on the slope below Sotira, with boulders laid on the chest and almost nothing else
Obsidian all but disappears; a Ceramic Neolithic village holds one or two pieces at most
The Sotira culture ends, perhaps after earthquakes; at Sotira most of the houses collapsed
The last Sotira-culture villages, Vrysi among them, are given up; a further break of several centuries follows
ERAS.region: Ubaid culture unites Mesopotamia. Predynastic Egypt begins along the Nile. Copper metallurgy is emerging in Anatolia and the Balkans.

life.economy: Farming was mixed and local: sickle-gloss flint blades and quantities of grinding equipment show cereal cultivation, and Ayios Epiktitos-Vrysi adds olives and grapes to the wheat, barley and pulses, while fallow deer, sheep, goats and pigs supplied the meat. The new craft was pottery, Combed Ware in the south and Red-on-White in the north, made for household use rather than for exchange, and stone bowls went out of fashion as it came in. Anatolian obsidian, the one clear import of the previous age, now dwindles almost to nothing, and the island looks more inward-facing in these centuries than at almost any other time in its history.
life.language: Unrecoverable, and here the island's isolation makes even indirect inference harder than before. Whether these villagers descended from the Aceramic population or from fresh arrivals is itself unsettled, since a gap of several centuries whose length is still debated separates the two, so nothing certain can be said about linguistic continuity. Nothing was written; the sharp difference between northern and southern pot decoration says something about community identity but nothing at all about speech.
life.religion: Still no sanctuaries, no cult buildings and no named gods. Burial remained a village affair, in simple pits inside or on the edge of the settlement with few or no goods, and Sotira-Teppes has yielded the largest group of Ceramic Neolithic human remains on the island. Small stone and clay figurines continue to be made, and pottery or a quern placed with a body is usually read as ritual, though the reading rests on very little.
life.people: These were small communities living in free-standing single-room huts, sunk into the ground at Vrysi and clustered around open yards at Sotira-Teppes, where about fifty such structures have been traced; no published population estimate exists for either. Skeletal work in the Limassol district shows a diet high in terrestrial protein with little marine input, along with the joint wear and heavy dental attrition expected of a population grinding its own grain by hand. A pilot strontium study suggests that some individuals moved between districts during their lives, but the settlements themselves were short-lived, rarely lasting more than a few generations before being given up.

pop.n: No island-wide figure. The Sotira-culture villages were small and rarely outlasted a few generations.

reading.n: Covers the gap after the Aceramic villages and the arrival of the first pottery-making communities.

reading.t: Sotira
reading.n: The excavation report for the type-site of the Ceramic Neolithic, a hilltop village of fifty houses.

reading.t: Early Society in Cyprus
reading.n: Essays on how the island's first societies were organised, from villages to the beginnings of rank.

ERAS.name: Chalcolithic
events: Villagers at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia cut two long parallel ditches across their site, the earliest enclosure works known on the island
First copper objects, hammered rather than cast
The dead at Souskiou are moved out of the village into deep rock-cut shafts, the first extramural cemeteries on Cyprus
Picrolite from the Kouris and Dhiarizos beds becomes the island's first widely traded material, worked into pendants at Souskiou-Laona
Cruciform picrolite figurines are worn as pendants across the south-west; rich shaft graves at Souskiou show the first ranked burials
Kissonerga-Mosphilia, the largest Chalcolithic village known, builds its Red Building and buries a hoard of figurines with a clay house model
A copper axe of foreign form is packed into a storage jar at Chlorakas-Palloures with a stone axe, four pig-tusk fish hooks and a copper spiral
The Pithos House at Kissonerga, nine metres across and packed with storage jars, copper slag and a stamp seal, burns down
Ore and two possible crucibles appear in the last houses at Kissonerga; whether anyone on Chalcolithic Cyprus actually smelted is still disputed
Contact with Anatolia intensifies as the Philia phase begins
Lemba, Kissonerga and Souskiou are all given up within a few generations, with no destruction to explain it
ERAS.region: Uruk and the first cities of Sumer. Egypt is unified under the first pharaohs around 3100 BCE. Troy is founded and the Cycladic islands flourish.

life.economy: Farming broadened to cereals, legumes and orchard crops of olive, grape, fig and pistachio, and while fallow deer were still hunted in quantity, herded sheep, goats and pigs came to outnumber wild game in the bone counts by the end of the period. Copper appears for the first time, native metal hammered cold into pins, hooks and small chisels, worked in tiny amounts and nowhere near the scale that later made the island's name. The signature craft was picrolite, a soft blue-green stone picked out of the Kouris and Diarizos river beds and carved into pendants and figurines; imported faience beads in the Souskiou graves are among the few certain traces of contact overseas.
life.language: Unrecoverable. The island was largely self-contained and entirely unlettered, and the picrolite figurines, however expressive, carry no writing of any kind. The idea that the later Eteocypriot language descends from a Chalcolithic or earlier substrate is possible but untestable, and no linguist claims more than that.
life.religion: The cruciform picrolite figurines, worn as pendants in life and then buried with their owners, are the clearest ritual objects of the age, though the once-standard reading of them as fertility goddesses or birthing scenes is now widely doubted and they are as often taken for personal charms or markers of identity. Kissonerga-Mosphilia produced a deliberate deposit of figurines packed inside a model of a building, which looks like the residue of a ceremony rather than a household accident, and the site's Red Building and Pithos House may have had some communal function. Burial was in pit graves inside the village, single and flexed, with infants sometimes placed in pots, while at Souskiou rock-cut shaft graves outside the settlement took several bodies in succession with much richer goods, the earliest sign on Cyprus of ranking in death.
life.people: Villages grew well beyond Neolithic scale: Kissonerga-Mosphilia extended over as much as twelve hectares across its successive phases, though only part of that was occupied at any one time, and buildings became larger and more formal. Grave goods begin to differ sharply from one burial to the next, at Souskiou above all, and the argument over whether this reflects real social inequality or only differences of age, sex and household is still live. Diet remained terrestrial with almost no fish, and the strontium evidence for movement between districts is suggestive rather than conclusive.

pop.n: No island-wide figure. Kissonerga-Mosphilia, the largest settlement known, covered about twelve hectares.

reading.n: The excavation volumes for Lemba and Kissonerga, the villages that define the Cypriot Chalcolithic.

reading.n: Reads the cruciform figurines and birth imagery of the Chalcolithic as evidence for how gender was lived.

reading.n: The first copper, the picrolite figurines and the growth of villages, set in their wider context.

ERAS.name: Early Bronze Age
events: At Sotira-Kaminoudhia, beside the old Neolithic village, Philia-phase settlers build multi-room rectangular houses
Tombs at Vasilia on the north coast receive a spearhead and a sword of central Taurus copper, imported ready-made
Philia culture: Anatolian settlers, the plough, and rectangular houses
The plough, the mould-made mudbrick, the rectangular house and new ways of cooking and spinning arrive together, which is why many argue for migrants rather than fashions
The great cemetery at Vounous begins, with its scenes of ritual in clay
The cemetery on the Kafkalla plateau at Deneia begins to fill; over 1,200 of its tombs will eventually be robbed
Politiko-Troullia is founded beside the pillow lavas, its households smelting their own copper and carving the largest stone plank figure known
Red Polished ware is at its most elaborate; Marki-Alonia has grown to a village of about four hundred people
At Pyrgos-Mavroraki one complex smelts copper, presses olive oil, weaves cloth and blends perfumed oil, burning the oil as furnace fuel
Miners at Ambelikou-Aletri sink shafts beside the Skouriotissa orebody, the earliest copper mining yet proved on Cyprus
Copper from Alashiya is soon recorded in texts from Mari on the Euphrates (c. 1800 BCE), the first written trace of Cyprus's export trade
ERAS.region: Akkadian Empire under Sargon of Akkad. Egypt's Old Kingdom, builder of the great pyramids, collapses around 2180 BCE. The first Minoan palaces rise on Crete.

life.economy: Cattle returned to Cyprus after some three thousand years, and with them the ard plough, which opened the heavier soils of the central lowlands and supplied traction, milk and hides; isotopic work on Philia-phase cattle confirms that these were kept and worked animals rather than hunted ones. Copper was now smelted and cast rather than merely hammered, the first real metal industry on the island, and Red Polished ware, the most inventive pottery Cyprus ever produced, was made in every village. Export begins just as the period closes: cuneiform tablets from Mari on the Euphrates, of the first half of the eighteenth century BCE, record purchases of copper and bronze from Alashiya and distinguish its ordinary, mountain and refined grades.
life.language: Still unrecoverable and still unwritten. The Philia newcomers from southern Anatolia brought ploughs, cattle and rectangular house plans but no script, and if they brought a language with them it left no direct trace; attempts to tie it either to Anatolian Indo-European or to the later Eteocypriot are speculation. The first written word for the island is a foreign one, the Akkadian Alashiya of the Mari tablets, and even the equation of Alashiya with Cyprus, though now generally accepted, was disputed for a century.
life.religion: Cult has to be inferred almost entirely from cemeteries and from clay. The Red Polished models, above all the bowl from Vounous with figures ranged around an enclosure and bulls' heads set on its wall, are usually taken to depict a ceremony, but what the ceremony was, and whether the scene shows a rite or a story, is genuinely contested. Bulls recur throughout the pottery, rock-cut chamber tombs outside the village replace burial under the floor, and the dead were given large numbers of vessels, which implies eating and drinking at the graveside.
life.people: Marki-Alonia, the most thoroughly excavated village, grew to something like four hundred people living in agglomerated multi-room rectangular houses, and the great cemetery at Bellapais-Vounous served a community of similar order. The household remained the unit of production, with craft work done at home and only elementary specialisation, and there is no archaeological sign of any authority above the village. Diet was cereals, pulses, dairy, sheep, goat and pig, with deer now a minor part of it, and the move to extramural chamber tombs makes the dead more visible and differences in their wealth easier to read.

pop.n: No island-wide figure. Marki-Alonia, an ordinary village, is estimated at about four hundred people.

ERAS.name: Middle and Late Bronze Age
events: An earthquake flattens the workshops at Pyrgos-Mavroraki and preserves the perfumers' equipment where it stood
White Painted juglets in the pendent line and cross line styles reach over thirty sites in the Levant and Tell el-Dab'a in Egypt, the first Cypriot pottery exported in quantity
Fort building begins in earnest: a ditched double wall at Barsak above the Yialias, cyclopean walls at Nitovikla, and watchposts at either end of the Agirda pass
Fortresses such as Nitovikla guard the routes from the copper mines to the coast
The hilltop workshop at Erimi-Laonin tou Porakou dyes cloth around a central court and casts axe-shaped copper ingots in terracotta moulds
Copper is smelted at Politiko-Phorades in the Troodos foothills, the earliest smelting workshop yet excavated on the island
Cypriot White Slip and Base Ring pottery, made in quarters like Toumba tou Skourou, is traded from Egypt to the Aegean
Cypro-Minoan script in use; Enkomi becomes a metalworking city
The Hittite king Arnuwanda I claims Alashiya as Hittite territory; real control is doubtful
The king of Alashiya writes to the pharaoh in the Amarna letters, offering copper by the hundred talents
The king of Alashiya apologises to the pharaoh for a small shipment of copper: the hand of Nergal is in his land and there is no copper worker left
A ship wrecked at Uluburun off Turkey carries ten tonnes of Cypriot copper in oxhide ingots, the largest Bronze Age metal cargo known
Ashlar buildings at Kalavasos, Alassa and Maroni store olive oil by the tens of thousands of litres and press the first Cypriot wine
Miners at Apliki in the Solea district cut the ore behind almost every oxhide ingot yet analysed, at home and abroad
Aegean settlers found Maa-Palaeokastro; Hittite kings Tudhaliya IV and Suppiluliuma II defeat Alashiya and impose tribute
Pyla-Kokkinokremos and Maa-Palaeokastro are abandoned with their gold still hidden under the floors
Locally made Mycenaean IIIC pottery, Aegean cooking pots and Aegean loomweights appear at Enkomi, Kition, Sinda and Maa
The harbours close: Hala Sultan Tekke's bay silts into a salt lake and the channel at Enkomi fills
Earthquakes and upheaval: Enkomi is abandoned, Salamis founded nearby
ERAS.region: The Hittite Empire and New Kingdom Egypt compete for the Levant. Ugarit and the Mycenaean palaces trade with Cyprus. Around 1200 BCE the Bronze Age world collapses.

life.economy: Copper made the island. Slag heaps at smelting camps such as Politiko-Phorades and the flat oxhide ingots stacked in the towns belong to an industry far beyond local need: the king of Alashiya tells the pharaoh in Amarna letter EA 35 that he is sending five hundred talents, and the ship wrecked at Uluburun about 1320 BCE carried some ten tonnes of Cypriot copper. In return came Mycenaean fine pottery in quantity from the fourteenth century, Canaanite jars of oil and wine, gold, ivory, glass and faience, while Cyprus sent out copper, timber, its own painted wares and, on the usual reading of the poppy-shaped Base Ring juglets, opium.
life.language: For the first time something was written on Cyprus, in Cypro-Minoan, a syllabary of roughly a hundred signs descended from Cretan Linear A and in use from about the sixteenth century BCE. It is undeciphered: the corpus is small and mostly very short, and even the number of distinct scripts it represents is argued over, so the language behind it is unknown, though a non-Greek local tongue possibly ancestral to Eteocypriot is the usual assumption. Greek arrives only at the very end, with Aegean settlers after about 1200 BCE, and the language in which Alashiya wrote to Egypt, Ugarit and the Hittites was Akkadian, the diplomatic lingua franca of the age.
life.religion: Urban sanctuaries with fine ashlar masonry stand at Kition, Enkomi and Palaepaphos, several of them built alongside copper workshops, which suggests that metallurgy and cult were bound together. Two bronzes from Enkomi carry most of the argument: the so-called Ingot God, a helmeted armed figure standing on an oxhide ingot, and the Horned God, a youth in a horned cap, both known by those modern names because no inscription tells us who they are. The great goddess of Palaepaphos, later identified with Aphrodite, was worshipped there from about 1200 BCE and is addressed in later Cypriot inscriptions simply as Wanassa, the Lady; her cult shows heavy Near Eastern influence from Ishtar and Astarte.
life.people: The island urbanised. Hala Sultan Tekke covered perhaps twenty-five to fifty hectares, which would make it one of the largest Bronze Age towns in the Mediterranean, and Enkomi was walled in cyclopean masonry and crowded with workshops, though firm population figures for either are simply not available. Society was plainly stratified, with ashlar residences, elite chamber tombs full of gold, glass and ivory, and craftsmen working in dedicated workshops rather than at home, and movement was constant: Levantines and Aegeans lived in the ports, and after 1200 BCE Aegean settlers arrived in numbers at Maa-Palaeokastro and elsewhere, changing pottery, dress and cooking habits as they came.

pop.n: No island-wide figure, though the towns were far larger than anything before them: Enkomi and Hala Sultan Tekke each ran to tens of hectares.

ERAS.name: Iron Age
events: Amathus is founded by indigenous 'Eteocypriots', who keep their own non-Greek language into the fourth century BCE
New towns at Salamis and Lapithos; the older centres of Palaepaphos and Kourion grow into kingdoms
A cremation at Kourion-Kaloriziki is buried with a gold sceptre headed by two falcons in cloisonné enamel, the earliest hint of a Cypriot ruling house
Greek is spoken and written in the Cypriot syllabary: the Opheltas spit from Palaepaphos is the island's earliest Greek text
The Skales cemetery at Palaepaphos fills with bronze roasting spits, bimetallic knives and Aegean-style pottery
Cypriot bronze rod tripods and stands turn up in Crete and the Aegean, carried west by Cypriot smiths
Phoenicians from Tyre settle at Kition and build a temple to Astarte
Cypriot copper and worked bronze go east again as Tyre and Sidon rebuild their trade
A Phoenician named Moula scratches a dedication to Lady Astarte on a bowl at Kition, the oldest Phoenician writing on the island
Chytroi, Ledra, Tamassos and Idalion emerge inland, each sitting on a route from the copper to the sea
Homer's Iliad remembers Kinyras, a king of Cyprus who sent Agamemnon a breastplate; the first royal tombs at Salamis follow in the late eighth century
ERAS.region: The Greek Dark Ages give way to Homer's world. Phoenician cities expand across the Mediterranean. The Neo-Assyrian Empire begins its rise.

life.economy: Copper mining went on but at reduced scale, and the metal of the moment was iron, worked early on Cyprus and probably passed on from here to the Aegean; iron spits, knives and weapons become normal tomb furniture. Cypriot White Painted and Bichrome pottery was exported eastward from the tenth century onwards and turns up at Tel Dor, in the Amuq valley and in Cilicia, shipped mainly from Salamis and Kition. The Phoenician settlement at Kition, planted from Tyre around 850 BCE, tied the island into the Levantine network that would soon carry Cypriot goods much further west.
life.language: This is the age when the island's languages become visible. Greek is written for the first time in the Cypriot syllabary, a descendant of Cypro-Minoan, on the bronze spit from Palaepaphos inscribed with the name Opheltas in the genitive, dated to about the eleventh century BCE; the dialect is Arcado-Cypriot, closest of all Greek dialects to that of inland Arcadia. Beside it stood Eteocypriot, a non-Indo-European language written in the same syllabary and still undeciphered, spoken at Amathus and probably elsewhere, and Phoenician arrived with the settlers at Kition, where a dedication to the Lady Astarte scratched on a bowl about 800 BCE is the oldest Phoenician writing on Cyprus.
life.religion: Sanctuaries become archaeologically loud. The temple at Kition-Kathari was rebuilt on its Late Bronze Age footings, and an inscribed Red Slip bowl of about 850 to 800 BCE names Astarte as its goddess, which makes her the first securely attested divine name on the island; worship of the Paphian goddess continued unbroken at Palaepaphos, and open-air enclosures such as Ayia Irini began to accumulate crowds of terracotta worshippers around a central altar. At the end of the period the built chamber tombs of Salamis take a strikingly Homeric form, with broad ramps, sacrificed pairs of yoked horses still wearing their bits and blinkers, and amphorae of oil, though whether this was conscious imitation of epic or simply a shared aristocratic fashion is debated.
life.people: New towns were founded at Salamis and Lapithos while Palaepaphos, Kourion and Amathus grew from older roots, and Amathus was settled around 1100 BCE by people who kept their non-Greek language for the next seven centuries. Population seems to have risen through the period, and authority lay with basileis, kings whose right to rule at Paphos rested on their priesthood of the goddess. Not one of them is known: no Cypriot king is attested by name before 673 BCE, and the Kinyras whom the Iliad makes king of Cyprus is legend.

pop.n: No figures survive from the age when the city-kingdoms formed.

ERAS.name: Archaic
events: Seven kings of Cyprus submit to Sargon II of Assyria (709–707); his stele is set up at Kition
A Phoenician silver bowl engraved with a city under siege is buried in a rich tomb at Amathus
Esarhaddon of Assyria lists ten kings of Iadnana (Cyprus) who sent materials for his palace at Nineveh, the first roll-call of the Cypriot kingdoms
Country shrines at Achna, Arsos, Golgoi and Ayia Irini fill with limestone and terracotta worshippers, paid for by villagers rather than kings
Cypriot painters invent the Free Field style: a single bird, fish or bull drawn on an open ground
Cypriot limestone sculpture and terracottas reach their height
Amasis of Egypt makes Cyprus tributary; Evelthon of Salamis strikes the first Cypriot coins
A rural sanctuary at Meniko, inland from Kition, is built for the Phoenician god Baal Hamman
Cyprus passes to the Persian Empire of Cyrus the Great (certainly Persian by 525)
Cypriot ships join Cambyses's fleet against Egypt, Herodotus says 'of their own accord'
Onesilos of Salamis leads the island's revolt against Persia and is killed; Soli holds out for five months
Paphos falls to a Persian siege ramp and Kourion changes sides in mid-battle; the Amathusians hang Onesilos's head above their gate, and when bees nest in it an oracle tells them to worship him
ERAS.region: Assyria conquers and then falls to Babylon. Saite Egypt revives. The Achaemenid Persian Empire stretches from India to the Aegean. Greek cities colonise the Mediterranean.

life.economy: Copper from Tamassos and the Troodos foothills, timber from the same slopes, and wine, olive oil and grain were the island's exports, and the ten kings of Esarhaddon's list in 673 BCE sent building materials to his new palace at Nineveh. Craft output was extraordinary for so small a place: limestone votive statues, mass-produced terracottas and painted pottery, made largely for the sanctuaries and traded around the eastern Mediterranean. Coinage arrives late, when Evelthon of Salamis struck the first Cypriot silver in the middle of the sixth century, and tribute was the recurring cost of trade, to Egypt under Amasis from about 560 BCE and to Persia from about 545.
life.language: Greek written in the Cypriot syllabary is the language of most inscriptions, in the Arcado-Cypriot dialect; the Greek alphabet, standard everywhere else in the Greek world by now, made almost no headway here, which is one of the odder facts of the island's history. Phoenician was the language of Kition and increasingly of Idalion and Tamassos, written in the Phoenician alphabet, while Eteocypriot continued at Amathus. Assyrian scribes called the island Iadnana, and because the earliest Cypriot royal names reach us only in Akkadian spellings, several of the identifications on Esarhaddon's prism remain contested.
life.religion: The island filled with sanctuaries, urban and rural, and Cypriot worship is best seen through the thousands of terracotta and limestone figures left standing in them; the open-air temenos at Ayia Irini held something like two thousand terracotta figures ranged around its altar when the Swedish expedition uncovered it in 1929. The great goddess of Paphos is called only Wanassa or simply the goddess in Cypriot inscriptions, and the male god of Kourion later known as Apollo Hylates, together with the lion-slaying figure conventionally labelled Cypriot Herakles or Herakles-Melqart, are named by modern convention rather than by any Archaic dedication. Phoenician Kition, by contrast, names Astarte, Melqart and Reshef outright, and the temple accounts from its Astarte sanctuary are among the fullest Phoenician economic documents anywhere.
life.people: Population rose markedly, and about ten kingdoms held between them a landscape of dispersed farmsteads, mining villages and rural sanctuaries that served as markers of territory. Society was aristocratic under a basileus, with chariot-owning elites whose tombs at Salamis and Tamassos were furnished on a princely scale, above a countryside of peasant cultivators about whom the evidence is mostly indirect. Greeks, Phoenicians and Eteocypriots lived alongside each other, sometimes in the same town, and there is no sign that the island's communities were sealed off from one another.

pop.n: No figures survive. Assyrian and Egyptian records count kings and tribute, not people.

ERAS.name: Classical
events: Cypriot ships, 150 of them, fight for Persia at Salamis in Greece
Pausanias of Sparta leads the Hellenic League fleet to Cyprus and drives out Persian garrisons, but the Greeks sail on without holding the island
Idalion contracts with a physician on a bronze tablet while Persians and Kitians besiege it, the earliest written agreement from Cyprus
Idalion falls to the Phoenician kings of Kition, who govern it from a palace archive of inked potsherds
The Athenian general Kimon dies besieging Kition
Evagoras I takes Salamis and makes it a beacon of Greek culture
Milkyaton takes Kition and dedicates a trophy to Baal Oz for a victory won in his first year
The King's Peace formally assigns Cyprus, with the Greek cities of Asia, to the Persian king
Evagoras loses a sea battle off Kition and is shut up inside Salamis
After a ten-year war Evagoras makes peace with Persia; he pays tribute but keeps his throne 'as a king to a king'
Evagoras I is murdered; his son Nikokles reforms the coinage and drops the old syllabary from it
Nine Cypriot kings join the Phoenician revolt against Artaxerxes III; it is put down by 344
Pasikypros of Tamassos sells his kingdom and his crown to Pumayyaton of Kition for fifty talents and retires to Amathus
After Issus the Cypriot kings send 120 ships to Alexander's siege of Tyre
ERAS.region: The Persian Wars and the Athenian Empire. Athens and Sparta fight the Peloponnesian War. Philip II and Alexander of Macedon conquer Persia.

life.economy: The kingdoms fought over copper: Kition seized Idalion in the middle of the fifth century and later bought Tamassos outright, gaining direct control of the mines, and the Phoenician administration at Idalion left more than a thousand inscribed pottery fragments, almost all of them economic records. Timber was the other strategic commodity, going into the fleets the kings supplied first to Persia and then to Alexander, a hundred and fifty ships at Salamis in 480 BCE and a hundred and twenty at the siege of Tyre in 332, and wine, oil and grain went out beside it. Each kingdom struck its own coin, in silver on a Persian standard and, from the reign of Melekiathon of Kition, in gold and bronze as well.
life.language: Greek in the Cypriot syllabary remained the standard written language, and the longest surviving syllabic text, the bronze Idalion Tablet of the mid fifth century, records King Stasikypros and the city paying a family of physicians in silver and land for treating the wounded during a siege. Phoenician was the administrative language of Kition and its dependencies, and bilingual inscriptions in Phoenician and syllabic Greek become common. Eteocypriot survived at Amathus into the fourth century, where the bilingual inscription published in 1914 gives what appears to be the same dedication in Greek and in the native tongue; the language is still undeciphered, and the Greek half is all that allows even a partial reading of the other.
life.religion: The old cults continued and grew more Greek in appearance: the Paphian goddess is still Wanassa in inscriptions until the name Aphrodite appears for the first time late in the fourth century, and the kings of Paphos ruled by virtue of her priesthood. Kition's Astarte and Melqart, the Apollo-Reshef of Idalion, and Zeus Ammon in his Cypriot guise show a habit of blending rather than replacing, and Cypriot votive sculpture of the period adopts Greek poses and drapery while keeping local dress and local gods. Rock-cut chamber tombs remained the norm, and the ostentatious built tombs of the Salamis kings had already been abandoned before the period began.
life.people: Salamis was the largest city by far, holding on one estimate thirty-five to thirty-seven thousand people in the time of Evagoras I, and the island supported nine or ten kingdoms of very unequal size around it. The courts Hellenised fast, with Athenian orators addressing Cypriot kings and Greek craftsmen and physicians working on the island, while the population as a whole stayed mixed, Greek-speaking in most places, Phoenician at Kition, Eteocypriot at Amathus. Political violence was frequent, with revolts in 498, in the 390s and again in the 350s, and the kings' habit of changing sides means the same families appear as Persian loyalists and Greek champions within a single generation.

pop.n: No figures survive. Herodotus counts Cypriot ships, not Cypriots.

reading.n: An Athenian orator's encomium for the king of Salamis who Hellenised his city and defied Persia.

ERAS.name: Hellenistic
events: Four Cypriot kings (Salamis, Soli, Paphos, Amathus) side with Ptolemy I against the regent Perdiccas
Ptolemy deposes the pro-Antigonid kings of Kition, Marion, Lapithos and Kyrenia and makes Nikokreon of Salamis governor of the island
Nikokreon dies; Ptolemy's brother Menelaos takes over as governor and the last city-kingdoms disappear
Demetrius Poliorcetes wins the naval battle of Salamis; the Antigonids hold Cyprus
Demetrius lands at Karpasia and takes it and Ourania before marching on Salamis
Zeno of Kition begins teaching in the Painted Colonnade in Athens and founds Stoic philosophy
Ptolemaic rule restored for good
Ptolemy II plants cities named Arsinoe, among them the ancestor of Famagusta and the refounded Marion
Onesagoras the barber begins dedicating inscribed jars to the Nymph at Kafizin, the last dated use of the Cypriot syllabary
Pelops son of Pelops, the first strategos securely attested by inscriptions, governs from Salamis
Nea Paphos becomes the seat of the Ptolemaic governor
Antiochus IV of Syria seizes Cyprus and invades Egypt; a Roman ultimatum at Eleusis forces him to give both back
Ptolemy, brother of Ptolemy XII, becomes king of Cyprus as a separate Ptolemaic kingdom
Building begins on Yeronisos island off Cape Drepanon, a sanctuary of Apollo and a lookout in the last Ptolemaic years
ERAS.region: Alexander's successors carve up his empire. Seleucids and Ptolemies fight six Syrian Wars. Rome defeats Carthage and enters the Greek East.

life.economy: The Ptolemies worked the island as a royal estate, and the proceeds of its copper, timber and wine went to the treasury at Alexandria. Its forests kept the fleet in hulls, Cyprus being the main base of the Ptolemaic navy outside Egypt for close to two centuries, with the chief yard at Nea Paphos. Mints at Paphos and Salamis struck large quantities of Ptolemaic silver and bronze between about 200 and 80 BCE, the island being better supplied with silver than Egypt itself, and Athens and Alexandria were the steady partners in trade.
life.language: Koine Greek became the language of government, and the Greek alphabet finally displaced the Cypriot syllabary that had carried the island's Greek for some six centuries. The last securely dated syllabic inscriptions come from the rural shrine at Kafizin and belong to about 225 to 218 BCE, though some scholars would keep the script alive later still; the three hundred or so inscribed vessels dedicated there by a man named Onasagoras are mostly alphabetic, with a handful still syllabic or written in both scripts at once. Phoenician, the language of Kition's kings, went out with the dynasty Ptolemy I destroyed in 312 BCE, and the island's last Phoenician inscriptions are third century.
life.religion: Aphrodite's sanctuary at Palaipaphos remained the greatest shrine on the island, its cult image not a statue but a tall conical black stone, and its chief priests were the Cinyradae. The Ptolemies added themselves to the pantheon: about thirty Cypriot inscriptions honour Arsinoe Philadelphus, many of them plain sandstone altars set up privately at Soloi, Chytroi, Idalion, Kourion and Salamis, and a text from Idalion dated 254 BCE names her eponymous priestess. By the late third century the strategos who governed Cyprus was also archiereus, high priest of the whole island, with its sanctuaries and their revenues in his hands.
life.people: Ptolemy I put an end to the city kingdoms: Pumayyaton of Kition was executed in 312 BCE, Stasioikos of Marion was arrested and his city destroyed with its people moved to Nea Paphos, and Nikokreon of Salamis was forced to take his own life in 311 or 310 BCE, the sources differing. Garrisons sat in every town under a single governor who was general and high priest together, residing first at Salamis and later at Nea Paphos, founded about 312 BCE and the first place to serve as capital of the entire island. No usable population figure survives for the period, and any number offered for Hellenistic Cyprus is a guess.

pop.n: No figures survive from Ptolemaic rule, for all its careful accounting of grain, copper and timber.

reading.t: A History of Cyprus, Volume I: To the Conquest by Richard Lion Heart
reading.n: The Ptolemaic governors, the naval battle of Salamis in 306 and the end of the kingdoms.

reading.t: Library of History, Book 20
reading.n: Demetrius Poliorcetes takes Cyprus in 306 BCE: the siege of Salamis and the great sea battle.

reading.t: Cyprus: From the Stone Age to the Romans
reading.n: Ptolemaic Cyprus in a single chapter, for orientation.

reading.t: The Inscriptions of Kourion
reading.n: The inscriptions of one city, Hellenistic and Roman, and what they reveal of civic life.

ERAS.name: Roman
events: Cato the Younger annexes Cyprus for Rome
Caesar hands Cyprus back to Cleopatra's family; it returns to Rome after Actium in 30 BCE
Cyprus becomes a senatorial province under a proconsul
An earthquake levels Nea Paphos; Augustus pays for the rebuilding and the city takes the title Augusta
Paul and Barnabas preach at Salamis and Paphos
Sergius Paulus, the proconsul who heard Paul at Paphos, is next recorded at Rome as a curator of the Tiber's banks
An earthquake and its wave wreck Salamis and Paphos; Trajan and Hadrian pay for the new gymnasium and baths at Salamis
Milestones record the coastal and mountain roads laid out under Augustus and Titus
The koinon of the Cypriot cities strikes its own bronze coinage and takes charge of the imperial cult
The Jewish revolt of 115–117 devastates Salamis and is crushed; Jews are banned from the island
Caracalla's builders convert the Kourion theatre for wild beast shows
Cypriot bishops, Spyridon of Trimithous among them, attend the Council of Nicaea; legend has St Helena founding Stavrovouni in 327
An earthquake brings down the warehouses at Dreamer's Bay on Akrotiri, five years before the shock that ends Kourion
ERAS.region: The Roman Republic becomes an empire under Augustus. Christianity spreads through the eastern provinces. Crisis and recovery in the third century.

life.economy: Copper was the island's name and its business: Roman aes cyprium, Cyprian metal, gave Latin cuprum and eventually the English word, and the hundred or so ancient slag heaps in the Troodos hold an estimated four million tonnes of waste, the by-product of perhaps 200,000 tonnes of metal smelted over some three thousand years on the geologist George Constantinou's reckoning. Radiocarbon dating puts the great red heap at Skouriotissa at between 73 and 26 BCE, and output there rose to a genuinely industrial scale in late antiquity. In 13 or 12 BCE Augustus gave Herod the Great half the revenue of the Cypriot mines and the management of the other half, a grant known only from Josephus; wine, olive oil, grain, timber, glass and shipbuilding filled out the trade, and provincial coin was struck at Paphos and Salamis.
life.language: Greek was the language of daily life and of nearly all writing, and the whole Roman period has left no more than about eighty Latin inscriptions on the island, a fair measure of how little Latin travelled beyond the governor's offices. The coinage tracks the shift neatly, issues under Augustus and Tiberius being in Latin, Claudian ones bilingual and everything after that in Greek. Paphos and the west kept an imperial calendar devised for Augustus, while Salamis went on using the Egyptian calendar it had inherited from the Ptolemies.
life.religion: Three shrines held the right of asylum and Tacitus names them: Aphrodite at Paphos, Aphrodite at Amathus, and Zeus at Salamis, the first and last of which appear on the island's coins. Emperors were worshipped alongside the old gods rather than in temples of their own, and how much authority the koinon of Cyprus actually exercised over the island's religion is disputed among scholars. Christianity came early, Paul and Barnabas landing at Salamis about 45 CE and converting the proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos, though it spread slowly in the countryside; the Jewish revolt of 115 to 117 CE under Artemion wrecked Salamis and ended with the Jews expelled, Cassius Dio's figure of 240,000 dead being rhetoric rather than a count.
life.people: Cyprus became a senatorial province under a proconsul in 22 BCE with Nea Paphos as its capital, garrisoned so lightly that there is no evidence of anything beyond the governor's bodyguard. No reliable population figure exists for the province, though the theatre at Salamis seated some 15,000 and the city's necropolis sprawled across several square kilometres. Earthquakes shaped the age: the shock of 76 CE brought down three cities, which the ancient sources decline to name, and those of about 332 and 342 CE left Salamis and Paphos in ruins, after which Constantius II remitted four years of taxes and rebuilt Salamis on a smaller scale as Constantia.

pop.n: No census survives. Dio Cassius put the dead of the Jewish revolt of 115-117 at 240,000, a figure modern historians treat as far too high.

ERAS.name: Byzantine
events: Bishops of Paphos, Salamis and Trimithous attend the Council of Nicaea, the first Cypriots on record at an ecumenical council
By tradition Helena is driven ashore on her way home from Jerusalem and leaves a fragment of the True Cross on the peak later called Stavrovouni
Earthquakes (332 and 342) wreck Salamis; Constantius II refounds it as Constantia, the new capital
Earthquakes between 365 and 370 flatten Kourion; it is rebuilt as a Christian town
The Church of Cyprus is declared independent at the Council of Ephesus
Zeno grants the archbishop of Cyprus an imperial sceptre, a purple mantle and the right to sign in cinnabar red, the three privileges still used
Archbishop Anthemios finds the tomb of St Barnabas near Salamis (c. 478–488); Emperor Zeno confirms the Church's independence
The apse at Kiti is set with a gold-ground mosaic of the Virgin between two archangels, and Kanakaria in the Karpas gets another
Arab fleet under Muawiya sacks Salamis-Constantia
A second Arab fleet takes Constantia and storms Lapithos with mangonels; a garrison from Baalbek is left on the island
Treaty between Justinian II and Abd al-Malik makes Cyprus a shared, demilitarised island taxed by both empires
Justinian II moves much of the population to Nea Justinianoupolis near Cyzicus; they return in 698
The Quinisext Council in Constantinople confirms the exiled archbishop's rank and the title Nea Justinianoupolis that the Church of Cyprus still carries
Cyprus, half outside the empire, is barely touched by Iconoclasm; the plain painted crosses at Geroskipou are a rare local trace
Raiders sack Karpasia; its people abandon the port and move inland to Rizokarpaso
Cypriots are carried off from Chytroi, and Bishop Demetrianos follows them to the caliph's court to argue them free
Niketas Chalkoutzes recovers the island for Byzantium; Cyprus becomes a theme
The governor Theophilos Erotikos revolts, is beaten and is paraded through the Hippodrome in women's clothes
Rhapsomates revolts; Alexios I sends John Doukas and Manuel Boutoumites, and Eumathios Philokales stays on as governor
The chapel of the Holy Trinity at Koutsovendis is painted for the governor Eumathios Philokales, the earliest dated wall painting on the island
The painted church of Asinou opens a golden age of Cypriot wall painting
Raynald of Chatillon and Thoros II of Armenia plunder Cyprus for three weeks, sparing neither churches nor convents
Theodore Apseudis, trained in Constantinople, paints the cave hermitage of Neophytos above Paphos
Isaac Komnenos seizes Cyprus and rules as a self-styled emperor
Richard I lands at Limassol in May, defeats Isaac and takes the island within a month
Isaac surrenders at Cape St Andreas and is jailed by the Hospitallers at Margat in chains said to be silver, because Richard had promised him no irons
ERAS.region: Constantine founds Constantinople. Justinian, the Arab conquests, Iconoclasm and the Macedonian revival. The Seljuk Turks and the First Crusade arrive in the Levant.

life.economy: Justinian's law of 536 detached Cyprus from the eastern prefecture and attached it to the quaestura exercitus, so that its grain, olive oil and wine went by sea to provision the Danube army, and the island's economy grew steadily more tied to Constantinople. Copper mining reached its peak here rather than its end: the exposed slag at Skouriotissa formed between about 320 and 520 CE, and Vasiliki Kassianidou has shown extraction surviving the Arab raids and continuing into the eighth century in the north west. Cypriot cooking pots from Dhiorios, made in something like factory conditions, were still reaching Palestine and even the Adriatic in the eighth century, which is the best evidence against the old picture of total collapse.
life.language: Greek replaced Latin in the imperial administration during the seventh century, and Cyprus followed the empire. Modern Cypriot Greek descends not from the ancient Arcadocypriot of the syllabary but from Byzantine medieval Greek, and its divergence is usually put down to the island being cut off from the rest of the Greek world between the seventh and tenth centuries; no vernacular Cypriot text survives from the period, so the early dialect is reconstructed rather than read. Arabic was present through the condominium and through the Maronite communities, some of whom were settled well before 1191, but no word in the dialect can be securely traced to that contact.
life.religion: The Church of Cyprus won its independence from Antioch at the Council of Ephesus in 431, and the Quinisext Council of 692 confirmed it; when Justinian II moved the Cypriots to Nea Justinianoupolis near Cyzicus in 691 the archbishop kept his rank, and after the return in 698 or 699 he kept the title of Nea Justiniana and All Cyprus that his successors bear still. Tradition holds that Archbishop Anthemios found the tomb of Barnabas about 478 and that a grateful Emperor Zeno granted the archbishops the right to sign in red ink, wear imperial purple and carry a sceptre rather than a crosier, though Joseph Huffman has argued that these regalia privileges were in truth a sixteenth century construction. The condominium made the island a refuge during iconoclasm, and the great monasteries followed: Saint John Chrysostomos at Koutsovendis about 1070, Kykkos about 1100 under Alexios I, and Machairas, granted its whole mountain and stavropegial standing by Manuel I in 1172.
life.people: No scholarly population estimate for Byzantine Cyprus can be had, and the figures in circulation should be treated as guesses. Earthquakes struck Salamis in 332 and again ten years later, the second reportedly levelling whatever the sea had not taken, and Jerome found Paphos with nothing but ruins to show what it had been; the plague of Justinian is nowhere actually attested for the island, though Sir George Hill thought it inconceivable that Cyprus escaped. The Arab raids from 649 emptied the coast, Constantia being sacked and its people drifting to Famagusta while Kourion's survivors moved inland to Episkopi, and people came the other way too, with some 3,350 Armenian and Persian prisoners deported to the island under Maurice and Armenian troops settled after the reconquest of 965, although Luca Zavagno argues the destruction has been much overdrawn.

pop.n: No figures survive from eight centuries of Byzantine rule, through the Arab raids and the shared period.

reading.n: Icons and painting on an island where Orthodox and Latin met.
