ERAS.name: Lusignan
events: Richard I takes Cyprus and marries Berengaria at Limassol
After the Templars give up the island they bought from Richard, it passes to Guy de Lusignan, the ousted King of Jerusalem
Aimery is crowned first King of Cyprus and a Latin archbishopric is founded at Nicosia with sees at Paphos, Limassol and Famagusta
The fourteen Orthodox bishoprics are cut to four and moved out of the cathedral towns; the Greek clergy are made subject to Latin bishops
Frederick II's partisans and the Ibelin regents fight the War of the Lombards around St Hilarion and Kyrenia
Thirteen Orthodox monks of Kantara are burned in Nicosia for refusing Latin rites
The Bulla Cypria places the Greek Church under the Latin archbishop
Acre falls; Famagusta booms as the last Christian port in the East
The Templars of Cyprus are tried at Nicosia after the order's suppression, and Kolossi passes to the Hospitallers
Plague reaches the island and returns repeatedly, emptying villages and pushing up the price of labour
Peter I takes Korykos and Antalya, carrying the war to the Anatolian coast
Peter I's crusade sacks Alexandria, the high point of Lusignan power; he is murdered by his own knights in 1369
Genoa seizes Famagusta after a Genoese-Venetian brawl at Peter II's coronation, and holds it until 1464
Mamluk invasion; King Janus captured at Khirokitia, Cyprus pays tribute to Cairo
A peasant rising under a leader called King Alexis is crushed after the Mamluk defeat
James II drives the Genoese out of Famagusta after ninety years
James II marries Caterina Cornaro, whom Venice has declared a daughter of the Republic
James II dies and a Catalan plot murders Caterina's uncle and her chamberlain at Famagusta; Venetian officers take over the government
Queen Caterina Cornaro cedes the kingdom to Venice
ERAS.region: The Crusader states fall to the Mamluks. Genoa and Venice fight for eastern trade. The Ottomans take Constantinople in 1453.

life.economy: Sugar was the kingdom's great industry, grown and refined at Kouklia and Akhelia on the royal estates, at Kolossi under the Knights of Saint John and at Episkopi under the Venetian Cornaro, whose refinery employed four hundred hands in 1494; no sound export tonnage survives, though Pegolotti thought Cypriot sugar the best made anywhere and much of it went to the Martini house in Venice. Salt from the lake at Larnaca was a crown monopoly which every adult on the island was obliged to buy, raising some 80,000 besants a year in the 1390s and shipped on to Syria and Venice, while the camlet cloth woven by the women of Famagusta served as the very currency in which the kingdom paid its tribute, valued in Egypt at twenty ducats the piece. The fall of Acre in 1291 made Famagusta the chief entrepot of the Levant, its customs farmed in 1395 for 37,700 white besants, but the Genoese seizure of the port in 1373 and the Mamluk victory at Khirokitia in 1426, after which Janus was ransomed for 200,000 ducats and the island owed Cairo 5,000 ducats a year, broke the kingdom's finances for good.
life.language: French was the language of the court and of the Haute Cour, and the Assizes of Jerusalem were written in it before being turned into Greek in the fifteenth century and into Italian by 1531; Latin served the church and the charters, Italian rose with the Genoese and Venetians, and Greek remained the tongue of the great majority. The Cypriot Greek dialect became a literary language in its own right, Leontios Machairas writing his Recital concerning the Sweet Land of Cyprus in it in the 1420s and Georgios Boustronios carrying the story on to 1489, while a collection of Petrarchan sonnets in Cypriot Greek, once owned by the humanist Natale Conti and now in the Marciana at Venice, is the only known Petrarchism in the Greek language. Old French had its writers here too, chief among them Philippe de Novare, whose chronicle of the war against Frederick II survives inside the Gestes des Chiprois, and Guillaume de Machaut, who wrote nine thousand verses on Peter I's sack of Alexandria without ever setting foot on the island.
life.religion: A Latin hierarchy was installed in 1196 with an archbishop at Nicosia and suffragans at Paphos, Limassol and Famagusta, and the settlements of 1220 and 1222 cut the Greek bishops to four and banished them to the villages of Solia, Arsinoe, Lefkara and Karpasia, agreements to which the Greeks were not even a party. Alexander IV's Bulla Cypria of 3 July 1260 made the Latin archbishop sole metropolitan and provided that after Germanos died the Greeks should have no archbishop at all, yet it also capped Latin visitation fees and left the Greek courts standing, which is why Chris Schabel has called it the Magna Carta of the Greeks; it governed the island until 1570. Coercion was rare but memorable, thirteen monks of the house of Kantariotissa being tried over the use of leavened bread in 1231, one dying in prison and twelve burned at Nicosia, an episode without parallel in the Latin east; the Maronites numbered perhaps seven or eight thousand in some thirty villages, the Armenians held a quarter of Nicosia still called Armenia, and the Nestorian merchants of Famagusta, the Lakhas brothers among them, built their own church there about 1360.
life.people: Gilles Grivaud, the standard authority, insists that no population count survives from the Lusignan period and that the curve cannot be drawn in absolute numbers; he works from a deliberately low figure of about 70,000 peasants for the royal accounts of 1412 and 1413, and rejects the 300,000 that circulates without evidence. Nine epidemics between 1347 and 1471 covered eighteen years in all, the Black Death of 1347 and 1348 costing between a third and two thirds of the people according to which chronicler one follows, though J. C. Russell's estimate of about twenty per cent is the sober corrective, and locusts stripped the crops for three or four years after 1409 until Janus ordered the eggs dug out and buried in 1413. Below a Frankish nobility that amounted to only a thousand or twelve hundred people in the thirteenth century sat the paroikoi, who owed two or three days' labour a week and a third of their crops and could be sold or flogged at their lord's will, then the perperiarii and the freed francomati; after Khirokitia the countryside rose in 1426 and a peasant styling himself King Alexis held Lefkoniko until he was hanged on 12 May 1427.

pop.v: Unknown for almost all of it
pop.n: No count survives until the very end of the period. The plague of 1348 and its returns are thought to have carried off a large share of the island.

ERAS.name: Venetian
events: Venice takes formal possession of the island
In Venice's first year Turkish raiders carry off villagers from the Karpas
The citadel of Famagusta is remodelled for artillery under Captain Nicolo Foscarini; the Sea Gate follows in 1496
With the Ottoman conquest of Egypt, the island's annual tribute is redirected from Cairo to Istanbul
An Ottoman fleet raids and burns Limassol
Sanmicheli begins modernising Famagusta's walls; the Martinengo bastion is finished by 1562
A conspiracy against Venetian rule led by Iakovos Diassorinos is uncovered; he is executed in Nicosia
Nicosia's new walls by Giulio Savorgnan, with eleven bastions
The Pedieos is turned into the new moat and the royal palace and scores of churches are pulled down for Savorgnan's walls
Ottoman landing near Limassol in July; Nicosia stormed on 9 September
Nicosia is stormed on 9 September and the luogotenente Nicolo Dandolo is killed; Kyrenia surrenders days later without a fight
Famagusta surrenders on 1 August after ten and a half months; Bragadin is flayed despite the terms
Bragadin is flayed on 17 August; his skin is stolen back from the Ottoman arsenal in 1580 and buried in Venice
Ten weeks after Famagusta falls, the Holy League destroys the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto, too late for Cyprus
Venice makes peace and formally cedes the island
ERAS.region: Ottoman power at its height under Suleiman and Selim II. The Reformation divides Europe. The battle of Lepanto is fought weeks after Famagusta falls.

life.economy: Cotton became the boom crop, known as the plant of gold, and by about 1600 it had driven out sugar, whose Cypriot plantations were already failing against Madeira, a competitor the Venetian diarist Marino Sanudo named as early as 1496. Salt from Larnaca was a state monopoly so strict that Venetian ships calling at the island had to dump their ballast and load salt for Venice, and John Locke reported in 1553 that a Venetian caught carrying an ounce out of the city lost an ear; estimates of what the Signory made from it range from 100,000 to 800,000 ducats a year, and Hill thought 300,000 near the truth. Grain was the largest crop of all, its export licensed only after eighteen months' supply had been set aside, and the Proveditor Bernardo Sagredo reckoned the island's whole revenue in 1585 at 546,000 ducats, of which 300,000 came from salt, leaving 361,669 net of the garrison's pay; fortification swallowed much of the rest, 178,092 ducats going on Famagusta between 1491 and 1528 and the Martinengo bastion alone costing 50,000.
life.language: Italian, and specifically the Venetian dialect, became the written language of government, and by 1531 the Assizes had been rendered into it; a French visitor named Mesenge complained in 1507 that pleadings once made in French were now made in Italian, and that Cypriot gentlemen, as good Frenchmen as any in France, were wonderfully ill content to be subjects of Venice. Greek remained the language of the countryside and of the church. The chronicles of the transition make the point neatly, Georgios Boustronios writing his account of 1456 to 1489 in Cypriot Greek prose while his relative Florio Bustron, an administrator under Venice, wrote his Historia overo commentarii de Cipro in Italian, and the 156 Petrarchan poems in Cypriot Greek preserved in the Marciana were probably assembled between 1546 and 1570.
life.religion: The Latin church stayed on top and the Greek church stayed subordinate, with four bishops each answering to the Latin diocesan above him and the Greek archbishopric still vacant under the terms of the Bulla Cypria. Nicholas Coureas argues that in practice the Greek church grew stronger rather than weaker, because the Latins were few and town bound, Rome was distant and the Ottoman threat made enforcement of papal directives unwise; the four Greek bishops drew 1,400 ducats between them about 1500, while eighteen Greek monasteries were reported in 1529 with 6,600. The Maronites lost people back to the Levant under heavy taxation, and the Armenians dwindled too, though they had held their Nicosia quarter and the church of Notre Dame de Tyre since before 1504 and kept shops in Famagusta, Limassol, Paphos and the capital.
life.people: Venetian reports put the island's population somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 and disagree wildly among themselves: 106,000 from the Cypriot deputation of 1490, 90,000 from the Syndic of 1504 against his Lieutenant's 130,000, 121,179 in the census of 1523, 126,179 from Minio in 1529, 197,000 from Attar about 1540 and 200,000 from Graziani about 1570, on which evidence Hill concluded the population probably rose rather than fell. Serfdom was the ordinary condition: Martin von Baumgarten wrote in 1508 that all the inhabitants were slaves to the Venetians, paying a third of everything and working two days a week for the state, and Hill computes the paroikoi's burden at about forty per cent of produce, a third plus the tithe; every villein, male or married female over fifteen, also paid a besant a head for salt, and in 1490 the Cypriots said many had fled the island rather than bear it. Nicosia held perhaps 21,000 people before the siege of 1570 and roughly that number died in it, the Ottoman survey of 1572 finding between 1,100 and 1,200 left; Famagusta held out from September 1570 to 5 August 1571, and contemporaries put the total Venetian and Cypriot loss at 56,000 killed or enslaved.

pop.n: The first real numbers. A Cypriot deputation told Venice in 1490 that the island held some 106,000 souls; a Venetian survey later counted 147,701, and 197,000 was claimed for the eve of the Ottoman conquest.

reading.t: Cyprus, the Franks and Venice, 13th-16th Centuries
reading.n: The essential scholar of Venetian Cyprus on its administration, taxes and population.

reading.t: Villages désertés à Chypre (fin XIIe-fin XIXe siècle)
reading.n: The abandoned villages of Cyprus over seven centuries, and what they say about population and rural life.

reading.t: Description de toute l'isle de Cypre
reading.n: A Cypriot Dominican's account of his island written in exile just after its fall.

reading.t: The True Report of All the Success of Famagosta
reading.n: An eyewitness on the eleven-month siege of Famagusta, translated into English within the year.

reading.t: A History of Cyprus, Volume III: The Frankish Period, 1432-1571
reading.n: The fullest narrative of Venetian rule and the war of 1570-71.

reading.t: Othello
reading.n: Four of its five acts are set in a Venetian garrison port on Cyprus with the Turkish fleet expected: the island's most famous fiction.

ERAS.name: Ottoman
events: Cyprus becomes an Ottoman province; the Latin church is suppressed and the Orthodox archbishopric restored in 1572
The Latin cathedrals of Nicosia and Famagusta become the Selimiye and Lala Mustafa Pasha mosques; the first Friday prayer in Nicosia is held on 15 September 1570
Anatolian families are ordered to settle the island; Timotheos is installed as the first Orthodox archbishop since 1260
A ruined church beside Selimiye is granted to the Haramayn foundation as the Bedesten, the covered cloth market
A Tuscan squadron raids Famagusta, the last western attempt on the island
The fort at Larnaca is rebuilt; Larnaca becomes the port of trade and the seat of the European consuls
The Archbishop comes to be recognised as spokesman of the Greek community, with direct access to the Porte (1660s)
Cyprus is downgraded to a sanjak under the Kapudan Pasha, admiral of the fleet
Boyacioglu Mehmed Agha leads a revolt of local aghas that holds the island for about two years
Cyprus is granted as an arpalik to the Grand Vizier and run by a muhassil who farms its taxes
Ebubekir Pasha begins the aqueduct that will carry water about ten kilometres to Larnaca; it serves the town until 1939
The Archbishop becomes the tax intermediary for the Christians
Greeks and Turks together storm the governor's palace and kill the extortionate governor Çil Osman after a tax revolt
The dragoman Hadjigeorgakis Kornesios builds his Nicosia mansion; the dragomans are the richest men on the island
Muslim townsmen and peasants riot in Nicosia against the tax power of the archbishop and the dragoman
Hadjigeorgakis Kornesios is executed at Constantinople and his property seized
Archbishop Kyprianos founds the Hellenic School of Nicosia, later the Pancyprian Gymnasium
Archbishop Kyprianos and leading Greeks executed in Nicosia on 9 July
The three bishops are beheaded and Archbishop Kyprianos hanged in Nicosia on 9 July; executions and confiscations follow for months, and Kykkos loses its abbot and its lands
The Tanzimat reforms make Cyprus a sanjak under a mutasarrif; the Ottoman land code of 1858 follows
Ottoman reform permits Christians to build bell towers; the belfry of Ayios Lazaros rises at Larnaca
The Cyprus Convention hands administration to Britain
The Cyprus Convention is signed on 4 June; the British flag is raised at Nicosia on 12 July by Lord John Hay and Wolseley lands at Larnaca on 22 July
ERAS.region: Ottoman decline and reform. The Greek War of Independence. The Eastern Question and the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 redraw the Balkans.

life.economy: The Porte farmed the island out, first through timars granted to Lala Mustafa's soldiers and later through annual iltizam and lifetime malikane leases, and the cizye or poll tax on non-Muslims was set in 1572 at eleven, five and a half or three piastres according to means. The imperial rescript of 1754 fixed the island's liability at 10,066 warrants of assessment at twenty-one and a half piastres each, some 216,400 piastres a year, and required that number to be issued whether the population rose or fell; by the 1760s barely 7,500 people were left to pay it, which explains eighteenth century Cyprus better than anything else does. Cotton was the chief export, about 3,000 quintals or 750 tons a year around 1750 going to Britain, France, Holland and Venice, with the French houses at Larnaca acting as factors for merchants of Marseille; Mahmud II fixed the annual tribute at 3,179,082 piastres in 1837, and a British consular return of the 1870s puts total regular revenue at 16,836,874 piastres, of which the salt monopoly alone yielded 2,929,550.
life.language: Ottoman Turkish was the language of administration and of the kadi courts, which non-Muslims and foreigners could also use, while Greek remained the language of the great majority and of the church that collected their taxes. Cypriot Turkish grew out of Ottoman Turkish and the Yoruk dialect of the Taurus, brought by settlers moved from the Karaman region under the settlement law of 22 September 1572, and Sir Harry Luke thought the community had preserved the purity of its Turkish to a degree matched almost nowhere else; the British census of 1881 found 95 per cent of the island's Muslims giving Turkish as their mother tongue, the Greek-speaking remainder falling below two per cent by the 1920s. No literacy rate for Ottoman Cyprus appears to survive, but Archbishop Kyprianos founded the Hellenic School of Nicosia in 1812, the island's first secondary school and now the Pancyprian Gymnasium.
life.religion: The Latin church was suppressed after 1571 and the Orthodox archbishopric restored, Timotheos taking office in 1572 as the first Greek archbishop since 1260, while Saint Sophia in Nicosia and Saint Nicholas in Famagusta became mosques, taking the names Selimiye and Lala Mustafa Pasha only in 1954. Under the millet system the archbishop and his three suffragans rose from spokesmen for their flock, a role the chronicler Kyprianos dates to about 1660, to being the tax intermediaries of the settlement of 1754, so that one British traveller reported that Cyprus was in fact governed by the Greek archbishop and his clergy; that ascendancy ended on 9 July 1821, when the governor Kucuk Mehmet had Archbishop Kyprianos and the three bishops killed along with some 470 to 486 leading Greeks, the count varying by source. Latins, Venetians, Maronites and Armenians converted to Islam to escape the taxes and disabilities laid on non-Muslims and became the Linobambaki, the linen and cotton people who kept a Christian and a Muslim name apiece across seventeen to twenty villages depending on which list one follows, while at Larnaca the Hala Sultan Tekke grew around the tomb of Umm Haram, a shrine built in 1760 with its mosque completed in 1817.
life.people: The conquest emptied the island: 76 villages of the Mesaoria and Mazato were recorded with no inhabitants at all in 1572, Nicosia fell from perhaps 21,000 people to between 1,100 and 1,200, and famine followed the war. The enumerations counted taxpayers rather than people and must be read as such, an examiner about 1641 finding hardly 25,000 rayahs after the dearth of 1640 and the plague of 1641, Archimandrite Kyprianos publishing the census of 1777 as 10,487 Christian tax-paying families in 564 villages, giving 37,000 Christians and 47,000 Muslims while warning that the estimate was approximate and that doubts about the Muslim figure were grave, and the Ottoman register of 1831, which counted males only, returning 14,983 Muslim and 29,190 non-Muslim males, 44,216 in all. Plague took perhaps a third of the island in 1692 and again in 1760, drought and locusts brought a famine in 1757 and 1758 that sent a great number fleeing to Syria and Anatolia, and the tax revolt of 1764 ended with the muhassil Cil Osman and eighteen of his followers killed in the burning palace; the first British census, taken in 1881 three years after the handover, found 186,173 people, 137,631 of them Greek Orthodox and 45,458 Muslim.

pop.n: A sharp fall after 1571, then slow recovery. Travellers and Ottoman counts through the 18th and early 19th centuries suggest well under 100,000; by 1881 the island held 186,173.

reading.t: Christians and Muslims in Ottoman Cyprus and the Mediterranean World, 1571-1640
reading.n: From the Ottoman court records: how the two communities actually lived side by side in the first decades.

reading.t: Cyprus under the Turks, 1571-1878
reading.n: A colonial administrator's history of the Ottoman centuries, dated in tone but still the only general narrative.

reading.a: Michalis N. Michael, Matthias Kappler and Eftihios Gavriel (eds)
reading.t: Ottoman Cyprus: A Collection of Studies on History and Culture
reading.n: Recent scholarship on the province from Ottoman sources, correcting the old picture of neglect.

reading.t: A Provincial History of the Ottoman Empire: Cyprus and the Eastern Mediterranean in the Nineteenth Century
reading.n: The last Ottoman century on the island, reform and all.

reading.t: Excerpta Cypria: Materials for a History of Cyprus
reading.n: Every traveller's account of the island from antiquity to 1878, translated: the source for most of what we know of Ottoman Cyprus from outside.

reading.t: Travels in the Island of Cyprus
reading.n: A Tuscan who lived on the island in the 1760s describes its towns, crops and people; Cobham's translation of 1909.

reading.t: Levkosia, the Capital of Cyprus
reading.n: A drawn and written portrait of Nicosia in the last Ottoman years, just before the British arrived.

ERAS.name: British Cyprus
events: British administration begins under the Cyprus Convention; Wolseley lands at Larnaca
A summer hill station is laid out on the Troodos; the governor's cottage is begun at 1,700 metres
A Legislative Council with elected members is created; the Cyprus Museum is founded
The Cyprus Government Railway opens from Famagusta to Nicosia on 21 October; it reaches Morphou in 1907 and Evrychou in 1915
Intercommunal rioting in Limassol and Nicosia, the first serious violence between the two communities under British rule
Britain annexes Cyprus when the Ottomans join the war
Britain offers Cyprus to Greece in return for joining the war; Athens declines
The Cyprus Mines Corporation is founded and reopens the ancient copper of Skouriotissa; Mavrovouni follows in 1929
The Treaty of Lausanne confirms British sovereignty; Turkish Cypriots are given two years to opt for Turkish nationality and thousands emigrate
Cyprus becomes a Crown Colony
The Cyprus Tribute is abolished; since 1878 Cyprus had paid about £92,800 a year of its revenues towards defaulted Ottoman loans
The October riots against colonial rule; Government House is burned and the legislature abolished
Seven demonstrators are killed, more than 2,600 arrested and ten leaders exiled after the October riots
About 30,000 Cypriots serve in the Cyprus Regiment and other units during the Second World War
Britain offers a Consultative Assembly and a constitution; the Greek Cypriot leadership boycotts it and the offer lapses in 1948
Long strikes in the copper mines and a growing left-wing labour movement under the Pancyprian Federation of Labour
A church-organised plebiscite records about 96 per cent for union with Greece; Makarios III is elected archbishop
EOKA begins its armed campaign for union with Greece on 1 April
A state of emergency is declared; the Turkish Resistance Organisation is founded in answer to EOKA and presses for partition
Makarios is deported to the Seychelles in March; nine men are hanged at Nicosia Central Prison between May 1956 and March 1957
Grigoris Afxentiou is burned out of his hideout at Machairas on 3 March
Four EOKA men die in the barn at Liopetri on 2 September; the Macmillan plan is rejected by both communities
The Zurich and London agreements settle independence with power-sharing and British bases
Grivas declares a ceasefire on 9 March; the emergency has cost about 500 lives, including 156 British servicemen and police
ERAS.region: The British Empire at its height, then two World Wars and decolonisation. Greek-Turkish rivalry, the Cold War and Suez shape British thinking about the island.

life.economy: Under the Cyprus Convention Britain undertook to pay the Ottoman treasury an annual fixed sum of 92,799 pounds, eleven shillings and threepence, more than half the island's average revenue, but the money never reached Istanbul: it was deposited at the Bank of England to service the Ottoman Crimean War loan of 1855 on which the Porte had defaulted, and it was Cypriots who paid both the tribute and the cost of their own administration. Churchill, visiting as Undersecretary in 1907, wrote that Britain had no right except by force majeure to take a penny of the Cyprus Tribute to relieve itself of its own obligations, and Parliament soon voted a permanent grant-in-aid of 50,000 pounds which reduced it accordingly. Copper came back with the Cyprus Mines Corporation, founded in 1916 after Charles Gunther noticed the Roman slag at Skouriotissa, and by 1955 its mines were the island's largest industry and furnished more than a quarter of all government revenue; asbestos was worked at Amiantos in the Troodos until 1988, the Cyprus Government Railway carried 3,199,934 tons of freight between 1905 and 1951 without ever making a profit, and by the 1960s Britain was drinking 13.6 million litres of Cypriot wine a year, half the island's production and most of it sold as sweet sherry.
life.language: English was the official language of the colony and continued in legal proceedings until 1989 and in the legislature until 1963, though Greek and Turkish remained in everyday and communal use. Schooling was divided between Greek and Turkish curricula, and British attempts to curtail Greek influence in the schools were among the stated causes of the revolt of 1931. No literacy rate from the colonial censuses could be traced for this entry, but the growth of Greek secondary education is plain enough in the expansion of the Nicosia Hellenic School into a lyceum in 1893 and the founding of a teacher training college the following year.
life.religion: The Church of Cyprus kept its standing and its politics, and the archbishop remained the ethnarch: Makarios III was elected on 18 September 1950 and the church at once organised the enosis plebiscite of that January, signed in open books placed in the churches, which returned 95.7 per cent in favour, a result taken by some as coerced. Muslim religious property was administered through the Evkaf, over which the 1878 Convention gave Britain a measure of control, with an Ottoman and a British delegate on a board that also seated the mufti and the kadi of Cyprus; Britain gave up that control only in 1956. The church then led the political struggle, Makarios becoming the political head of the EOKA campaign from 1955 and being exiled to the Seychelles in 1956.
life.people: The censuses run every ten years from 1881, with none taken in 1941, and show steady growth: 186,173 in 1881, 237,022 in 1901, 347,959 in 1931, 450,114 in 1946 and 573,566 in 1960, the Greek Orthodox share rising from 73.9 per cent to about 80 by 1946 before settling at 77.1 in 1960, and the Muslim or Turkish share falling from 24.4 per cent to 18.2. Emigration ran outward throughout, with some 30,000 Turkish Cypriots leaving for Turkey between 1881 and 1927 and a Turkish Cypriot community of about 8,500 established in Britain by 1958. The October 1931 riots left seven protesters dead and 2,606 people punished, nine camps at Caraolos, Dhekelia and Xylotymbou held 53,510 Jewish detainees between August 1946 and January 1949, and the malaria campaign begun in 1946 by the Turkish Cypriot health inspector Mehmet Aziz divided the island into 556 blocks and made Cyprus the first malaria-free country in the world by February 1950.

pop.n: The first reliable series. Censuses run from 186,173 in 1881 to 573,566 in 1960.

reading.t: Bitter Lemons
reading.n: Life in Bellapais as the EOKA emergency closed in: the most read book ever written about Cyprus, and a partial one.

reading.t: Closed Doors: An Answer to Bitter Lemons by Lawrence Durrell
reading.n: A Cypriot novelist's reply, the same years seen from inside a Nicosia family; English translation 2004.

reading.t: British Imperialism in Cyprus, 1878-1915: The Inconsequential Possession
reading.n: Why Britain took Cyprus and then did so little with it.

reading.t: Britain and the Revolt in Cyprus, 1954-1959
reading.n: The definitive account of the EOKA years from the British archives.

reading.t: Labour, Society and Politics in Cyprus during the Second Half of the Nineteenth Century
reading.n: The island's working people in the transition from Ottoman to British rule.

reading.t: Historic Cyprus: A Guide to Its Towns and Villages, Monasteries and Castles
reading.n: A colonial inspector of antiquities' village-by-village guide, still consulted for monuments since lost or altered.

reading.t: Logbook III
reading.n: The Nobel laureate's Cyprus poems, written on visits in 1953-55: 'Helen', 'Salamis in Cyprus' and the rest.

ERAS.name: Republic of Cyprus
events: The Republic of Cyprus becomes independent on 16 August; Britain keeps the Akrotiri and Dhekelia bases
Britain retains 254 square kilometres as the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, about three per cent of the island
Cyprus joins the Commonwealth and, in 1961, the Non-Aligned Movement
Constitutional breakdown and intercommunal fighting; the Green Line divides Nicosia
Major-General Peter Young draws the ceasefire line across Nicosia with a green chinagraph pencil on 30 December
United Nations peacekeepers (UNFICYP) arrive
Fighting at Kokkina in August; Turkish aircraft napalm the Tillyria villages and a UN ceasefire follows on 9 August
Fighting at Kophinou and Ayios Theodoros brings Greece and Turkey close to war
Coup by the Greek junta on 15 July; Turkish invasion from 20 July divides the island
About 160,000 Greek Cypriots are displaced south and some 45,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots move north; Turkey holds 36 per cent of the island
Larnaca airport opens in February; Nicosia's stays sealed inside the UN Protected Area
Makarios dies in August; the high-level agreement of that year accepts a bizonal federation in principle
The north declares itself the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, recognised only by Turkey
Security Council resolution 550 declares any resettlement of Varosha by others than its inhabitants inadmissible
The first large desalination plant opens at Dhekelia; the island begins to drink the sea
Crossing points on the Green Line open for the first time in nearly thirty years
The Ledra Palace crossing opens on 23 April and hundreds of thousands cross in the first months
Cyprus joins the European Union; the Annan reunification plan is rejected in referendum

The Annan plan is rejected by about 76 per cent of Greek Cypriots and accepted by about 65 per cent of Turkish Cypriots on 24 April; Cyprus joins the EU on 1 May with the acquis suspended in the north
Cyprus adopts the euro
Drought forces the Republic to ship drinking water from Greece by tanker
An ammunition store explodes at the Mari naval base on 11 July, killing thirteen and wrecking the Vasilikos power station
A ten-billion-euro bailout in March closes Laiki Bank and imposes losses on deposits over 100,000 euros
Reunification talks collapse at Crans-Montana in July after the closest approach to a settlement since 2004
Part of the Varosha beachfront is opened to visitors, drawing Security Council condemnation
Of 2,002 people listed as missing from 1963 to 1974, about 1,080 have been identified and returned to their families
ERAS.region: The Cold War, Greek and Turkish politics, and European integration. Lebanon's war, the Gulf wars and the Syrian conflict make Cyprus a haven and a base in a troubled neighbourhood.

life.economy: The events of 1974 cost the Republic about seventy per cent of its wealth-producing resources, tourist facilities falling by 65 per cent and industry by 46, after which growth averaged 6.1 per cent a year through the 1980s. Services now account for close to eighty per cent of the economy and agriculture for about two, and travel and tourism generate roughly a fifth of GDP, arrivals passing four million for the first time in 2024 and earning about 3.2 billion euros, with the United Kingdom, Israel and Poland the largest markets; the shipping registry is the third largest in the European Union. The euro replaced the Cypriot pound on 1 January 2008 at 0.585274 to one, and the banking crisis of March 2013 brought a ten billion euro programme, the closure of Laiki and the conversion of 47.5 per cent of uninsured deposits at the Bank of Cyprus into shares, some 3.8 billion euros in all; halloumi was registered as a protected designation of origin in 2021 under all three of its names, and the Aphrodite gas field, announced in December 2011, is not expected to produce before 2027.
life.language: Article 3 of the 1960 constitution makes Greek and Turkish the official languages, requires legislative and administrative acts to be drawn up in both, and allows anyone to address the authorities in either. In practice Standard Modern Greek is the high variety and Cypriot Greek, which is unintelligible to an unprepared speaker of the standard, is the language people actually use, and Cypriot Turkish stands in much the same relation to standard Turkish in the north, where the standard became the language of schools and media. English remains widely spoken, by about 73 per cent of the population according to Eurobarometer, and it served in the courts until 1989; Armenian was recognised under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages on 1 December 2002 and Cypriot Maronite Arabic in 2008, though at the 2011 census none of the 3,656 Maronite Cypriots in the government-controlled area declared it as a first language.
life.religion: Makarios III held the archbishopric and the presidency at once from 1960 until his death in 1977, and when three bishops demanded that he resign the presidency in 1972 he had them defrocked the following summer and enlarged the synod to dilute them. The constitution gives special standing to five bodies, the Church of Cyprus, the Vakif, the Maronites, the Armenian Orthodox and the Latins, and provides that citizens belonging to neither main community must opt to join one of them: the Armenians, recognised as a religious group under Article 2, chose the Greek Cypriot community in a referendum on 13 November 1960. The 2011 census gave the government-controlled area as 89.1 per cent Greek Orthodox among all residents, or 97.4 per cent among Cypriot citizens alone, and the 2021 figure of 74.5 per cent looks like a collapse but chiefly reflects a rise in those declining to state a religion, from 1.1 to 17.3 per cent; the Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage has meanwhile restored or protected more than a hundred churches and mosques on both sides of the line.
life.people: The 1960 census found 573,566 people, 77.1 per cent Greek and 18.2 per cent Turkish, and in the fighting of 1963 and 1964 nearly 25,000 Turkish Cypriots, about a sixth of their community, left their homes for enclaves, Pierre Oberling's figures giving 364 Turkish Cypriot and 174 Greek Cypriot dead. In 1974 between 140,000 and 200,000 Greek Cypriots were displaced from the north, the spread reflecting the difference between people counted crossing and the refugee caseload the government supported, and 50,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots moved north from the south, largely under the Vienna III agreement of August 1975; the Committee on Missing Persons lists 2,002 people missing from 1963 to 1974, 1,510 Greek Cypriots and 492 Turkish Cypriots, of whom 1,081 had been identified by July 2026. The 2021 census counted 923,381 residents in the government-controlled area, 77.9 per cent of them Cypriot citizens, with Greeks, Romanians, Britons, Bulgarians, Syrians and Russians the largest foreign groups, so that about a fifth of the population holds another nationality; the north's last agreed census, in 2011, gave 286,257, and the number of settlers from Turkey remains genuinely contested, the researcher Mete Hatay calling the higher claims wildly speculative.

pop.n: 573,566 at independence in 1960. The 2021 census counted 923,272 in the government-controlled area; the island as a whole is now roughly 1.2 million.

reading.t: Echoes from the Dead Zone: Across the Cyprus Divide
reading.n: A Greek Cypriot anthropologist lives on both sides of the line and tests what each was taught about the other.

reading.t: The Past in Pieces: Belonging in the New Cyprus
reading.n: Lapithos after the crossings opened in 2003, and what home means to the displaced of both communities.

reading.t: Hostage to History: Cyprus from the Ottomans to Kissinger
reading.n: A polemic on the great-power politics behind 1974; partisan, and influential.

reading.t: The Cyprus Problem: What Everyone Needs to Know
reading.n: The division and the negotiations explained in plain question-and-answer form.

reading.t: Journey into Cyprus
reading.n: A six-hundred-mile walk across the whole island in 1972, two years before it was cut in two.

reading.t: The Island of Missing Trees
reading.n: A Greek Cypriot and a Turkish Cypriot fall in love in Nicosia in 1974; a fig tree tells the rest.

reading.t: The Sunrise
reading.n: Famagusta in the summer of 1974, and the emptying of Varosha.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Akrotiri-Aetokremnos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A collapsed rock shelter on a sea cliff where hunters camped around 10,000 BCE. It is the earliest evidence of people on Cyprus, and it holds nearly 300,000 bones from at least 500 pygmy hippos and a handful of dwarf elephants, the island's now-extinct native fauna.

finds.t: Remains of more than 500 dwarf hippos, burnt and broken, mixed with stone tools. Whether the hunters caused the extinction is still debated; one dating study argues the bones piled up naturally before people arrived.
Remains of at least three Cyprus dwarf elephants among the hippo bones, the last trace of the species.
About a thousand flints, small blades and thumbnail scrapers of a type found in the Levant of the same date.
Stratified fire features with burnt hippo bone, shells, bird and fish remains. Whether the fires cooked the hippos or merely burnt older bone is the crux of the extinction debate.
finds.w: Largely excavated; samples with the Department of Antiquities

finds.t: About 160 beads worked from marine shell, most of them dove shell, with dentalium and cone shell among them. They are the oldest ornaments known from Cyprus, and they are made from the sea.
finds.w: Limassol District Archaeological Museum; Department of Antiquities

finds.t: Over 73,000 fragments of marine invertebrates, roughly 21,000 individual animals: topshell, limpet, crab, cuttlefish and sea urchin. Whatever the argument about the hippos, these people unquestionably lived off the shore.
The remains of 73 individual birds, including bustards, geese and ducks, so the rock shelter was also used as a fowling station.

Eighteen bones of pig, an animal with no place in the island's native fauna. Boar were brought over from the mainland, most likely to stock the island with something worth hunting, and their descendants were still being hunted at Klimonas two thousand years later. This is the first animal introduction to Cyprus and one of the earliest anywhere.
One bone of a coastal fish. Small, but the earliest evidence of fishing from Cyprus, and the beginning of a habit that runs unbroken through the whole of the island's prehistory.

Age-structured population modelling combined with hindcast climate, published in PNAS, argues that Cyprus was permanently peopled between about 14,250 and 13,180 years ago by two or three organised movements of roughly a thousand to fourteen hundred people each, reaching four to five thousand inhabitants within three centuries. If that is right, Aetokremnos is not a first landfall but a late episode in a longer settlement, and the island was never the empty, hostile place the older accounts assumed.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Khirokitia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The best-preserved Neolithic village of the eastern Mediterranean and a UNESCO World Heritage site. Several hundred people lived in round stone-and-mudbrick houses packed inside a great wall on a hillside above the Maroni river. They buried their dead under the house floors.

finds.t: Round houses with stone footings up to ten metres across, some with internal piers for an upper floor. Five have been reconstructed at the site.
Deep bowls and trays carved from hard grey volcanic stone, some with spouts and relief decoration. There was no pottery.
Schematic human heads and figures, including a unique head in unbaked clay.
Volcanic glass imported from central Anatolia, proof of sea contact.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Two successive walls, the first 2.5 m thick and still 3 m high, with a built passage and stairs leading up into the village; the western wall marks a later expansion.
Necklaces of imported carnelian beads, dentalium shell and picrolite pendants placed with the dead, especially women and children.
Crouched burials beneath house floors, often with a grinding stone laid on the body; 254 have been found.
finds.w: In situ; skeletal material with the Department of Antiquities

finds.t: A small carved fish, found on the surface by Dikaios and unique on the island. It is probably a grouper or a sea bream, which happen to be the two species the villagers actually caught, six kilometres from the sea.

Pebbles scored with grids of lines, and small cones decorated with chevrons on the sides and a chequered pattern on the base. Weights for fishing nets, pictures of nets, and tokens in a system of social storage or exchange have all been proposed and none has won. Identical objects turn up in the Levant from the Natufian onwards, which suggests a shared symbolic world rather than parallel invention.

About forty beads of orange-red carnelian, including one shaped like a butterfly. This is by far the largest carnelian group on Cyprus, out of only fifty known pieces island-wide. Portable XRF on twenty-seven of them found at least two chemical groups, but the source, somewhere in Anatolia or the Caucasus, has not been identified.

A number of the skulls appear to have been reshaped by binding the head in infancy, and the practice is recorded roughly twice as often in women as in men. The interpretation goes back to Lawrence Angel's study in the 1950s and is still contested, with some arguing the flattening is a result of burial conditions rather than deliberate moulding.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Department of Antiquities

finds.n: Andesite and diabase from the Troodos rivers
finds.t: The stone the bowls are made of is not local. Hard igneous cobbles of andesite and diabase were collected from river beds draining the Troodos ophiolite, carried to the village and hollowed out with stone tools, the same rocks that supplied the querns, axes and adzes. At Kalavasos-Tenta the ground stone comes from riverbeds in the same way, so this was an island-wide habit and not one village's trick.

finds.n: Sea food carried six kilometres inland
finds.t: Nearly 650 marine molluscs and around 250 fish bones, mainly grouper and sea bream, all of them large fish. Khirokitia sits six kilometres from the coast, so somebody was making that walk regularly, and more of the material still waits to be published.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Sotira-Teppes
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The type-site of the Ceramic Neolithic. About fifty single-roomed houses stood on a hilltop, home to a community of farmers and herders who made the island's first pottery.

finds.t: Bowls and flasks whose slip was dragged with a comb into wavy bands, the signature of the culture named after this village.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; some in the Penn Museum, Philadelphia

finds.t: Stone footings of about 47 sub-rectangular, horseshoe and circular houses excavated by Porphyrios Dikaios in 1947 and 1951–54, partly with the Penn Museum.
A small schematic human figure in limestone, one of very few figurines from the Sotira culture.
A house floor found with a flint-worker's tools left in place, together with a stone axe still fitted to an antler handle.

Twelve pit graves cut into the eastern slope below the village. The dead have moved out of the houses, a clean break with the Aceramic habit of burying people under the floor, and the largest group of Ceramic Neolithic burials known from Cyprus.
finds.w: In situ; skeletal material with the Department of Antiquities

finds.t: An adult man of about thirty-nine, loosely contracted with his head to the south and his face east, a limestone boulder laid on his chest and a small stone set behind his head. Twelve potsherds and a single flint came from the soil of the grave, and that was all: grave goods are essentially absent, in sharp contrast to the necklaces buried with the dead at Khirokitia.
finds.w: In situ; skeletal material with the Department of Antiquities

finds.n: The earthquake at the end of Phase 2
finds.t: The densely packed houses and narrow lanes of the village's second phase came down together. What followed was a brief patched-up reoccupation, Phase 3, with repairs and a new retaining wall, before Sotira was left for good. It is the clearest destruction horizon in the Cypriot Neolithic and the reason earthquakes are blamed for the end of the Sotira culture.

A hook cut from bone, found at a hilltop village 330 m up and several kilometres inland. Together with the grooved stones from the same site it shows fishing was still part of the economy of a community that mostly farmed and hunted.

The village occupies a defensible plateau at 330 m above the Kouris valley with two or three perennial springs beside it, controlling a small well-watered valley with access both to the coast and inland. Where the Sotira-culture villages chose to sit is one of the few things about them that looks like a deliberate strategy.

Thin sections show the pots were made locally, household by household, each using its own clay recipe. Nobody at Sotira was a full-time potter, which makes the sharp regional split between combed pottery in the south and painted pottery in the north harder to explain as anything other than a deliberate statement of identity.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Penn Museum, Philadelphia

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayios Epiktitos-Vrysi
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Ceramic Neolithic village on a headland above the sea, where houses were sunk into deep hollows and rebuilt so often that the settlement rose into a mound.

finds.t: Painted vessels with bold linear designs, a northern counterpart to the Sotira wares of the south.
Eighteen semi-subterranean dwellings, many rebuilt two or three times, excavated by Edgar Peltenburg in 1969–73.
Household kit from the sunken houses: polished stone axes, bone beads and tools, with hearths and raised sleeping benches built against the walls.
Two narrow sunken passages and open yards linking the house-hollows, giving the village its partly underground plan.

Thirty-six mollusc species with over 1,500 examples, mostly edible limpet and topshell, along with 159 crab fragments and bones identified as marine turtle. Only sixty fish bones were recorded from twenty deposits, which almost certainly reflects the absence of water-sieving rather than the diet of a village on a sea cliff.

A hook cut from bone, matching examples from Paralimni-Nissia on the far side of the island and stone ones from Sotira. Between them these three sites are most of what we know about how Ceramic Neolithic Cypriots fished.

One lump of volcanic glass. After three thousand years in which Anatolian obsidian reached Cyprus in thousands of pieces, this is the entire haul of a substantial north-coast village, and it sits at the bottom of a decline that nobody has satisfactorily explained.

Grooved and pierced stones and flat discs, called spindle whorls in the excavation report. Net sinkers is the likelier reading, given that spinning equipment of this date is otherwise unknown on the island.

Because the houses were sunk into hollows and rebuilt two or three times in the same spot, Vrysi accumulated deposits deep enough to give a proper sequence, which is exactly what the shallow southern villages lack. Peltenburg's excavation records were formally handed over in 2016, so a site now beyond the reach of most archaeologists can still be worked on.
finds.w: In situ; archive with the Department of Antiquities

SETTLEMENTS.name: Lemba-Lakkous
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Chalcolithic village of round houses on the coastal plain north of Paphos, excavated by Edgar Peltenburg from 1976 to 1983. Together with nearby Kissonerga it is the best-excavated village of the Erimi culture, which takes its name from Erimi near Limassol.

finds.t: A 36 cm limestone figurine of a woman with a long neck and outstretched arms, found in 1976: one of the largest and the most famous Chalcolithic figures from Cyprus.
Small pendants of blue-green stone from the Troodos rivers, shaped like a person with arms spread into a cross.
Experimental reconstructions built with Chalcolithic methods stand at the site, the first experimental-archaeology programme in the eastern Mediterranean (1982).
One of the earliest recognisable metal tools on Cyprus, from the last phase of the village.
A round house with a covered porch, an internal corridor and generous storage, showing how houses grew more formal late in the period.

The Lemba Lady came out of the fill of an ordinary roundhouse, not a shrine. Nothing about the building marks it as special, so calling the figure a fertility goddess is an interpretation resting mainly on her size.
finds.w: In situ, Lemba-Lakkous (figure in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia)

finds.t: Babies buried inside pots set beneath and beside house floors, a rite shared with Kissonerga and typical of the Erimi culture. The dead here stayed inside the village, which is what makes the shaft graves at Souskiou so startling.

Sixty-two axes and adzes plus querns, rubbers and pounders from the Lemba region, studied by Carole Elliott into the standard typology for Chalcolithic ground stone on Cyprus. Every later find, including the Palloures axes, is measured against it.
Broken limestone and terracotta figures besides the famous one, which is a useful corrective: these things were made in numbers and mostly ended up smashed.
Lemba was abandoned in the Late Chalcolithic, as Kissonerga and Souskiou were, with no destruction to explain it. The whole south-western settlement pattern simply dissolves.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Erimi
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Erimi-Pamboula gave its name to the Chalcolithic culture when Dikaios dug it in 1933. Two thousand years later Erimi-Laonin tou Porakou was a Middle Bronze Age hilltop settlement with a workshop complex for dyeing textiles.

finds.t: Painted pottery with lattice, chevron and dotted designs that defines the Chalcolithic sequence.
Basins, spindle whorls and traces of dye in a large workshop compound at Laonin tou Porakou.
Long regarded as the oldest copper object found on Cyprus, with a hook and a knife fragment from the same site.

finds.n: Central building at Laonin tou Porakou
finds.t: A 220 m² building with massive walls, a dog-leg entrance with monolithic thresholds and a courtyard ringed by six roofed units, with a pithos storeroom.
A complete terracotta mould for casting axe-shaped copper ingots, found in the destruction levels of the workshop complex in 2022. The textile people were handling metal too.
Unit SA IX, five metres by under four, interpreted as a small shrine inside the production complex, apparently attached to the work rather than to the households.
A woman of fifteen to twenty buried prone beside a stone basin inside the residential area, an anomalous rite in a period of tidy chamber tombs, found in 2019 and still unexplained.
A fixed installation holding three grinding slabs side by side, for processing on a scale beyond one family's needs.
A complete Red Polished vessel modelled as a duck, deliberately filled and then sealed under a later plaster floor, so it was put out of use on purpose.

A central open working court closed on three sides by ranges of rooms, with cut-rock basins for dyeing at their edges. Erimi is the only Middle Bronze Age site on Cyprus where a whole industrial layout can be walked.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Marki-Alonia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: An Early and Middle Bronze Age village in the copper-bearing foothills, occupied for some six or seven centuries and excavated by La Trobe University in 1990–2000. Its rebuilt houses show how village life changed after the Philia settlers arrived.

finds.t: Jugs and bowls with a burnished red surface, some with incised decoration and relief animals.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Rectangular multi-room houses around courtyards, the new Anatolian-influenced way of living.
Rectangular mudbricks made in moulds, an Anatolian technique that arrived with the Philia settlers and made rectilinear houses possible.
Bones of sheep, goat, cattle, deer, pig and donkey, with seeds of wheat, barley, grapes, olives and figs, from a village that grew from about fifty to about four hundred people.

Ten flat Red Polished human figures, all highly burnished, all saying much the same thing in the same way. Frankel and Webb read them as statements of belonging to the group rather than portraits of individuals or gods.
Large numbers of clay whorls in coarse fabrics with wildly variable incised patterns, apparently decorated by whoever was going to spin with them.

Houses rebuilt on almost the same footprints through phase after phase for six or seven centuries. Marki is the reason we can talk about continuity of individual households in Bronze Age Cyprus at all.
Ore and slag brought up from sources a few kilometres south and worked inside the village, although the site was placed for its farmland rather than its metal.
Frankel and Webb's report, one of the few complete accounts of an Early and Middle Bronze Age village on Cyprus, and the model every later project has worked from.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Bellapais-Vounous
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A cemetery of more than 160 rock-cut chamber tombs on the north slope of the Kyrenia range, dug by Dikaios in 1931–32 and by James and Eleanor Stewart in 1937–38. Its grave gifts are the richest source of Early Bronze Age Cypriot art.

finds.t: A clay model of a walled enclosure with some eighteen human figures and four penned cattle around a ceremony, perhaps a shrine or a chief's court. One of the most discussed objects in Cypriot archaeology.
A Red Polished clay scene of two pairs of oxen drawing hook-ploughs with their ploughmen, the clearest picture of the new cattle-drawn agriculture.
Flat, incised human figures in Red Polished ware, sometimes holding infants. A few come from Vounous; Lapithos was the main centre of the tradition.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Ashmolean Museum; Metropolitan Museum

finds.t: Bronze daggers with Cretan parallels and a piece of sheet gold, the earliest signs of overseas luxury reaching Cyprus.

finds.n: Red Polished vessels from the Stewart seasons
finds.t: Twenty-three jugs and bowls from the 1937–38 excavations passed via Cambridge to Liverpool in 1952; a Vounous tripod vase is in the Louvre.

A mudbrick feature at Alambra-Mouttes closely resembling the finials on the three-columned throne in the Vounous Bowl, found in a room beside human remains. Andrew Sneddon argued in 2019 that this pushes the bowl towards a burial or ancestor rite and away from village genre scene.

finds.n: Bulls' heads and snakes in relief
finds.t: Red Polished vessels with modelled cattle heads on the shoulders and snakes crawling up the sides. Cattle and snakes are the two recurring animals of Early Bronze Age Cypriot imagery and nobody has explained either.
Pots joined into groups, sets of miniature bowls on a single stand, and vessels with spouts that cannot pour, made for the grave rather than the table.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; World Museum, Liverpool

finds.t: The metalwork of the tombs: dress pins for pinning a cloak and tanged daggers, the ordinary wealth against which the gold and the Cretan blades stand out.
Vounous lies in the occupied north and has not been excavated since. Everything known about the richest source of Early Bronze Age Cypriot art comes from four seasons in the 1930s.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Enkomi
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The great city of Late Bronze Age Cyprus, often identified as the capital of Alashiya, though this is debated. A real city from about 1550 BCE, laid out on a grid in the twelfth century, with ashlar buildings, workshops smelting Troodos copper, and a harbour on a channel that has since silted up. Abandoned after earthquakes around 1050 BCE in favour of Salamis.

finds.t: A 54 cm bronze statue of a young god wearing a horned helmet, found by Dikaios in 1948 in a pit in his sanctuary. The emblem of Bronze Age Cyprus.
A 35 cm bronze warrior standing on an oxhide-shaped copper ingot, found by the French mission in 1963, linking divine protection to the copper trade.
Clay tablets in the island's undeciphered Bronze Age script; Enkomi is the only Cypriot site to have yielded them.
Large Greek wine-mixing bowls painted with chariots and gods, including the so-called Zeus Krater, from about a hundred tombs dug by the British Museum in 1896.

finds.n: Silver cup with inlaid bull's heads
finds.t: A silver cup inlaid in gold and niello with a frieze of bull's heads and flowers, the finest Bronze Age Cypriot metalwork.
A rectangular ivory box carved with a chariot hunt of bulls and goats, used for a race game, from the 1896 British Museum tombs.
A broad collar of gold sheet in Egyptian style from Tomb 93, described as unique outside Egypt.

A defensive circuit built of stone orthostat slabs, some up to 3.5 metres long, with gates on the north, west and south. Behind it the city was replanned on a grid, with a main street running the length of the town from north to south.

A block about 32.5 by 28.5 metres with some 38 rooms around a tripartite core, its faces in dressed ashlar and probably carrying an upper storey. It is the largest secular building known from Bronze Age Cyprus, and no one has settled whether it was a residence, an administrative centre or both.

A courtyard shrine with rubble walls, lime-coated benches, mudbrick niches and pillars of massive masonry, its floor scattered with close to a hundred skulls of bulls and other cattle. The bronze Ingot God stood here, divine protection standing literally on the island's export.

finds.n: Clay cylinder with the longest Cypro-Minoan text
finds.t: A clay cylinder found in 1967 carrying about 217 signs, the longest legible inscription in the script. Only some 250 inscribed objects survive in all, and with no bilingual text and so small a sample every proposed decipherment remains improbable.

Three ingots cast in the shape of a stretched hide, each around 30 kg, found in the town beside the furnaces and workshops that handled the metal. Ingots of the same form and the same Cypriot copper turn up from Sardinia to Bulgaria.

Enkomi stood on a navigable inlet fed by the Pedieos. The river's silt closed it, the sea withdrew, and a city built on shipping found itself stranded, which is part of why Salamis replaced it on the new coast.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Hala Sultan Tekke
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Late Bronze Age harbour city on what was then a sheltered bay and is now the salt lake. Dug by the British Museum in 1897–98 and by Swedish teams under Paul Åström (1971–2008) and Peter Fischer (since 2010), it is one of the largest towns of its age, trading with Egypt, the Levant, Anatolia, Sardinia and the Aegean. The salt lake later became holy ground: the shrine of Umm Haram, a companion of the Prophet who died during the Arab raid of 649, gives the site its name.

finds.t: Diadems, earrings and beads from wealthy tombs, including Egyptian and Mycenaean imports.
Copper-working installations, with about a tonne of slag recovered, and a vat and heaps of murex shells from purple-dye making.
Imported drinking sets showing the reach of the town's trade, alongside grey burnished pottery from Sardinia, the farthest western imports yet found on Cyprus.
A faience sceptre-head with the cartouche of the pharaoh Horemheb, an Egyptian royal object attributed to the Hala Sultan Tekke tombs.
Faience and haematite seals from the city's administrative quarter, evidence of record-keeping in a trading town.

finds.n: Shrine of Umm Haram (Hala Sultan Tekke)
finds.t: Domed mausoleum and Ottoman mosque beside the salt lake, one of the most venerated Muslim shrines in the Mediterranean.

A chamber tomb holding the remains of at least 137 people, with more than a hundred pots, many imported from Mycenaean Greece, Minoan Crete and Hittite Anatolia, and jewellery of gold, silver, bronze, faience and carnelian along with seals, scarabs and ivory.

Thin sheets of gold laid over the brows and mouths of the dead, from seven chamber tombs and one shaft tomb. A 2026 study argues they were made on the island but blend Minoan, Mycenaean, Egyptian and Near Eastern design, which is what a port city's goldsmiths would produce.

finds.n: The offering pit with chariot kraters
finds.t: A pit packed with figurines and more than sixty vessels, among them several Mycenaean kraters painted with chariots and a large jar bearing an oversized woman in Minoan dress. Offerings were made above the tombs, not only in them.

The Bronze Age city itself lies under fields about a kilometre from the shrine, and it is there, not at the mosque, that the Swedish trenches are. Peter Fischer's team has worked the urban centre since 2010 and the cemetery since 2014.

finds.n: The bay that became a salt lake
finds.t: Ships once came in to a sheltered inlet here. The bar closed, the water turned to brine, and Larnaca Salt Lake is what remains. The town died roughly as its harbour did, around 1150 BCE.

Three great stones over the grave, the uppermost a single slab several metres long, which local tradition held had been set there by angels and hung unsupported in the air. Umm Haram bint Milhan was a companion of the Prophet and a distant aunt, a nurse at Uhud and Hunayn, who sailed with Muawiya's fleet against Cyprus in the caliphate of Uthman and died on the island after a fall from her mount.

The hadith collections report the Prophet foretelling a naval expedition and Umm Haram sailing on it, but the identification of this particular grave beside the Larnaca salt lake with hers is medieval and Ottoman rather than early, and the year of her death is given variously. The Turkish name Hala Sultan, meaning maternal aunt, belongs to that later tradition.

A domed mosque, cells and a courtyard grew around the tomb from 1760, and the minaret was finished in 1817 under Sultan Mahmud II, turning the grave into a dervish tekke with gardens and a cypress grove on the lake shore.

Ottoman ships passing the bay are said to have lowered their flags and fired salutes, and Ottoman writers ranked the tekke among the holiest places in Islam, a claim modern scholarship does not accept but which explains the scale of the buildings.

finds.n: The lake that was a harbour
finds.t: The sheltered bay that made the Bronze Age town rich silted into a lagoon and then into the salt pan that supplied Larnaca's salt trade for centuries. The shrine and the buried city sit on the same shoreline, three thousand years apart.

Three large stones, two upright and one laid across them, cover the grave of Umm Haram bint Milhan, a kinswoman of the Prophet's foster-mother who is said to have fallen from her mule and died during the Arab raid of 649. Local tradition holds that the top stone hung unsupported in the air; the shrine was venerated by Ottoman sailors, who saluted it from the sea.

The mosque and minaret beside the tomb were built under the governor Seyyid Mehmed Emin, completing a complex whose tomb chamber and enclosure had been raised from about 1760; the inscription over the door records the work. It is among the most important Muslim monuments on the island.

finds.n: The takke's garden and dervish lodge
finds.t: Cells, a fountain, cypresses and palms around the mosque, laid out as a lodge for the dervishes and pilgrims who kept the shrine; the tekke held property in the district endowed for its upkeep.

finds.n: The salt lake and its flamingos
finds.t: The lake that once salted Larnaca's export trade now fills and dries each year and holds thousands of greater flamingos in winter; it is a Natura 2000 site and the setting that makes the tekke's silhouette famous.

The tekke lies in the government-controlled area but is maintained for Muslim worship, and access for Turkish Cypriots to pray here has been one of the small confidence-building measures negotiated since the crossings opened in 2003.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Maa-Palaeokastro
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A short-lived fortified settlement on a narrow headland with massive walls on both landward and seaward sides, dug by Karageorghis in 1979–86. Founded around 1230 BCE, perhaps by Aegean newcomers, it is one of the sites most often cited for the arrival of Greek settlers on Cyprus, though its culture mixes Cypriot, Aegean and Levantine habits.

finds.t: Walls of huge boulders about 3.5 metres thick and some 70 metres long, barring the neck of the headland.
Locally made Greek-style tableware, among the earliest produced on the island.
finds.w: Paphos District Museum; Museum of the Mycenaean Colonisation, Maa

finds.t: A large building of dressed stone with a central hearth of Aegean type, the best evidence for the newcomers' domestic habits.
A copper-domed museum sunk into the headland to spare the landscape, designed by Andrea Bruno.
Rows of small rooms holding large storage jars set behind the fortification, provisions on a scale that suggests a community expecting to sit out trouble rather than a trading post.

Coarse hand-shaped cooking pots of a kind at home in Italy and the western Aegean, found here and at Pyla-Kokkinokremos. It is the strongest hint that some newcomers came from further west than Mycenae, though pots can travel without their makers.

Unbaked clay reels and spools for weaving, a type unknown on Cyprus before this and ordinary in the Aegean. Textile tools are domestic, which is why they are used to argue that whole households arrived and not just traders.

The settlement was raised, given up, briefly reoccupied and left for good within about three generations. Vassos Karageorghis and Martha Demas published the sequence in 1988, and it is that short, broken occupation that makes the site so hard to read.

A neck of rock at Coral Bay with sea on three sides and no harbour, walled on the landward and the seaward side alike. Whoever built it wanted safety rather than trade, and feared attack from both directions.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kition
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Bronze Age harbour town that became a Phoenician city around 850 BCE and, from the fifth century, a kingdom whose Phoenician kings were vassals of Persia. Its temple of Astarte was one of the largest in the Phoenician world. The city continued as Larnaca and is the birthplace of the philosopher Zeno the Stoic.

finds.p: Founded 13th century BCE, Phoenician from c. 850 BCE
finds.t: A huge temple with a hall of pillars built over Bronze Age sanctuaries, with ship graffiti scratched on its walls.
A basalt stele recording the submission of seven Cypriot kings to Assyria. Found at Larnaca in 1845.

finds.n: Kition Tariffs and other Phoenician inscriptions
finds.t: Two marble tablets with painted accounts of a month's temple expenses (builders, barbers, sacrificers, singers), found in 1879, plus dedications from the sanctuaries: the largest body of Phoenician writing from Cyprus.
finds.w: British Museum, London; Larnaca District Museum

finds.t: At least six slipways, about 6 m wide and 38 m long, of the war harbour of the last Phoenician kings, dug by a French mission in 1984–99.
Built by Emperor Leo VI over the tomb of Lazarus after its discovery, with a carved Baroque iconostasis; a mosque briefly after 1571, bought back by the Orthodox in 1589.
Furnaces and slag abutting the Kathari sanctuaries, showing how closely metal-working and cult were bound.
A 20-metre Roman floor mosaic of the Labours of Hercules found in 2016 during drainage works and conserved in place.

A Phoenician text found at Larnaca in 1990 recording a trophy set up by Milkyaton, king of Kition and Idalion, in his first regnal year, to the god Baal Oz, Lord of Strength, for a victory the god had granted. The enemy is not named; most scholars supply Evagoras of Salamis and his allies, which would make this the only contemporary monument of that war.

finds.n: Phoenician funerary stelae from the Tourapi necropolis
finds.t: Four inscribed grave markers, one a white marble stele with a triangular top, found in 1894 by John Myres for the Cyprus Exploration Fund in the cemetery at Turabi Tekke. They name ordinary Phoenician-speaking Kitians and their families.
finds.w: British Museum, London; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Ashmolean Museum, Oxford

finds.t: The low mound beside the war harbour, dug by a French mission from 1976, with a sequence from the Late Bronze Age town to a Phoenician sanctuary and the classical port installations. It is the one part of ancient Kition excavated to modern standards over a long run of seasons.

Silver and gold struck through a reign of more than forty-five years, with the regnal year numbered on the coin, a habit almost unknown elsewhere in the Greek world. The numbers let historians date the annexation of Tamassos to his twenty-first year.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.n: Phoenician royal dedications from the Kathari temples
finds.t: Stone and marble dedications naming Kitian kings and temple officers, part of a corpus of more than 135 published Phoenician inscriptions from Cyprus, seven of them of the eighth century BCE or earlier. Together they make Kition the best-documented Phoenician city outside Lebanon.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Larnaca District Museum; British Museum, London

finds.t: The Roman city shrank to a small town around the church of Lazarus, its first bishop by tradition. Leo VI's masons building over the rediscovered tomb about 890 give the first firm evidence that anyone was still living here after the Arab raids.

A marble sarcophagus in the crypt under the church, empty: the relics went to Constantinople in 898 and on to Marseilles after the sack of 1204. Human remains found under the altar in 1972 are now shown as a relic of the saint.
finds.w: In situ, Church of St Lazarus, Larnaca

finds.t: The ancient acropolis mound was carted away in 1879 to fill the marshes and raise the new town, one of the most destructive acts in the island's archaeological history. What is known of Kition's upper city comes from what the diggers happened to notice.
finds.w: Site levelled; some finds in the Larnaca District Museum

finds.t: An Ottoman fort on the seafront built over the medieval castle, later a British prison and a place of execution, now a small museum with the medieval collection.

Bekir Pasha, the Ottoman governor, paid out of his own pocket for an aqueduct bringing water from Arpera to a town that had none. It supplied Larnaca until 1939 and thirty-three of its arches still stand beside the airport road.

A plaque over the entrance dates the Ottoman rebuilding of the fort to 1625, though a Turkish garrison had held the site since 1570 and there was a Lusignan work here before that. It carried the guns that saluted arriving consuls, then served the British as a prison with a gallows into the 1940s, and is now the Larnaca Medieval Museum.

Built over the tomb found in 890 inscribed 'Lazarus, four days dead, friend of Christ'. Taken as a mosque after 1571 and sold back to the Orthodox in 1589, it was then shared with Latin worshippers for about two centuries, an arrangement recorded in Latin graffiti in the walls. Its bell tower went up after the Ottoman reform of 1857 permitted belfries. A fire in 1970 destroyed much of the iconostasis, and in November 1972 human remains were found in a marble sarcophagus under the altar and identified as part of the saint's relics.

The Ottoman authorities required European consuls to live at Larnaca, and the town became the island's window on the world: French, Venetian, British, Russian and Swedish consulates, dragomans, merchants and the antiquities dealers who shipped much of Cypriot archaeology abroad. Cotton, carobs, salt, silk and wine went out through the roadstead by lighter because there was no harbour.

finds.n: The salt lake and the salt trade
finds.t: Salt raked from the lake beside the town was one of Cyprus's steadiest exports under Venetian, Ottoman and British rule; commercial harvesting stopped in the 1980s, and the lake is now protected for its wintering flamingos.

Thrown up in a few months on the edge of the salt lake after Nicosia airport was lost, initially with a converted cargo shed for a terminal; it became the Republic's main gateway and got a new terminal in 2009.

The town absorbed thousands of displaced people, took over the trade of Famagusta with a new commercial port, and grew a marina and a seafront palm promenade; the Turkish Cypriot quarter around the fort emptied in 1975. Modern Larnaca is a 1974 city as much as an ancient one.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Salamis
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Founded after the fall of Enkomi, by legend by Teucer of the Trojan War, Salamis was the leading city-kingdom of Cyprus for most of a millennium. Its kings Evagoras I and Nikokreon dominated the island. After earthquakes in the fourth century it was rebuilt by Constantius II as Constantia and made the capital, until the Arab raids of 647–649 and the sand took it.

finds.t: Great built tombs approached by ramps on which horses and chariots were sacrificed. Tomb 79 held an ivory-inlaid throne and bed of Homeric splendour.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; tombs in situ

finds.t: A colonnaded palaestra with marble statues, rebuilt under Trajan and Hadrian after earthquakes. Most statues are headless; whether by Christian zeal or by earthquake and later looting is debated.
The largest theatre in Cyprus, seating around 15,000, restored for performances.
The cathedral of Constantia and once the largest church on the island.

finds.n: Bronze cauldron with griffins and sirens
finds.t: A great bronze cauldron on an iron tripod from Tomb 79, its rim ringed with cast griffin and siren heads in Near Eastern style.
A three-aisled basilica with colonnaded courts and a bathhouse with a fine opus sectile floor, on the shore below the city.

finds.p: 7th century BCE; chapel from the 14th century
finds.t: A built tomb with two horse skeletons in its passage, vaulted over in Roman times and later venerated as the prison of St Catherine.

Sigloi with a recumbent ram and a plain reverse, carrying the king's name in the Cypriot syllabary, the first coins struck on the island. Their weight follows a local standard rather than a Persian or Greek one.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London; Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris

finds.t: The first gold coinage of Cyprus, with the head of Herakles and a recumbent goat, and legends in the syllabary and the Greek alphabet together. The double script is the whole policy of Evagoras in miniature: a Cypriot king advertising himself to Greeks.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.t: Gold thirds and small fractions with Aphrodite on one side and Athena on the other, on a new standard. Nikokles was the first Salaminian king to abandon the syllabary on his coins entirely.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris

finds.p: Archaic origins, monumental in Hellenistic and Roman times
finds.t: The city's chief temple, at the south of the site, whose Hellenistic and Roman phases survive as a platform and scattered capitals. The Archaic cult beneath is attested by dedications rather than by standing walls.

finds.n: The Iron Age town beneath the Roman city
finds.t: The Salamis visitors see is Roman and Early Christian; the kingdom's own city lies under it and has been reached only in small soundings near the harbour. That the leading kingdom of Cyprus is archaeologically its least known capital is a standing frustration of the field.

A semicircular public latrine off the gymnasium court with places for forty-four people at once, its flushing channels, water tanks and stone armrests still in place. It is the best preserved latrine in the eastern Mediterranean and says more about Roman daily life than any statue on the site.

finds.n: The agora and the temple of Zeus Olympios
finds.t: A colonnaded square 230 m by 55 m, among the largest in the Roman world, with the temple of Zeus Olympios on a podium about 28 m by 22 m at its southern end carrying twelve free-standing columns. One marble capital from it is carved with winged bulls in a manner that looks back to Achaemenid Persia.

Floors and wall mosaics in the bath block behind the palaestra, including Leda with the swan and the river god Eurotas, and a fight between men and Amazons, with patches of painted plaster surviving beside them.

finds.n: The mismatched columns of the palaestra
finds.t: The colonnade around the gymnasium court is made of columns of different sizes and stones, several of them lifted from the theatre during repairs after the earthquakes. The seam in the architecture is the clearest visible trace of the disasters.

A vaulted reservoir carried on thirty-six square pillars, fed by the aqueduct that brought spring water some 45 km from Kythrea. Built in the last years before the Arab raids, it is the final large public work of the ancient city.

Earthquakes in 332 and 342 flattened the Roman city. Constantius II rebuilt a smaller town on the same grid, remitted its taxes for four years and renamed it after himself, and it became the capital and metropolitan see of Cyprus. Its water came fifty kilometres by aqueduct from the spring at Kythrea because its own supply had failed.

An empty vaulted chamber under the south apse of his cathedral, where the heresy-hunting bishop who wrote the Panarion was buried. The relics were taken away at some point before the city was abandoned.

The apostle's body was moved from the tomb outside the city into the basilica of Ayios Epiphanios, which made Constantia a stop for pilgrims on the road to Jerusalem and gave the archbishop his standing at court.

The seaside basilica dug by Georges Roux from 1964 has colonnaded courts at both ends, a bathhouse and a floor of cut marble. The unusual double plan and a cross-shaped setting in the eastern court have led scholars to argue it was built to display a relic of the True Cross, though the case is circumstantial.

Muawiya's fleet met no resistance, went straight for the capital and camped in the bishop's residence, dividing the plunder between the Syrian and Egyptian contingents.
