A second fleet came a few years later. Constantia limped on into the eighth century, then the people moved to Ammochostos and the dunes came over the ruins.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Palaepaphos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Old Paphos was a Bronze Age town that became the Sanctuary of Aphrodite, the goddess said to have risen from the sea nearby. Pilgrims came from across the ancient world. It was also a city-kingdom whose last king, Nikokles, founded Nea Paphos before Ptolemy ended the dynasty.

finds.t: An open-air sanctuary of megalithic walls and later Roman courtyards. The goddess was worshipped as a conical black stone rather than a statue.
finds.w: In situ; the baetyl in Kouklia Local Museum

finds.t: A ramp built by Persian troops against the north-east gate, packed with about a thousand fragments of Archaic statues, altars and inscribed stones torn from a nearby shrine or from the city itself. One of the earliest siege ramps ever excavated, and the only one that can be tied to Herodotus's account.
finds.w: Kouklia Museum; Cyprus Museum; World Museum Liverpool; ramp in situ

finds.t: The largest group of texts in the Cypriot syllabary, including the royal dedications of the Paphian kings.
finds.w: Kouklia Local Museum; Cyprus Museum; World Museum Liverpool

finds.t: A royal manor and sugar mill, one of the island's medieval export industries.
A bronze roasting spit from a tomb at Kouklia-Skales inscribed 'of Opheltas' in the syllabic script: the earliest Greek name written on Cyprus.

finds.n: Royal palace on the Hadjiabdoullah plateau
finds.t: The University of Cyprus has located the Iron Age royal seat with storage and workshop complexes, and in 2025 exposed towered acropolis walls of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE.
Central panel of a Roman villa floor near the sanctuary; stolen in 1980 and recovered, now kept indoors with a copy in the original room.

The defenders dug galleries out under the Persian ramp and lit fires in them to collapse it, and the tunnels were found and followed by the Liverpool and St Andrews expedition in the 1950s. Siege and counter-siege survive together, which is very rare.

A sherd inscribed in the Cypriot syllabary with what reads as an administrative account, published in 2019 from the University of Cyprus excavations on the palace plateau. It is direct evidence that the Paphian kings kept written records.

A long series beginning with Siromos's kneeling bull with a human face, running through Stasandros's bull and ankh-holding eagle to Timarchos's gold, and ending with Nikokles, who signed his name in minute letters on Alexander's coinage. The man-faced bull is unique to Paphos.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.n: The Archaic and Classical acropolis walls
finds.t: Towered fortification walls of the fifth and fourth centuries BCE exposed on the Hadjiabdoullah plateau by the University of Cyprus, alongside the storage and workshop ranges of the royal seat. The kings of Paphos have finally acquired a palace.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Nea Paphos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Founded around 320 BCE as a harbour city, Nea Paphos became the capital of Ptolemaic and then Roman Cyprus. Its Roman villas hold the finest mosaics on the island. It declined after the fourth-century earthquakes and the Arab raids, but survived as a town around its harbour castle.

finds.t: Floors of a wealthy villa showing Dionysos, the seasons, Pyramos and Thisbe, Narcissus and the first wine. Found by a farmer ploughing in 1962.
The residence of the Roman governor, with a round mosaic of Theseus and the Minotaur.
Rock-cut peristyle tombs of Ptolemaic officials, imitating houses with Doric columns. No kings were ever buried here.
A castle first raised by the Byzantines to guard the harbour against Arab raids and remodelled by the Lusignans around 1200; wrecked by an earthquake in 1222 and never rebuilt.
Five mythological panels found by the Polish mission in 1983, often read as a late pagan reply to Christianity.

finds.p: Late 4th century BCE to 4th century CE
finds.t: A rock-cut theatre laid out when the city was founded, excavated by the University of Sydney; one of the oldest buildings of Nea Paphos.
The city's paved square with a small semicircular Roman theatre beside it, restored for summer performances.

A villa west of the Villa of Theseus with three mythological floors: Orpheus playing to the beasts, Hercules and the Nemean lion, and an Amazon with her horse. Excavated in the 1980s and still not open to visitors.
finds.w: In situ, Paphos Archaeological Park (closed to the public)

finds.p: 3rd century BCE to mid 2nd century CE
finds.t: A large courtyard house south of the Villa of Theseus with four courts, one a peristyle garden with Corinthian and Ionic porticoes. It was divided into two dwellings around 100 CE and brought down by an earthquake in the middle of the second century, one of several shocks the city absorbed between the disasters of 15 BCE and 365 CE.
The city's healing sanctuary, immediately beside the Odeon and the agora, so that the sick, the market and the concerts shared one civic centre.

Bronze coins struck for the league of the island's cities, whose reverses show the temple of Aphrodite at Palaepaphos with the conical stone standing inside it. The league ran the imperial cult, voted honours and set up statues of deified emperors, and it is the nearest thing Roman Cyprus had to a native government. Which city struck the coins is not certain.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.n: The milestones of the Paphos roads
finds.t: Thirty Roman milestones have been recorded on Cyprus, most of them in the hills, and they fall into phases: new roads under Augustus and Titus, civic repairs under the Severans, then old stones re-cut for propaganda. The Peutinger Table shows the island squashed flat and gives almost no road detail, so the stones are the real evidence.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Paphos District Archaeological Museum; several in situ

finds.t: A rectangular keep about 40 m by 20 m at the harbour mouth, built by the Lusignans after the earthquake of 1222 wrecked Saranta Kolones, fortified further by the Genoese in 1373 and taken over by Venice in 1489. Venice blew up the western tower in 1570 rather than leave it to the Ottomans, who rebuilt it in 1592; it later held a hundred men and twelve guns, then became a British salt store.

A Greek Cypriot of learning and ambition who plotted to raise the island against Venice with foreign help; the conspiracy was betrayed in January 1563, he was taken at Paphos in February and executed at Nicosia. The clearest evidence that Venetian rule was resented.
Tiepolo brought his Paphos militia across the island to Famagusta and served through the siege; he was among the officers put to death when the city fell in August 1571.

finds.n: The harbour and the salt trade
finds.t: The Lusignan and Venetian port shipped sugar from Kouklia, copper brought down the camel road and salt from the pans; the castle stood over the mole and doubled as customs house and salt store into the British period.

The Venetians blew up the Lusignan harbour forts in 1570; the Ottomans rebuilt one tower with a vaulted hall and prison cells in 1592, and the British used it as a salt store before it was scheduled as an ancient monument in 1935. It is the working emblem of Paphos harbour.

Paphos was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1980 for the whole ensemble from Palaepaphos to the Tombs of the Kings and the Roman houses, one of the first sites listed for Cyprus and the reason the archaeological park was consolidated.

A destructive earthquake in the Paphos district killed dozens of people and wrecked villages and churches across the west; much of the district's plain vernacular architecture was rebuilt afterwards in concrete, which is why so little old fabric survives outside the hill villages.

The Turkish Cypriot quarter of upper Paphos, with its mosque and bath, emptied when its people moved north in 1975 and was allocated to Greek Cypriots displaced from the north; two displacements are stacked in the same streets.

An airport opened at Paphos in 1983 turned the quietest district of the Republic into a tourist and retirement coast, and Paphos was European Capital of Culture in 2017, which paid for the excavation and display of much of the old town.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kourion
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A city-kingdom on a limestone bluff above the sea, by tradition founded by Argives. Its king Stesenor deserted Onesilos in the battle of 497 BCE and handed Persia the victory. Under Rome it was a prosperous city of theatre, baths and villas until the earthquakes of 365–370 CE, after which a Christian city rose and then faded away after the Arab raids of 649.

finds.t: A house whose collapse trapped a family: a man of about 25 shielding a woman and an infant, a girl of about thirteen fallen from the upper floor, and a mule tethered in the yard. The destruction layer dates the end of the Roman city.
finds.w: In situ; remains in Kourion Museum, Episkopi, moving to the new Cyprus Museum in Nicosia

finds.t: A Greek theatre enlarged by the Romans and converted for animal fights, restored for concerts today.
Floors of an early Christian bath complex with fish, birds and inscriptions praising Christ.
A rural sanctuary of Apollo of the Woodland with a temple, a palaestra and a great pit of broken votives.
Gold, silver and jewellery removed by Luigi Palma di Cesnola in the 1870s, with disputed provenance.
finds.w: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

finds.t: The three-aisled cathedral of Christian Kourion with a separate baptistery, built over the ruins of the earthquake-struck Roman city.
A U-shaped track with seven rows of seats for about 6,000 spectators, one of the few stadia on the island.

finds.n: House of Achilles and House of the Gladiators
finds.t: Two villas by the Paphos road: one with Achilles recognised among the daughters of Lykomedes, the other with named gladiators fighting in its courtyard.
Kourion enters history as Damasu on Esarhaddon's prism, one of the ten Cypriot kings who sent materials for the Assyrian palace at Nineveh. The name is the Greek Damasos in Assyrian spelling.
finds.w: Prism in the British Museum, London

finds.n: The Archaic votive deposit of Apollo Hylates
finds.t: A great pit of offerings including gold and silver bull figurines, East Greek painted pottery and Egyptian bronze bowls, with the burnt bone of large-scale animal sacrifice. The imports show a country sanctuary plugged into the whole eastern Mediterranean.
finds.w: Kourion Museum, Episkopi; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: A paved ring with a low kerb and post-holes in the Apollo sanctuary, usually explained as a place for ritual dancing around a planted tree or a sacred grove. No other Cypriot sanctuary has one.
finds.w: In situ, Sanctuary of Apollo Hylates

finds.t: Herodotus names Stesenor of Kourion as the commander who changed sides in the middle of the battle against the Persians, taking his chariots with him and losing the Cypriot revolt. No inscription or coin of him is known, which is itself telling.
A conduit running some 22 km from a spring near Souni and crossing a 60 m bridge to reach the city, one of two aqueducts built as Kourion outgrew its rainwater cisterns.
finds.w: In situ, fragments between Souni and Kourion

finds.n: The rock-cut cistern in the agora
finds.t: A large colonnaded reservoir cut into the bedrock of the agora, part of the same programme as the aqueducts. Water, not marble, was the expensive part of building a Roman city on a dry limestone bluff.
The civic square formalised in the second century with long colonnaded stoas on its north, west and south sides, the setting for the inscriptions that name Kourion's proconsuls.
A large house built in the same generation as the House of the Gladiators, with an apsed dining room and mosaic floors. Both were standing when the earthquake struck.

Under Caracalla the Greek theatre was rebuilt so that wild beast hunts could be staged in it, with the lower seats removed and a barrier put up. Later in the same century it was turned back into a theatre, a rare case of a Roman city changing its mind about blood sports.

Kourion's bishop was one of the four Cypriots who went to the Council of Ephesus in 431 and came home with canon 8, the charter of the island church's independence. The others were Rheginos of Constantia, Sapricius of Paphos and Evagrios of Soloi.
finds.w: Acts of the Council of Ephesus

finds.t: A building of its own north of the cathedral, with narthex, cross-shaped font and mosaic floors, put up when adults were still baptised by immersion and the bishop did it himself at Easter.

finds.n: Extramural basilica and the tomb of Ayios Ermogenis
finds.t: A second basilica outside the walls to the east, built over an older cemetery around a martyr's tomb. The little chapel of Ayios Ermogenis below the bluff still marks the spot and still draws its feast-day crowd.

finds.p: 2nd to 4th century CE, in use later
finds.t: A monumental fountain house at the head of the aqueduct, among the largest such buildings known on the island, still supplying the Christian town after the Roman city fell.
The village below the site is called Episkopi, the bishop's place, because Kourion's see came down off the bluff when the city was given up. The name is the last working trace of the Christian town.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Amathus
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The kingdom of the Eteocypriots, who kept a pre-Greek language into the fourth century BCE. Amathus stayed loyal to Persia during the revolt of Onesilos and later prospered under the Ptolemies and Rome, with a temple of Aphrodite on its acropolis. Abandoned after the Arab raids.

finds.t: A limestone vase 1.85 m tall and 3.2 m across, weighing about fourteen tonnes, carved with a walking bull on each of its four handles. One of a pair; the other lies broken on the acropolis. Removed by Edmond Duthoit in 1865.
Texts in the Cypriot syllabary in a non-Greek language that has never been read.

A Roman temple with Nabataean-style capitals, begun in the last quarter of the first century CE over a Hellenistic predecessor and a far older sanctuary; demolished in the sixth century for a basilica.
Breakwaters built for Demetrios Poliorketes around 315 BCE and abandoned under Ptolemy I, probably never used; now under the waves.
A painted limestone coffin from the north cemetery showing a chariot procession, with Astarte and Bes figures on the ends; probably a royal burial and the star of the Cesnola collection.
finds.w: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

finds.t: A colonnaded market square below the acropolis with a nymphaeum and bath complex, rebuilt after the earthquake of 77 CE.
A Christian basilica built over the demolished temple of Aphrodite, marking the site's last phase before the Arab raids.

A silver bowl, gilded and worked in repoussé, taken from a looted Amathus tomb by Luigi Palma di Cesnola before 1877. Concentric bands show sphinxes, Assyrian-dressed worshippers at a sacred tree, and an outer scene of a city under siege by soldiers in Greek, Egyptian and Urartian gear, the fullest picture of a siege to survive from the Phoenician world.

Under the Roman temple of Aphrodite lie earlier cult terraces with a great rock-cut cistern and votive deposits, the shrine of the goddess the Amathusians worshipped before Greek names were attached to her. The French mission traced the sequence from the 1970s.

finds.n: Lion coinage of the Amathusian kings
finds.t: Sigloi of Rhoikos I with a recumbent lion, followed by issues of Rhoikos II, Pyrrhos, Zotimos, Lysandros and Epipalos, several of them known only from their coins. The mint kept a local weight standard long after its neighbours changed.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.t: A massive circuit of mudbrick on stone footings around the lower town, one of the earliest fortifications of the Cypriot kingdoms. It is why Onesilos had to besiege the place in 498 BCE instead of walking in.

The tombs that produced the Amathus sarcophagus and the silver bowl were dug out by Cesnola and by the British in the nineteenth century, with two chambers alone yielding fragments of fifteen sarcophagi. Almost nothing of that context was recorded.
finds.w: In situ (emptied); objects in the Metropolitan Museum, New York, and the British Museum, London

finds.n: The Hellenistic collapse and the Antonine revival
finds.t: Under the Ptolemies Amathus lost out to Paphos: the harbour silted, the acropolis was largely abandoned and the city shrank. It was rebuilt in the second century CE, when the gates, fountains, nymphaea and agora were all renewed. The stratigraphy of that gap is the clearest thing on the site.

Amathus became a bishopric, and its most famous bishop, Tychon, gave his name to the modern village of Agios Tychonas beside the ruins. The church built at his tomb was one of a cluster of basilicas that mark the city's Christian centuries.

Amathus was one of only three cities, with Tamassos and Soli, still named as producing copper under Rome. The slag from its workings lies as much as 3 km from the mines, so ore was hauled to the fuel.
finds.w: In situ, the hills north of Amathus

finds.t: Amathus was already almost deserted when Richard I took the island in 1191, and its cut stone went into the buildings of Limassol and, in 1869, into the works of the Suez Canal. A large part of the city is not lost but relocated.
finds.w: Dispersed; some blocks reused in Limassol

SETTLEMENTS.name: Idalion
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A city-kingdom on two acropolis hills near the copper mines, with temples to Athena and Aphrodite. In the mid-fifth century BCE (c. 470–450) it was conquered by the Phoenician kings of Kition and administered from a palace archive. The site was one of the first ever excavated on Cyprus, by Cesnola and Lang in the 1860s.

finds.t: A bronze plaque in the Cypriot syllabary recording the city's contract with a physician who treated the wounded during the siege by Persians and Kitians. The longest syllabic text known.
More than 730 inscriptions, mostly Phoenician ink on sherds, from the palace on the west acropolis, excavated by the Department of Antiquities in 1991–2012: the largest Phoenician archive anywhere.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities; Idalion Local Museum, Dali

finds.t: A fortified sanctuary of Athena on the west acropolis, excavated by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition in 1928.
finds.w: In situ; finds in the Medelhavsmuseet, Stockholm, and the Cyprus Museum

finds.t: A limestone pedestal dedicated to Apollo Amyklos and Reshef-Mikal in both Phoenician and Cypriot syllabic, found by Robert Hamilton Lang in 1869; it provided the key to deciphering the syllabary.
Some 142 limestone worshippers and deities from the sanctuary of Apollo on the east hill, dug in 1868–69 and shipped to London.
A fortified complex of courts and storerooms where the kings of Idalion and later the governors from Kition kept their records.
finds.w: In situ, Dali; finds in Idalion Local Museum

finds.n: Crowned head of Apollo from Potamia-Ellines
finds.t: A limestone head wearing a laurel crown, found in 1933 in the Ellines locality of Potamia, the next village east of Dali, and long the best-known object from Idalion's hinterland. Later trenching at Ellines confirmed a settlement there within the kingdom's territory.

finds.n: The destruction layer of the west acropolis
finds.t: A burnt horizon across the fortified summit at Ambelleri, marking the day the Phoenician army of Kition took the city. Everything above it is Kitian administration; everything below is an independent kingdom.
Small silver thirds and twelfths of a siglos with a syllabic legend, the last coins struck by an independent Idalion. Stasikypros is the king named on the Idalion Tablet.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.n: Sanctuary of Aphrodite on the east acropolis
finds.t: The hill opposite the Athena temple carried shrines of Aphrodite and Apollo, cleared by Cesnola and Lang in the 1860s. Idalion is where the myth of Adonis dying in Aphrodite's arms was localised, and the Cypriot Aphrodite was worshipped here as much as at Paphos.
finds.w: In situ, Dali; sculpture in the British Museum, London, and the Metropolitan Museum, New York

finds.n: The double acropolis and the lower town wall
finds.t: Two flat-topped hills flanking the Yialias river, joined by a walled lower town, the clearest plan of a Cypriot city-kingdom anywhere. Copper from the Troodos passed through it on the way to the coast.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Tamassos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The copper kingdom. Homer's Temese, where Athena in disguise sails to trade iron for copper, is usually identified with Tamassos. Its wealth came from the mines of the north-east Troodos, its royal tombs are among the finest built on the island, and it lived on as a bishopric into Byzantine times.

finds.t: Two ashlar-built chamber tombs with carved pilasters and false windows imitating a wooden house or a Phoenician shrine.
A life-size bronze head of Apollo from a statue found by villagers in 1836; the body was broken up for scrap.
Heaps of smelting waste around the mines record extraction from the Bronze Age to Roman times.
A temple built around 600 BCE, twice destroyed and rebuilt in the Hellenistic period, with copper furnaces and slag beside it: metal and goddess were tended together.
Six intact life-size limestone guardians, two sphinxes and four lions with traces of red and blue paint, found in 1997 near the royal tombs.
A rural sanctuary packed with votive statues, some colossal, dug by Ohnefalsch-Richter in 1885 and then lost; relocated in 2021 by the Universities of Frankfurt and Kiel.
finds.w: In situ, Pera valley; 1885 finds in the Cyprus Museum and Berlin

finds.t: Built over the tomb of Herakleidios, first bishop of Tamassos, marking the city's Christian afterlife.
One of the built ashlar tombs, its grave goods including an iron sword with silver rivets in the hilt. Tamassian tombs are smaller than those at Salamis but their masonry is finer.
finds.w: In situ, Politiko; sword in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Dedications inscribed in both Phoenician and the Cypriot syllabary, set up after the kingdom passed to Kition. They are the documents historians use to work out what actually changed for a Cypriot city when a Phoenician king bought it.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.n: Sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods
finds.t: A shrine inside the city walls, distinct from the Aphrodite sanctuary and the Apollo shrine at Frangissa, showing three separate cults served by one small town. Its votives are mostly terracotta.

Syllabic texts from the Frangissa sanctuary that call the god Alasiotas, 'of Alashiya', the Bronze Age name of the island still attached to a deity a thousand years later. It is the longest survival of that name anywhere.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Staatliche Museen zu Berlin

finds.n: Copper smelting workshops beside the goddess
finds.t: Furnaces and slag from the smelting of copper sulphide ores, and casting debris, immediately next to the Aphrodite sanctuary. The technical detail matters: sulphide ore needs roasting before smelting, and Tamassos was doing it at scale.

Duris of Samos records that Pasikypros, king of Tamassos, sold his city and his royal title to Pumayyaton of Kition for fifty talents and went to grow old at Amathus. Pumayyaton's dated coins confirm he held Tamassos from his twenty-first year.
finds.w: Literary source; coins in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

SETTLEMENTS.name: Marion, later Arsinoe
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A city-kingdom of the north-west with close Athenian ties and a lively trade in painted pottery. Ptolemy I destroyed it in 312 BCE for siding with Antigonus and moved its people to Paphos. It was refounded as Arsinoe and lived on into Byzantine times.

finds.t: Thousands of imported Greek vases from the cemeteries, one of the largest groups on Cyprus; much of the 1880s material went abroad.
finds.w: Local Museum of Marion-Arsinoe, Polis Chrysochous; Cyprus Museum

finds.t: Limestone votaries and lively terracotta figures from the sanctuaries.
finds.w: Local Museum of Marion-Arsinoe, Polis Chrysochous

finds.t: Two early Christian churches, one with fragments of early Byzantine wall painting, excavated by Princeton University in 1983–2007.
A hilltop shrine burned around 500 BCE, packed with thousands of terracotta votaries, bronze bowls and an iron roasting spit.
finds.w: Local Museum of Marion-Arsinoe, Polis Chrysochous

finds.t: A wall three metres wide thrown hastily across a sanctuary as Ptolemy's army approached, sealed under ash.
A rare marble youth in Greek style from Ohnefalsch-Richter's 1880s digs.
The first gold struck at Marion, by the king Ptolemy arrested in 312 BCE, with legends in both the Cypriot syllabary and Greek letters. They were minted within a few years of the city's destruction.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.n: The Sasmas coin with Phrixos and the ram
finds.t: A silver issue of an early Marion king showing Phrixos riding the golden ram, the only appearance of that myth on Cypriot coinage. Why a north-western Cypriot king chose it is unexplained.
finds.w: British Museum, London; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: The ore body a few kilometres east of Polis, worked from antiquity and again industrially until 1979, which gave Marion its wealth and its reason to exist. Ancient galleries and slag heaps survive around the modern workings.

Princeton University's excavations from 1983 traced streets and houses of the kingdom's town beneath the later Arsinoe, including workshops and a paved square. It is the best-planned Cypriot Classical townscape yet exposed.

After Ptolemy I destroyed Marion in 312 BCE and moved its people to Paphos, Ptolemy II refounded the place as Arsinoe, one of the string of towns he named for Arsinoe II. The new name stuck for a thousand years, and Byzantine sources still use it.

finds.n: The Hellenistic and Roman town quarters
finds.t: Princeton University's excavations between 1983 and 2007 found streets, houses and workshops of the Hellenistic to Late Roman town under the modern streets of Polis. Digging a living town in small plots is slow, and the plan is still patchy.

The cemeteries that produced the famous Classical Attic pottery stayed in use for centuries afterwards, yielding mould-made bowls, glass and lamps of the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. These later graves attracted far less nineteenth-century looting than the painted vases did.
finds.w: Local Museum of Marion-Arsinoe, Polis Chrysochous

SETTLEMENTS.name: Soli
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Greek city-kingdom on Morphou bay, said, doubtfully, to have been renamed for the Athenian lawgiver Solon. It joined the revolt of 498 BCE and held out for five months. On the hill beside it stands Vouni, a palace of the Persian period that its excavator thought pro-Persian Marion built to watch Soli.

finds.t: A marble statue of the goddess, probably a Roman copy of a Hellenistic type, found by a farmer ploughing in 1902; it has become the island's emblem, appearing on its coins and stamps.
A theatre for about 3,500, rebuilt in 1962–64 after most of its stone had been carted off in the nineteenth century to build the harbour at Port Said.
Floors of an early Christian cathedral with a famous swan among geometric patterns.
A colonnaded market square with a monumental fountain, excavated by Université Laval in 1964–74 and in use until the seventh century.
Marble statues of Aphrodite, Isis and other gods from the hillside temples west of the theatre.

A sanctuary of Apollo on the coast west of the city, excavated by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition in 1929, with limestone and terracotta votaries running from the Archaic period into Roman times. Half the sculpture went to Stockholm under the division of finds.

Herodotus says Soli held out five months against the Persians, longer than any other Cypriot city, and fell only when they undermined the wall. Traces of the Archaic circuit survive on the acropolis above the theatre.

Issues with Apollo and Aphrodite struck by the last king of Soloi, who married Eirene, a daughter of Ptolemy I, and so outlasted every other Cypriot dynasty. He was still on his throne after 312 BCE, when the rest were gone.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.t: The kingdom's first appearance in history is as 'Erisu king of Sillu' on Esarhaddon's prism, among the ten Cypriot kings who sent building materials to Nineveh. The Greek story that Soli was renamed after Solon of Athens cannot be reconciled with a kingdom already there in the seventh century.
finds.w: Prism in the British Museum, London

finds.n: The inscription of the proconsul Paulus
finds.t: An inscription found at Soli in 1887 naming a proconsul called Paulus, long taken as the Sergius Paulus who heard Paul at Paphos in Acts 13. D. G. Hogarth dated it to the first century; Terence Mitford argued on epigraphic grounds that it is considerably later, and the identification remains open.

The Skouriotissa mines lay in Soli's hinterland, and Soli was one of three Cypriot cities still named as producing copper under Rome. The city's wealth and its position on Morphou bay both come from the ore behind it.

finds.p: 1st century CE by tradition; basilica 4th to 6th century
finds.t: Cypriot tradition makes Auxibios the first bishop of Soli, ordained in the generation of Barnabas and Mark, and the great basilica on the site is usually identified as his church. The tradition rests on a Life written centuries later and cannot be checked.

The great basilica on the terrace above the theatre is dedicated to Auxibios, whom tradition makes the first bishop of Soloi, baptised by Mark and ordained by Barnabas. In its first form it was among the largest churches on the island, five aisles wide with an atrium.

A reduced basilica built inside the walls of the first, reusing its columns and its apse. It is the clearest picture anywhere on Cyprus of a congregation shrinking before the raids ended the town altogether.
Greek texts worked into the mosaic floor asking for the salvation of the people who paid for each stretch, alongside the famous swan and the geometric carpets.
Soloi's bishop Evagrios was one of the four Cypriots at Ephesus in 431. When the town was abandoned the see moved inland to Morphou; refounded in 1973, its holder is still titled President of Soloi.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Lapithos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A settlement since the Early Bronze Age and a city-kingdom of the north coast said to have been founded by Spartans. Its Bronze Age and Iron Age cemeteries are among the richest on Cyprus, and it kept its royal line until Ptolemy deposed King Praxippos in 312 BCE. Two hoards of Byzantine silver, the Lambousa treasures, were found here in 1897 and 1902.

finds.n: Vrysi tou Barba Bronze Age cemetery
finds.t: Rock-cut chamber tombs with Red Polished pottery, bronze weapons and gold ornaments, dug by the Swedes in 1927 and the Penn Museum in 1931.
finds.w: Medelhavsmuseet, Stockholm; Cyprus Museum; Penn Museum, Philadelphia

finds.t: Chamber tombs with bronze vessels, iron weapons and fine painted pottery excavated by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition and the Penn Museum.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum; Medelhavsmuseet, Stockholm; Penn Museum

finds.n: Second Cyprus Treasure and the David Plates
finds.t: Nine silver plates telling the story of David, stamped in Constantinople under Heraclius, plus gold jewellery, found at Lambousa in 1902.
finds.w: Metropolitan Museum, New York (six plates); Cyprus Museum, Nicosia (three plates)

finds.t: Twenty-eight silver liturgical pieces, including 25 spoons and a censer, probably buried before the Arab raids; found in 1897.

One of the largest Early and Middle Bronze Age cemeteries on the island, whose settlement has never been found. Buxton dug 47 tombs for Oxford in 1913 and Menelaos Markides, the first curator of the Cyprus Museum, another eighteen in 1917.
finds.w: In situ, Lapithos; finds in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia and the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford

finds.t: The flat clay figures came to light here, cut from slabs up to 35 cm high and incised with faces, headdresses, necklaces, earrings and patterned clothes. Lapithos remains the main centre of the tradition.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Ashmolean Museum, Oxford; Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

finds.n: Gold jewellery and masses of copper
finds.t: The plank figures were laid in tombs alongside gold ornaments and large quantities of copper, at the moment when Cyprus was becoming the eastern Mediterranean's main source of the metal.

Jennifer Webb has reconstructed the 1913 and 1917 tomb groups from scattered records and museum stores, with metals analysis by Marcos Martinon-Torres. A hundred-year-old excavation has effectively been dug again on paper.

Silver with the head of Athena on both faces, one of the earliest coinages of the north coast. Lapethos struck under Greek, then Phoenician, then Greek names again, and the mint is the main record of who was in charge.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.t: Ba'alzakor, Sidqmilk and Barik Shamash struck coins with Phoenician legends, and the issue of Sidqmilk is the one Cypriot coin that names both the king and his kingdom. A Greek-founded city with Phoenician rulers is a reminder that the island's two cultures were not neatly divided by geography.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London

finds.t: Small bronzes inscribed in Greek letters, struck by the last king, whom Ptolemy I arrested in 312 BCE for dealing with Antigonus. The kingdom was abolished with him.

Dedications from the site in Phoenician and Greek, equating Melqart with Herakles and Anat with Athena, among the latest Phoenician inscriptions on Cyprus. They show the language surviving here long after Kition had gone over to Greek.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris

finds.t: Built on the ruins of a sixth-century church on the Lambousa headland and rebuilt so often that early Christian, Byzantine, Gothic and Frankish work all show in the same walls; it now has two domes and a Gothic narthex. It was the seat of the bishop of Lambousa, one of the fourteen sees, until 1222. Since 1974 it has stood inside a Turkish army camp and is closed.

The name means not made by human hands. The story is that the Virgin carried the icon across the sea from Asia Minor to save it from destruction. A second tradition, with nothing at all behind it, made the monastery the home of the shroud that went to Turin in 1452.

Tanks cut into the reef on the Lambousa shore for keeping fish alive until they were wanted, among the best-preserved sets of their kind in the eastern Mediterranean and still filling and emptying with the sea.

The monastery of the icon 'not made by hands' at Lambousa, a domed Byzantine church given a Gothic porch, refectory and vaulted ranges in the Lusignan and Venetian centuries; it stands inside a military zone and is effectively inaccessible.

Lapithos was one of the main centres making Cypriot sgraffito ware, lead-glazed bowls and jugs incised through a white slip with birds, fish, knights and dancing figures. It is the everyday art of the Lusignan kingdom and turns up on every medieval site on the island.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Medieval Museum, Limassol Castle

finds.t: The Lapithos springs drove a string of mills and watered terraced gardens; the casale was known for silk, lemons and its pottery, and its water made it one of the richest villages of the north coast.
The ancient city site became a monastic and quarry landscape, its cut blocks reused in the abbeys and castles of the coast; rock-cut fish tanks by the shore were still in use.

A monastery on the shore beside ancient Lambousa, with a domed church of Byzantine and Gothic phases, whose name means 'made without hands'. It stands inside a Turkish military area and has been inaccessible and largely unmaintained since 1974.

Lapithos was the island's best-known pottery town, turning out glazed and slip-decorated earthenware jugs, bowls and storage jars on the wheel; museum collections of Cypriot folk pottery are largely Lapithos work, and the craft died with the displacement of 1974.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum and Folk Art Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Springs on the Kyrenia range fed terraced gardens of lemons, mulberries for silk and vegetables, made the town unusually prosperous and gave it a reputation for water in a dry island; the channels and washing places survive in the lanes.

Lapithos's Greek Cypriot population, several thousand strong, fled or was expelled in 1974 and now lives scattered in the south; the town, renamed Lapta, was settled by Turkish Cypriots from the south and by families from Turkey and is today a tourist village. Both displacements are documented village by village in the PRIO displacement project.
finds.w: In situ, Lapta; PRIO Cyprus Displacement Centre

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kyrenia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A small ancient kingdom, first named among the city-kingdoms in the fourth century BCE, that grew into a walled Byzantine harbour town with a great castle rebuilt by Lusignans and Venetians. The castle houses the Kyrenia ship, one of the best-preserved ancient Greek merchant ships ever found.

finds.t: A 14-metre merchant ship, built in the later fourth century BCE and already old and much repaired when she sank. Found by the diver Andreas Cariolou in 1965 and excavated in 1967–69 with about 380 wine amphorae, most from Rhodes, more than 9,000 almonds and 29 millstones as ballast. More than half her hull survived.
A Byzantine fort against Arab raids, enlarged by John of Ibelin and turned into a gun fortress with round towers by Venice; it surrendered to the Ottomans in 1570 without a fight.

Kyrenia is not among the ten kings of Esarhaddon's prism and surfaces only in the late fourth century, when Diodorus has Ptolemy I remove its ruler along with Praxippos of Lapithos in 312 BCE. It may never have been more than a dependency of its larger neighbour.

The rock-cut and built moles under the modern quays enclose the same small basin the Iron Age town used, one of the few natural harbours on the north coast. The line of the ancient works can be seen from the castle wall in calm water.

finds.n: Cypro-Archaic and Classical tombs in the town
finds.t: Chamber tombs with painted pottery have been found in and around Kyrenia during building work, the main evidence that the site was occupied throughout the age of the kingdoms. There has been no systematic excavation of the ancient settlement.

The first fort on the rock was thrown up against the Arab raids. Stretches of its curtain and a horseshoe tower survive inside the later Lusignan and Venetian shells, and it was still the strongpoint of the north coast when Richard I's men took it in 1191.
A small domed church of the Byzantine town, swallowed by the Venetian north-west bastion and now standing in the castle courtyard with its columns reused around it.

While Richard chased Isaac Komnenos east, Guy de Lusignan took Kyrenia, where Isaac's wife and daughter were lodged. The daughter, whom the chroniclers call the Damsel of Cyprus, passed into Richard's household, and Isaac gave up the island soon after at Cape St Andreas.
finds.w: Recorded by Neophytos the Recluse and the Latin chroniclers

finds.t: The ship's hull is shown in a climate-controlled hall with the cargo she went down with: hundreds of amphorae, thousands of almonds, and the millstones that ballasted her. It is one of the few places in the world where a whole ancient merchant hull can be walked around.

A full-scale working copy built from the excavation drawings, which sailed from Piraeus to Cyprus in 1986 and later crossed to Japan and America to prove what the original could do. She now lies in the south of the island, on the far side of the line from the wreck she copies.

finds.n: Icon museum in the church of the Archangel Michael
finds.t: The old parish church on the bluff above the harbour now displays icons gathered from the churches of the Kyrenia district after 1974.

Venice buried John of Ibelin's square and horseshoe towers inside squat rounded bastions with walls thick enough to take cannon and gun ports at three levels, one of the first fully artillery-age reworkings of a crusader castle in the Levant. It surrendered to the Ottomans in 1570 without being fired on.
A small domed Byzantine church, once outside the walls, swallowed whole by the Venetian north-west bastion and now standing inside the fortress with reused Roman columns holding up its dome.

finds.n: Lusignan works of John of Ibelin
finds.t: A new entrance, square and horseshoe towers, archers' embrasures and the dungeons, built by the regent who made Kyrenia the crown's strongest harbour; the castle stood a siege in 1232 during the war between Frederick II's men and the Ibelins, and again in the 1460s.
The grave of the Ottoman commander who took the castle in 1570, in the courtyard; a rare case of the conqueror buried inside the prize.

A full-scale sailing reconstruction of the Kyrenia ship built by the Hellenic Institute for the Preservation of Nautical Tradition, which sailed to Greece, Cyprus, New York and Japan and settled long-running arguments about how such a hull handled.
finds.w: Thalassa Museum, Ayia Napa (verify current display)

finds.t: The oldest Ottoman building in the town, a small stone mosque with a squat minaret and a fountain, built for the garrison a decade after the conquest, just above the old harbour.

finds.n: The castle as a colonial prison
finds.t: The British used the Venetian fortress as a prison and, during the 1955 to 1959 emergency, as a detention centre for EOKA suspects; the cells and the exercise yards are shown to visitors alongside the medieval work.

Turkish forces came ashore on Five Mile Beach west of Kyrenia at dawn on 20 July 1974 and pushed inland to link with the Turkish Cypriot enclave in Nicosia. A monument and a museum now stand at the landing point, and the anniversary is a public holiday in the north.

finds.n: Bitter Lemons and the house at Bellapais
finds.t: Lawrence Durrell bought a house in Bellapais, taught in Nicosia and worked for the colonial information service, and wrote Bitter Lemons about watching the island slide into the emergency; the book shaped how a generation of British readers understood Cyprus, and the house is still pointed out.

finds.n: The harbour and the tourist town
finds.t: The horseshoe harbour with its carob warehouses converted to restaurants was the postcard image of Cyprus before 1974 and is now the tourist centre of the north, ringed by hotels and casinos serving visitors from Turkey.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ledra, later Nicosia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A minor Iron Age kingdom called Ledra, listed on Esarhaddon's prism in 673 BCE, then a village and a bishopric, Nicosia became the capital when the Arab raids drove life inland. Lusignan kings built its Gothic cathedral and palaces, Venice ringed it with eleven bastions, and it has been the seat of every government since.

finds.t: A near-circle of ramparts about 5 km round, with eleven heart-shaped bastions and three gates, designed by Giulio Savorgnan and Francesco Barbaro. Still unfinished when the Ottomans stormed the Podocattaro bastion on 9 September 1570, and still complete today.
The coronation church of the Lusignan kings, in French Gothic style, where the Templars were tried in 1310. A mosque since 1570, named Selimiye in 1954.
The grandest of the three Venetian gates, a vaulted passage through the Caraffa bastion modelled on Sanmicheli's gate at Candia; now a cultural centre.
One of the first Ottoman buildings on the island and its largest caravanserai, 68 rooms around a courtyard with a small mosque.
The national archaeological museum, holding most of the finds named in this atlas; present building 1924.

The only ruler of Ledra known by name, listed on Esarhaddon's prism as Unasagusu among the ten kings of Iadnana who sent tribute to Nineveh. After that the kingdom vanishes from the record, absorbed by stronger neighbours.
finds.w: Prism in the British Museum, London

finds.t: Nobody knows where the Iron Age town stood. It is assumed to lie under the walled city or on the banks of the Pedieos, and only chance finds during building work ever touch it.

finds.n: Cypro-Archaic and Classical tombs under the modern city
finds.t: Rock-cut chamber tombs with painted pottery turn up regularly in rescue excavations across Nicosia and its suburbs. They are the strongest argument that a substantial settlement of the kingdoms' age lies beneath the capital.

Nicosia was a minor bishopric called Ledra until the coast became dangerous. The governor of the new theme settled inland after 965, and the island's capital has sat ten miles from the sea ever since, which is why Cyprus is the one Mediterranean country whose capital has no harbour.

The Archbishop Makarios III Foundation's gallery beside the archbishopric holds the largest icon collection in Cyprus, running from the ninth century onwards, together with the recovered fragments of the Kanakaria mosaic and the icons brought back from the Netherlands and Athens.

finds.p: Byzantine core, rebuilt from the 14th century
finds.t: A tangle of six building phases next to Selimiye that began as a small Byzantine church, grew into the Orthodox metropolitan cathedral of Nicosia under Frankish rule, and ended as an Ottoman cloth market. Restored between 2004 and 2009, it is now a concert hall.

finds.n: The medieval walls and the diverted river
finds.t: The Lusignan circuit was far larger and looser than the Venetian one. In 1567 Venice pulled it down along with the royal palace and a great many churches and monasteries, and turned the Pedieos river out of the city, in order to fit the town inside eleven bastions it could actually hold.

The oldest church still in use inside the walls, said to have been founded by Helena Palaiologina, the Greek queen of Cyprus, and until 1974 the home of a celebrated icon collection now in the Byzantine Museum.

The church beside the cathedral, identified by T. C. Papacostas as the site of the first Saint Sophia and proposed by Camille Enlart as a Latin church of Saint Nicholas served by English followers of Thomas Becket, a reading not universally accepted. Under Venice it was the seat of the Orthodox metropolitan as Panagia Hodegetria; the Ottomans turned it into the covered market that gave it its present name. Restored between 2004 and 2009.

To build the new walls Venice pulled down the Lusignan fortifications and, inside and outside the new line, houses, palaces, churches and monasteries of both rites, including the royal palace, partly for a clear field of fire and partly for cut stone. The Pedieos was diverted out of the city into the new moat in the same year. Nicosia lost most of its medieval fabric to the defence that then failed.

finds.n: Eleven bastions named for eleven families
finds.t: Pentagonal bastions with rounded orillons, on the model of Palmanova, each named for an Italian noble house of the city that paid towards it: Caraffa, Podocattaro, Constanza, D'Avila, Tripoli, Roccas, Mula, Quirini, Barbaro, Loredan and Flatro. The upper half of the curtain was left unfaced so it would absorb shot, and the gates were tucked beside the bastions.

finds.n: The storming of the Podocattaro bastion
finds.t: The walls were still unfinished, without piazze basse, cavaliers or outworks, and the curtains were low. After seven weeks the Ottomans broke in on the fourth assault; contemporaries put the dead at some twenty thousand, and the luogotenente Nicolo Dandolo was killed. Kyrenia surrendered days later without a fight.

finds.n: Omeriye Mosque, the Augustinian church of Saint Mary
finds.t: One of the few Latin churches to survive the 1567 clearances, converted to a mosque after 1571 on the belief that the caliph Umar had prayed on the spot; medieval Frankish tombstones are reused in its floor.

A grey granite column brought from the ruins of Salamis and raised in the square outside the governor's palace under the Lion of Saint Mark. Thrown down after 1570 and re-erected by the British in 1915, now carrying a globe instead of the lion.

The Augustinian church of Saint Mary, wrecked in the siege, was converted by Lala Mustafa Pasha in 1571 in the belief that the Caliph Omar had rested on the spot; Lusignan tomb slabs are reused in its floor. The hamam of the same complex was restored in 2002 to 2004 under the Nicosia Master Plan, still works as a bath house, and won the top Europa Nostra conservation prize in 2006.

The sandstone mansion of the dragoman, the Greek interpreter and tax intermediary who was the richest and most hated man on the island, built round a courtyard with its own three-room hamam. Kornesios was executed at Constantinople in 1809. Saved from demolition in the 1950s, opened as a museum in 1960 and given a Europa Nostra award in 1988, it is the best surviving picture of how power actually worked in late Ottoman Cyprus.

The Ottoman authorities gave a ruined Byzantine and Gothic church beside Selimiye to the Haramayn foundation in 1573 for use as a covered cloth market; it fell out of use when the municipal covered market, the Bandabuliya, opened in 1932 next door. The two buildings, forty metres and 360 years apart, are the Ottoman and the colonial versions of the same function.

finds.n: Faneromeni church and the Marble Mausoleum
finds.t: The largest church of the walled city, rebuilt in 1872 on the site of an older convent, with a marble mausoleum to its east holding the relics of Archbishop Kyprianos, the three bishops and the clergy executed by the Ottoman authorities on 9 July 1821. Faneromeni School opposite is one of the oldest on the island.

Founded by Archbishop Kyprianos as the Hellenic School, on a site that had held a school since 1753, and reorganised as the Pancyprian Gymnasium in 1893; the present neoclassical building followed a fire in 1920. Its pupils include Makarios III, Glafcos Clerides, Tassos Papadopoulos, Georgios Grivas and the Nobel economist Christopher Pissarides, and its classrooms were a nursery of both enosis and the 1931 and 1955 movements.

finds.n: Government House, now the Presidential Palace
finds.t: The first Government House was a prefabricated building shipped from England in 1878, intended for Ceylon and carried up from the coast by camel. A crowd of about 5,000 burned it on 21 October 1931 and the cost was charged back to the population; Maurice Webb designed the sandstone replacement, built between 1932 and 1937 for £70,000. It became the Presidential Palace in 1960, was burned again in the coup of July 1974 and was rebuilt in 1977 with Greek money.

Thirteen graves in the yard of the Central Prison holding the men the British hanged during the emergency, among them Michalakis Karaolis and Andreas Demetriou on 10 May 1956 and the eighteen-year-old Evagoras Pallikaridis on 14 March 1957, together with fighters killed in action including Markos Drakos, Grigoris Afxentiou, Stylianos Lenas and Kyriakos Matsis. The gallows and cells are shown as a national monument.

finds.n: The Green Line through the city
finds.t: Major-General Peter Young drew the ceasefire line across Nicosia with a green chinagraph pencil on a map on 30 December 1963; the buffer zone it became runs 180 km across the island and covers 346 square kilometres, from twenty metres wide in the old city to seven kilometres in the plain. Nicosia has been the last divided capital in Europe since 1974. The Ledra Palace hotel, opened in 1949 and shell-scarred in 1974, has served as the United Nations barracks, and the crossing beside it was the first to open, in April 2003, followed by the pedestrian crossing on Ledra Street in the old city in 2008.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Famagusta
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Founded as Arsinoe by the Ptolemies around 274 BCE, a fishing town that inherited the people of Salamis after the Arab raids, Famagusta exploded into one of the richest cities in Christendom after Acre fell in 1291. Lusignan kings were crowned Kings of Jerusalem in its cathedral. Genoa held it for ninety years, Venice fortified it, and the Ottoman siege of 1571 left it a ghost town within its walls.

finds.t: A Rayonnant Gothic cathedral often compared to Reims, where the Lusignans took the crown of Jerusalem until 1372. A mosque since 1571, named Lala Mustafa Pasha in 1954.
About 3 km of ramparts up to 18 m high and 9 m thick, with fourteen bastions; the Martinengo bastion by Sanmicheli (1550–62) was among the most advanced fortifications of its day.
A Lusignan castle refaced by Venice under Captain Nicolò Foscarini, later linked to Shakespeare's 'seaport in Cyprus' by nineteenth-century visitors.
Venetian harbour gate with a marble Lion of St Mark and an iron portcullis.

finds.n: Church of St George of the Greeks
finds.t: The Orthodox cathedral of Famagusta, a Gothic-Byzantine hybrid whose apse still carries wall paintings and cannonball scars from 1571; one of more than a dozen ruined churches within the walls.
The Lusignan royal palace refronted by Venice with columns from Salamis; later an Ottoman prison where the poet Namık Kemal was held.

Ptolemy II founded a town called Arsinoe here, one of several he named for his sister and wife Arsinoe II, and it lived quietly in the shadow of Salamis for nine hundred years. Practically none of it has been excavated: it lies under the medieval walled city, and Famagusta's ancient phase is known almost entirely from texts.

finds.n: Ancient stone in the medieval city
finds.t: Granite and marble columns and cut blocks from Salamis and from Arsinoe itself were carried into Famagusta's churches, palace and walls. The Venetian Palace front stands on columns from Salamis, so the ancient city is visible in the medieval one.

The reef-sheltered anchorage that made Arsinoe worth founding is the same basin that made Famagusta the richest port in Christendom after 1291 and is still the harbour today. Salamis, 6 km north, lost its harbour to silt; this one never silted.

Ptolemaic Arsinoe was a fishing village with a good roadstead until Constantia was given up. Its Greek name means hidden in the sand, and it took in the refugees from up the coast and, in time, their bishop.

Famagusta was quarried out of Constantia. Granite columns carted down from Salamis stand in the Venetian palace, and reused ancient blocks turn up throughout the walls and the churches, which is why the ruins of Salamis are so much barer than their size suggests.

The church of the Syrian and Nestorian merchants, built by the brothers Francis and Nicholas Lakhas, whose walls carry paintings and layers of graffiti in Greek, Syriac and Armenian left by pilgrims and prisoners. The nickname means George the exiler, from a story that dust from the floor would drive an enemy off the island within a year.
A tiny single-aisled domed church in the ruined Greek quarter, one of the few buildings inside the walls built to a Byzantine rather than a Gothic plan, with fragments of painting still on the vault.

finds.n: The twin churches of the military orders
finds.t: Two small churches side by side near the palace, built for the Templars and the Hospitallers and joined by a common wall. Both have been restored and serve now as a theatre and a gallery.

finds.n: Church of Saints Peter and Paul
finds.t: One of the largest Gothic churches in the city, said to have been paid for out of a third of the profit of a single trading voyage to Syria by the Famagusta merchant Simone Nostrano. Massive flying buttresses were added after the sixteenth-century earthquakes. A mosque from 1571 as Sinan Pasha, a British grain and potato store, then a library and exhibition hall.

finds.n: Nestorian church of Saint George the Exiler
finds.t: Built by the Lakhas brothers, Syriac Christian merchants rich enough to found their own cathedral, with three apses, frescoes of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries and Syriac inscriptions. Reduced to a camel stable after 1571 and opened once a year for the saint's feast; a cultural centre of the Eastern Mediterranean University since 1989.

A small fortress-like church raised by Armenian refugees from Cilicia in Armenian style but Cypriot masonry, part of a monastic and teaching centre. Unused after 1571, leased back to the Armenian community in 1936 and reconsecrated in 1945; restored with the Carmelite church by the UNDP and handed over on 26 May 2018.

finds.n: Carmelite church and the tomb of Peter Thomas
finds.t: The church of the Carmelite friars, opposite the Armenian church, where Peter Thomas was buried. A Carmelite from Perigord, papal legate and Latin Patriarch of Constantinople, he pressed the Greeks hard towards Latin obedience, sailed on Peter I's Alexandria crusade in 1365 and died of his wounds at Famagusta in January 1366; he was canonised in 1628.

finds.n: Twin churches of the military orders
finds.t: Two small churches built shoulder to shoulder, traditionally the Templars' and the Hospitallers'; the Templar house and its Cypriot lands passed to the Hospitallers after the order was suppressed in 1312. Later used as a store, a theatre and an art gallery. The attribution is traditional rather than documented.

finds.n: The Ravelin, the Arsenal bastion and the siege of 1570 to 1571
finds.t: The outworks where the ten and a half month siege was decided: the Ottomans filled the ditch to the top of the walls, mined the Ravelin and stormed the Arsenal bastion, losing tens of thousands of men, while the huge Martinengo bastion was never even attacked. The Turkish name of the Ravelin, Akkule or White Gate, records the white flag raised there on 1 August 1571.

Famagusta's captain was mutilated at the surrender ceremony on 5 August 1571 and flayed alive in the square on 17 August; his skin was stuffed with straw and paraded. A young Venetian seaman, Girolamo Polidori, stole it from the arsenal at Constantinople in 1580 and brought it home, and it lies in an urn under Bragadin's monument in Venice.
finds.w: Basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, Venice

finds.t: After the siege the Ottoman authorities settled the walled city with Muslims and largely excluded Orthodox Cypriots from living inside it, which is why the Greek town grew as Varosha outside the gates. Travellers through the eighteenth century describe a garrison town of a few hundred people among two dozen ruined churches.

Cafer Pasha brought water into the walled city and built a domed bath house and a street fountain, the main Ottoman civic works in Famagusta; the fountain still stands near the cathedral square and the bath survives in part.

finds.n: Famagusta harbour and the railway terminus
finds.t: The British dredged and walled the silted harbour and made it the colony's main port, with the Cyprus Government Railway running from the quay to Nicosia from 21 October 1905. Locomotive No. 1 is preserved at the station.

The Republic declared Famagusta a closed port after 1974, so the busiest harbour on the island trades only with Turkey; the resulting legal argument about direct trade with the north has run through the European courts for decades.

The citadel was consolidated and reopened by the bicommunal Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage with United Nations and European Union funding, the most visible product of the one negotiating track that has kept working through every political freeze.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Limassol
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Neapolis, later Nemesos and Lemesos, grew up between Amathus and Kourion and took over as they declined; a bishop of the town sat at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Richard the Lionheart landed here in 1191, married Berengaria of Navarre, by tradition in a chapel on the site of the later castle, and destroyed Amathus. The Knights Templar and Hospitallers made the surrounding plain their estate, and it is the home of Commandaria, often called the world's oldest named wine still made.

finds.t: A fort built by Guy de Lusignan on a Byzantine site, demolished by Venice in 1567–68 and rebuilt as an Ottoman fort; a prison until 1950 and the Cyprus Medieval Museum since 1987.
Remains of a basilica and later Byzantine buildings found beneath the castle, evidence of the town before the Lusignans.

Almost nothing of Limassol's Late Roman and Byzantine beginnings has been excavated, because the ancient settlement lies directly under the modern city centre. What is known comes from rescue work on building plots, and there is no excavated urban core to visit.
finds.w: Beneath the old town of Limassol

finds.n: The inheritance of Amathus and Kourion
finds.t: Both of the district's ancient cities failed within a couple of generations, Kourion after the earthquakes and Amathus after the Arab raids, and their people moved to the small town between them. Limassol's rise is not a founding but a consolidation.
The district's collection, running from the Neolithic to the Roman period, and the place where much of the material from Amathus, Kourion and the Vasilikos valley sites is kept.

A bishop from the district sat at the Council of Chalcedon in 451. When Amathus and Kourion were abandoned after the Arab raids their sees were folded into that of the new town between them, and Limassol's bishops long carried Amathus and Kourion in their titles.

A monastery church on a knoll above the Kouris a short way north of Limassol, whose wall paintings were cleaned and published by Dumbarton Oaks in the 1970s and run in layers from the twelfth century to the sixteenth. The house flourished in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, declined in the eighteenth and ended as a parish church.

Cypriot tradition says three hundred hermits crossed from Palestine as the crusader states fell and scattered into caves across the island. A dozen villages and the monastery of Ayios Georgios Alamanos east of Limassol carry their names. Nothing outside the tradition attests any of them.
finds.w: Local cults across the Limassol district

finds.t: Two of Richard's ships were wrecked off Cyprus and a third, carrying his sister Joan and his betrothed Berengaria, lay at anchor off Limassol for a week rather than land within Isaac's reach. Richard arrived on 8 May, went ashore in a fury and had the island inside a month.

Richard I married Berengaria of Navarre at Limassol on 12 May 1191 and had her crowned Queen of England in the same ceremony, by tradition in a chapel where the castle now stands. She saw little or nothing of England in his lifetime, and the wedding took place only because a storm had driven her ship, and Richard's sister Joan, onto a Cypriot shore held by Isaac Komnenos.
finds.w: Tradition places it beneath Limassol Castle

finds.t: Richard sold Cyprus to the Templars for 100,000 bezants; after a revolt against them at Nicosia in 1192 they gave it back, and Richard passed the purchase on to Guy de Lusignan, the ousted King of Jerusalem. The last crusader kingdom began as a property transaction.
Frankish and Venetian tombstones, arms, coins, glazed pottery and architectural fragments gathered from across the island, in the vaults of the castle that was a prison until 1950.

finds.n: Commandaria and the Battle of the Wines
finds.t: The sweet wine of the Hospitallers' Grand Commandery above Limassol, named for the commandery itself. Henri d'Andeli's poem La Bataille des Vins, written about 1224, has the King of France judge the wines of Christendom and give the crown to the wine of Cyprus. A poem is not a tasting note, but Cypriot wine was genuinely a luxury export to western courts.
finds.w: Documentary; the wine still made in fourteen villages above Limassol

finds.n: The raid of 1539 and the demolition of the castle
finds.t: An Ottoman fleet burned Limassol in 1539. Venice, judging that a fort it could not hold would only serve the enemy, demolished the castle in 1567 to 1568; the Ottomans rebuilt it as a squat gun platform around 1590.

finds.n: The Grand Mosque and the Turkish quarter
finds.t: Djami Kebir, the Great Mosque, stands with its bath house a few steps from the castle in what was the Turkish Cypriot quarter of the old town; the quarter emptied in 1975 and its lanes are now bars and workshops. Limassol was a town where the two communities lived most closely mixed.

Stone warehouses on the shore beside the castle where carob pods, the black gold of Cyprus, were stored and shipped; the complex is now a museum, cinema and restaurant quarter. Carobs were among the colony's top three exports for decades.

Limassol became the island's wine town: ETKO dates its founding to 1844 and KEO was set up in 1927, with SODAP and LOEL following, all drawing grapes from the Troodos foothills. The Limassol Wine Festival has run since 1961.

A deep-water harbour finished just before the war, which then had to carry almost all the Republic's trade after Famagusta was lost; it remains the island's main port and a Mediterranean transhipment stop.

Limassol took the largest share of the displaced, and whole quarters of the eastern suburbs began as government refugee estates of identical low houses; the city's population roughly doubled in a decade and it overtook Famagusta as the island's commercial capital.

A marina and residential development beside the old town opened in 2014, followed by a line of high-rise towers along the seafront built partly on investment-for-citizenship money; the most conspicuous physical result of the post-2013 recovery.

SETTLEMENTS.name: St Hilarion Castle
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A tenth-century monastery that the Byzantines fortified in the eleventh century against Arab raiders, one of three castles guarding the northern range with Buffavento and Kantara. It commands the Kyrenia-Nicosia pass and was the prize of the 1228–1232 war between Frederick II's men and the Ibelins. The Lusignans turned the upper ward into a summer palace; Venice, trusting only the towns, stripped it after 1489.

finds.t: Gothic window of the royal apartments in the upper ward, looking over the north coast.
The monastery church in the lower ward, the castle's oldest part.

The Greeks called the twin-peaked ridge Didymos, the twins. The Franks heard it as Dieu d'Amour, the god of love, and that is the name the castle carries through the chronicles of the war of 1229 to 1232.

A ruined and partly restored church with a wide dome on eight pillars stands in the castle, one of only three buildings of the type known on Cyprus; the others are Antiphonitis and the lost church of St John Chrysostom at Koutsovendis.
St Hilarion, Buffavento and Kantara are spaced so that a fire lit on one summit can be seen from the next, a warning system for a coast that expected raiders from the sea.
finds.w: In situ across the Kyrenia range

finds.t: The mountain castles held the usurper's money and his household while he manoeuvred in the plain. They were handed over after he surrendered, and the plate and coin that came down from them helped pay for Richard's crusade.

The Ibelins held the castle for the boy king Henry I against Frederick II's five bailiffs. After the imperial defeat at Agridi in 1232 the garrison here gave in, which ended the war and settled Cyprus on the Lusignans.
Rock-cut tanks and a vaulted cistern that caught the winter rain. Without them the waterless summit could not have held a garrison for a single summer.
The upper ward that Hugh IV and Peter I used as a summer palace, with a hall, kitchens and cisterns cut into the crag at about 700 m; the court came up here to escape the heat of Nicosia and to hunt.

The tower from which, the chronicler Leontios Machairas relates, John of Antioch had his Bulgarian bodyguard thrown one by one over the cliff after being persuaded they meant to betray him; a story that captures how the castle was used in the dynasty's civil wars.

St Hilarion was the prize in the fighting between Emperor Frederick II's partisans and the Ibelin regents, and the child king Henry I was held here; the middle ward's barbican and gate belong to this phase.

Venice trusted only the walled towns, and had the mountain castles stripped of anything useful so that they could not shelter a rebel or a raider. The three castles of the range have been ruins ever since.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Buffavento Castle
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The highest of the three mountain castles at about 950 m, 'defier of the winds', a late eleventh-century Byzantine watchtower linking St Hilarion and Kantara by signal fire and guarding the pass from Kythrea to the coast. Under the Lusignans it served chiefly as a prison; Venice abandoned it.

finds.t: Vaulted rooms and pointed-arch towers cut to the rock.
Rainwater tanks that made the summit habitable for a garrison.

finds.n: Monastery of St John Chrysostom, Koutsovendis
finds.t: At the foot of the mountain below the castle stands the monastery founded about 1090 by the monk George, later bishop of Paphos. Its chapel of the Holy Trinity keeps wall paintings of about 1100 made for Eumathios Philokales, the imperial governor of the island, among the earliest closely dated Byzantine paintings on Cyprus. The main church was rebuilt at the end of the nineteenth century, and the site now lies inside a military zone.

The future recluse of Paphos fled an arranged marriage to Koutsovendis, was tonsured there in 1152, learned to read and write and served as assistant sacristan. His abbot refused to let him go off and be a hermit on the ground that he was too young.

finds.n: A watch post, not a fortress
finds.t: The summit at about 950 m held a signal station rather than a garrison town: Byzantine masonry survives in the lower ward, and the six rock-cut cisterns were what made the place habitable at all.
A local story makes the highest chamber the cell of a leper princess called Regina, walled up by her father. The name is on the signs at the top of the path and there is nothing whatever behind it.

Machairas records that Sir John Visconti, the knight who told Peter I of Queen Eleanor's infidelity while the king was abroad, was walled up at Buffavento and starved to death. The castle's chief Lusignan use was as a place to make people disappear.
At about 950 m Buffavento can see both St Hilarion to the west and Kantara to the east, which is the point of it; the three castles worked as one warning system along the range.
A Templar was held here during the arrest of the order in Cyprus, two years before the trials at Nicosia.
The Franks also called it the Castle of the Lion, and Cypriot folklore attached to it a queen with leprosy cured by the mountain's water; the name and the tale are both medieval, the cure is not.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kantara Castle
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The easternmost of the three mountain castles, 600 m above the Karpas, probably Byzantine of the late tenth or eleventh century. Isaac Komnenos fled here in 1191; it withstood the Ibelin siege of 1229 and the Genoese in 1373. Venice declared it obsolete in 1519 and had dismantled it by 1560.

finds.t: Lusignan entrance works with arrow slits.
Six rock-cut cisterns supplying the hilltop.

Beaten by Richard at Tremetousia, Isaac Komnenos rode for the Karpas and held out from Kantara before surrendering at Cape St Andreas. The Hospitallers jailed him at Margat in chains that the chroniclers insist were silver, because Richard had promised not to put him in irons.

Thirteen Orthodox monks from a house near the castle refused the Latin use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist, were tried for heresy, held for three years and burned in 1231. It is the sharpest single episode in the Latin church's dealings with the Cypriot Orthodox, and the Church of Cyprus still keeps them as martyrs.
finds.w: Documentary; commemorated by the Church of Cyprus

finds.t: The oldest masonry belongs to the chain of watch posts built after the reconquest of 965, when Byzantium had to defend a coast it had just recovered. A beacon here could be read from Buffavento.
The garrison held out against the Ibelins in 1229 and turned back the Genoese in 1373, which is the best evidence for how strong a small mountain castle could be before gunpowder.
Barrel-vaulted chambers and six rock-cut cisterns strung along the ridge at about 600 m, enough to keep a small garrison through a siege.
Kantara held out when Genoa overran the island and took Famagusta; the eastern castle covered the Karpas and the road to the Genoese-held port.
Venice declared the castle obsolete in 1519 and had it dismantled by 1560; what stands is what was not worth the labour of pulling down.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kolossi Castle
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The Grand Commandery of the Knights of St John, granted by Hugh I around 1210 and, after Acre fell in 1291, the order's headquarters until it moved to Rhodes. The Templars held it in 1306–1313. The square keep of 1454 stands beside a sugar refinery and aqueduct, and the knights' estates gave their name to Commandaria, the sweet wine still made in the villages above.

finds.t: A 21-metre three-storey Gothic tower with the commander's arms and a fresco of the Crucifixion.
Vaulted refinery where cane from the plain was boiled and cast, fed by a stone aqueduct from the Kouris river; sugar was one of the island's chief exports.

Excavation of the Hospitallers' sugar works, prompted by the Kouklia-Stavros project, exposed the mill room, furnaces and boiling floor and quantities of conical sugar moulds and syrup jars. Kolossi, Kouklia and Episkopi together make Cyprus the best-documented sugar landscape of the medieval Mediterranean.
finds.w: In situ, Kolossi; finds in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.n: Arms of Louis de Magnac and Jacques de Milly
finds.t: Carved coats of arms on the keep, including those of the commander who built it and of the Grand Master of Rhodes, dating the tower to the year and naming the order that owned the plain.
A wall painting on the first floor of the keep, all that is left of the decoration of a knight's residence rather than a church.
Mamluk raiders burned the commandery in the campaign that ended with King Janus captured at Khirokitia; the keep of 1454 is a replacement for what they destroyed.

After Acre fell the Hospitallers ran their order's western headquarters from here until they took Rhodes, and the commandery held some forty villages of the Kouris plain; the name Commandaria comes from this estate.

finds.n: The estate as an Ottoman chiftlik
finds.t: After 1570 the commandery's lands passed into Ottoman hands as a farm estate whose revenues went to state and pious foundations, and the keep became a store and a farmhouse. The sugar industry it had been built for was already dead, undercut by Atlantic and Madeiran sugar.

finds.n: The labour of the sugar works
finds.t: The cane fields and refinery were worked by a mixed force of Cypriot serfs, Syrian and Arab labourers and slaves, and the mill was driven by water brought by the aqueduct; the documentary record of this workforce is one of the fuller pictures of medieval Mediterranean plantation labour.

The Department of Antiquities took the castle in hand in the colonial period, cleared and consolidated the keep and the mill and opened them; the flat roof and its view over the Akrotiri plain date from that work.

The sweet wine named for the knights' commandery is now a protected designation of origin made in fourteen named villages above Limassol from sun-dried xynisteri and mavro grapes; the claim that it is the oldest named wine still in production rests on the medieval documents rather than on continuity of practice.

The village sits on the edge of the Akrotiri Sovereign Base Area, and part of its land was used to house Greek Cypriots displaced in 1974, so a Hospitaller estate now shares its fields with British sovereign territory and a refugee estate.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kykkos Monastery
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Founded around 1100 under Emperor Alexios I Komnenos around an icon of the Virgin attributed to St Luke, Kykkos is the richest and most famous monastery in Cyprus. Burned and rebuilt several times, its present church dates from 1745. Makarios III began as a novice here in 1926 and is buried at Throni nearby.

finds.t: Silver-covered icon of the Virgin, never shown uncovered.
Treasury of icons, manuscripts and vestments.

Kykkos answered to Constantinople, not to the local bishop, and that status carried it through the abolition of the Greek archbishopric in 1260 and the Latin centuries with its lands and its abbot intact.

The monastery burned repeatedly, which is why nothing medieval stands above ground and the present church dates from 1745; the icon was carried out each time, and each rebuilding was paid for by appeals across the Orthodox world.

Manuscripts, printed books, chrysobulls and firmans documenting the monastery's estates and its dealings with emperors, sultans and Latin archbishops; among the richest ecclesiastical archives in Cyprus.
Kykkos took on the conservation of the ruined Venetian-period monastery on the Xeros, work that won a Europa Nostra award in 1997; the wealthiest house in Cyprus still acts as patron to the poorest.

finds.n: Throni and the tomb of Makarios III
finds.t: The first president of the Republic, who began here as a novice in 1926, was buried on 3 August 1977 on the hilltop of Throni above the monastery at his own wish; a shrine to the Virgin stands beside the grave and the site draws pilgrims and tourists in equal numbers.

Kykkos was caught in the reprisals of 1821: its abbot was among those put to death and the monastery's property was seized, a reminder that the richest Orthodox house on the island held its wealth entirely at the sultan's pleasure.

Kykkos ran dependencies, farms and urban properties across Cyprus and beyond, and the income paid for village schools, scholarships and the printing of books; monastic estates were the main Greek Cypriot institution that survived the Ottoman centuries intact.

The Kykkos and Machairas forests sheltered EOKA groups and their caches, and the monastery is widely held to have helped them; British forces mounted repeated searches in the area. The monastery museum and the nearby memorials present the campaign from the Greek Cypriot side.

In drought the icon of the Panagia Kykkotissa was carried out of the mountains in procession to the parched villages, a practice recorded from the Ottoman centuries into living memory, and one of the clearest links between the island's religion and its water.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Troodos painted churches
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Ten villages across the Troodos range
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Ten small Byzantine and post-Byzantine churches under steep timber roofs, inscribed by UNESCO in 1985 for five centuries of wall painting: Ayios Nikolaos tis Stegis at Kakopetria, Asinou (1105/06), Panagia tou Araka at Lagoudera (1192), Ayios Ioannis Lampadistis, Moutoullas (1280), Pelendri, Platanistasa, Pedoulas (1474), Galata (1502) and Palaichori.

finds.t: Komnenian and Palaiologan cycles donated by Nikephoros Ischyrios.
The most complete late Komnenian painted programme in Cyprus.
A domed church near Kakopetria with a second pitched roof against the snow and layers of painting across six centuries.

Painted for Dimitre de Coron, a Greek in Venetian service, in the fully Italo-Byzantine manner: Renaissance architecture in the backgrounds, Latin as well as Greek inscriptions, and a Crucifixion with a kneeling donor.
