The clearest single statement of what two centuries of Latin rule did to Cypriot painting.

Painted for the priest Basil Chamados by an artist who signs himself Minas of Myrianthousa; a small barn-roofed church whose donor panel shows the priest, his wife and their children in fifteenth-century dress.

A church of the manor of Pelendri, held by John of Lusignan, son of Hugh IV, with a Tree of Jesse in the vault and painting of high Palaiologan quality; proof that the court itself commissioned Greek painters.

The earliest dated timber-roofed church of the Troodos type, painted for Ioannis Moutoullas and his wife Irene, whose portraits and inscription fix the year; the painting is provincial, forceful and untouched by Gothic taste.

finds.n: Latin chapel of Ayios Ioannis Lampadistis
finds.t: A chapel added to the Kalopanagiotis monastery holding the fullest Akathist cycle in Cyprus, painted in a frankly Italianate style with Renaissance settings; Greek subject, Italian handling, Latin patron.
Signed by Philippos Goul the year after he finished Stavros tou Ayiasmati, and the second half of the only securely identified painter's career in late medieval Cyprus.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayios Tychonas-Klimonas
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A village more than twenty centuries older than Khirokitia. Hunter-cultivators grew emmer wheat brought from the mainland, kept dogs, hunted the island's introduced wild boar, and gathered in a sunken circular communal building about ten metres across, the earliest of its kind found on an island. Excavated by a French-Cypriot team from 2009.

finds.t: A semi-subterranean round structure about 10 m in diameter, comparable to the communal buildings of the earliest Levantine villages.
Projectile points, sickle elements and charred emmer showing that cultivation had already reached the island.

finds.n: Wild boar bones and Sus scrofa circeus
finds.t: Over five hundred specimens, some 97 per cent of the animal remains from the village. Geometric morphometrics on teeth and heel bones, published in 2021, showed these boar were an island subspecies descended from animals brought from the northern Levant, and named it Sus scrofa circeus after the goddess who turned Odysseus's crew into pigs. They were 10 to 16 per cent smaller than their mainland ancestors, and the pigs of later Shillourokambos are their domesticated descendants: Cyprus domesticated its own pigs rather than importing them.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities; study collections, Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris

finds.t: The earliest dogs on Cyprus, shipped over with the first cultivators. Dogs and cereals arrived together, before any of the herd animals, which suggests the first colonists came as hunters who farmed rather than as herders.

The age and sex profile of the bones shows the hunters targeting females and their young. That is a pattern of management, not opportunism, and it is one of the reasons the Klimonas boar are read as a stocked and tended resource rather than simply wild game.
Three bladelets and one blade of Cappadocian obsidian, the sum of the village's imported stone. It is enough to prove the crossing was being made, and little enough to show it was not yet routine.

Besides the great communal building there were several small round houses and dedicated storage, so this was a real settlement with granaries and not a camp. The sea crossing that supplied it was 60 to 90 km of open water.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Parekklisha-Shillourokambos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: An early Neolithic village on a low plateau, excavated by Jean Guilaine's French mission from 1992 to 2004. Its early phases had post-built enclosures, deep wells and pens for cattle, with sheep, goat and pig arriving over time; about 300 blades of Anatolian obsidian show sea contact. Its most famous find is the burial of a man with a young cat beside him.

finds.t: A man over thirty buried with shells, a stone pendant, flints and ochre, and beside him an eight-month-old cat: the oldest evidence of cat taming.
About 300 imported Anatolian blades.

Deep shafts cut into the bedrock, dug from the earliest phase onwards and, with those at Kissonerga-Mylouthkia, among the oldest water wells known anywhere in the world. Cypriot wells span the second half of the ninth millennium to the middle of the seventh. Nothing comparable is known on the Levantine mainland until considerably later, so this looks like an island invention forced by island conditions.

Aurochs-sized cattle ferried across from the mainland and kept in post-built enclosures. Whether they arrived already domesticated or as managed wild animals is argued from morphology on one side and culling patterns on the other. What is certain is that cattle then died out on Cyprus during the eighth millennium and were not seen again for thousands of years, so the first herds could not sustain themselves.

Ninety per cent of the identified fish from Sector 1 are sea bass and large groupers weighing between four and seventeen kilograms. Fish that size are not caught from the beach, and the village sits several kilometres inland.

Small hollow cups of blue-green picrolite under 3 cm across, incised with vertical and horizontal hatching. Two near-identical pieces come from Akanthou on the north coast. Jean Guilaine and others have suggested they are models of boats, which would make them the earliest images of watercraft in the region; most specialists reserve judgement.

372 pieces of fossil and marine shell used as ornaments and tools, together with grooved stones carrying carved geometric motifs that may have served as net sinkers. The same engraved patterns turn up later at Khirokitia and Kholetria-Ortos, and in the Levant.

The projectile points of the early phases are straight out of the Levantine Pre-Pottery Neolithic B, and the first sickles were made of several small elements set in a haft. Around 7500 BCE the points vanish and the sickles become single robust blades, which is why the later Khirokitia-culture villages have no arrowheads at all: Cyprus had begun to go its own way.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kalavasos-Tenta
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A small Aceramic village on a low hill in the Vasilikos valley, dug by Ian Todd in 1976–84. Some forty round buildings of stone and mudbrick housed perhaps 150 people; around 7500 BCE the hill was ringed by a wall and ditch, and pillared round buildings on the summit anticipate those of Khirokitia. A conical shelter has protected the remains since 1995.

finds.t: Traces of at least two human figures with upraised arms, one in red and one in outline, on a wall of Structure 11: the earliest painting known from Cyprus.
About a thousand stone, bone and shell artefacts, some covered in ochre.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Larnaca District Museum

finds.n: The pillared buildings on the summit
finds.t: Three circular buildings with internal pillars, Structures 36, 17 and 14, each rebuilt on the ruins of the last on the western top of the hill. The form has its ancestors in the mainland Pre-Pottery Neolithic A, and only Tenta and Khirokitia have it on Cyprus. Whether they were the houses of important people or communal buildings for the village is unresolved.

finds.n: The wall and the rock-cut ditch
finds.t: In its fourth period the village ringed the hill with a substantial wall and an outer ditch cut into the havara, the soft local limestone. It was a large piece of communal labour and it is rare in Neolithic Cyprus, which is why Tenta keeps being described as fortified even though nobody can say against whom.

Fourteen graves holding at least eighteen people, adults, children and infants. Six were buried in pits under house floors, seven in pits outside the buildings and sometimes in rubbish layers, and grave goods are essentially absent. Against Khirokitia's 254 burials with their necklaces and querns, the contrast between two villages a few hours' walk apart is hard to explain.
finds.w: In situ; skeletal material with the Department of Antiquities

finds.t: Rings of white marble, a material not native to the island. Along with the obsidian and the carnelian at Khirokitia they show that the Late Aceramic Neolithic, usually painted as an inward-looking period, was still receiving things from across the sea.
finds.w: Larnaca District Archaeological Museum; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Including perforated dove and cone shells and the lips of two helmet shells, cut to be worn. The sea is three kilometres away down the Vasilikos valley.

Joanne Clarke and Alexander Wasse have argued that the pillared summit buildings belong to the same architectural tradition as Building 10 at Klimonas, and that Tenta's earliest phase, Period 5, may therefore reach back into the Initial Aceramic Neolithic rather than the Cypro-PPNB. That would make Tenta older than anyone had it, and older than the wall and ditch by well over a millennium. The case is not settled.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kissonerga-Mosphilia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The largest Chalcolithic settlement known in Cyprus, on the coastal plain just north of Lemba, excavated by Edgar Peltenburg in 1979–92. Around 3000 BCE a 'high sector' of imposing round buildings included the Red Building, the largest prehistoric building on the island. Later the nine-metre Pithos House held dozens of storage vessels, copper-working debris and a stamp seal before it burnt down. A roundhouse has been reconstructed on the site.

finds.t: A clay model of a round house, covered by two bowls and buried with about fifty deliberately broken objects, including stone and clay figurines of seated and birthing women.
Storage jars, copper slag and a stamp seal from the burnt building.
finds.w: Paphos District Museum; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: A round building of exceptional size in the settlement's high sector, with a red-painted floor, the largest prehistoric building known on Cyprus. Whether it was a chief's house, a meeting hall or a shrine is undecided.

The clay house model in the ceremonial deposit has a doorway, walls and an interior, and inside it lay a figurine of a woman giving birth. Diane Bolger read the whole assemblage as the equipment of a birth ritual, buried when its work was done.

finds.n: Two possible crucibles and copper ore
finds.t: Fragments identified as crucibles, with a few lumps of ore, in the latest houses. A 2018 reappraisal in Antiquity argued there is still no convincing evidence that anyone on Chalcolithic Cyprus actually smelted, so these remain the strongest and weakest case at once.
The first objects from the island that are unmistakably tools rather than ornaments, and with the Lemba chisel the beginning of a working metal industry.
A full-size roundhouse rebuilt on the site with Chalcolithic techniques, so that a visitor can stand inside one instead of reading a plan.

finds.n: The Pithos House stone tools in the jars
finds.t: Nests of small bowls and stone tools packed inside the storage vessels when the building burned, part of the same habit of caching things in jars later found at Chlorakas-Palloures.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Souskiou
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Souskiou, above the Dhiarizos river, Paphos district
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Middle Chalcolithic settlement with several cemeteries of deep rock-cut shaft graves, unusual for a period when the dead were normally buried under house floors. The graves were richly furnished with picrolite figurines, stone and clay figures and dentalium jewellery, and were heavily looted before excavation by the Department of Antiquities and Edinburgh's Lemba Archaeological Project.

finds.t: The finest series of the blue-green cross-shaped pendants, some wearing tiny figurines of their own.
A strip of metal twisted into nine loops, among the earliest metal on Cyprus.

Edgar Peltenburg's Edinburgh team dug here from 2001 to 2011 and found a village terraced into a steep hillside whose earlier phases were given over to working picrolite. Souskiou was not just a burial ground; it was where the pendants were made.
Shafts holding both articulated bodies and neatly rearranged loose bones, so the dead were returned to, moved and reordered over time rather than buried once.

Vathyrkakas was plundered for decades and unprovenanced cruciform figurines sold as 'Souskiou' flooded the market. Peltenburg's 2006 volume deliberately excluded every object without an excavated context, which is why the published corpus is so much smaller than the collectors' one.
finds.w: Dispersed in private and museum collections worldwide

finds.t: Strings of tiny tusk-shaped shells worn as necklaces and sewn onto clothing, among the commonest grave goods and a reminder that these people dressed for burial.
Narrow shafts cut metres down into rock, holding several people each. They are the first extramural cemeteries on Cyprus and the first burials that clearly separate the rich from everyone else.

The final report by Peltenburg, Diane Bolger and Lindy Crewe, which brought the settlement and the cemeteries together and settled Souskiou's reputation as a specialist producer rather than an oddity.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Sotira-Kaminoudhia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: An Early Bronze Age settlement and cemeteries 400 m from the old Neolithic village, excavated by Stuart Swiny for the Cyprus American Archaeological Research Institute. Its agglutinative multi-room buildings mark the break from the round houses that had dominated Cyprus for millennia; bones show beef, pork and goat on the table, and skeletons show signs of malaria.

finds.t: Tools and ornaments of pure and arsenical copper from the tombs.
Limestone slabs with rows of cup-marks, an early Cypriot board game.
Rooms added onto rooms in an agglutinative sprawl, the first Early Bronze Age settlement ever excavated on Cyprus. Before Swiny dug here the whole period was known from tombs alone.

Sturt Manning argued in 1994 that the site's radiocarbon dates were older than its pottery allowed, which forced a general rethink of when the Cypriot Bronze Age begins. The gap between the two kinds of evidence has narrowed but not closed.
Blue-green stone ornaments carried on from the Chalcolithic tradition, but now simple pendants rather than the elaborate cruciform figures of a few centuries earlier.
Chamber tombs beside the settlement, so that for once the same community's houses and graves can be compared directly.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities, Cyprus; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Swiny, George Rapp and Ellen Herscher's volume for CAARI and the American Schools of Oriental Research, with specialist studies of the pottery, chipped and ground stone, metals and terracottas.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Alambra-Mouttes
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Middle Bronze Age village in the copper-bearing foothills south of Nicosia, dug by Cornell University in 1974–85. Its rectangular multi-room houses are among the earliest of the type fully excavated on the island; bones of cattle, deer, pig and goat, clay figurines and copper objects were found, but no sign of smelting.

finds.t: Several multi-room dwellings on stone footings.
Small tools and Red Polished figurines from the houses.

A mudbrick element from a room containing a human burial, matching the ornaments on the columned seat modelled in the Vounous Bowl. Published by Andrew Sneddon in 2019, it is the only physical analogue for anything in that famous object.
A crucible and a double-sided terracotta mould, with ore samples and small quantities of slag, showing that copper was melted and cast inside the village even though nobody smelted here.
A tight hundred-year window for the occupation, which makes Alambra one of the few Middle Bronze Age villages whose dating does not have to lean on pottery style alone.
Magnetic and resistivity survey mapped walls across the unexcavated part of the site and, just as usefully, showed where the local geology defeats the technique.
Human remains in a room of a domestic building, at a period when the dead were normally taken out to a cemetery. It is the context that gives the finial its meaning.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kalavasos-Ayios Dhimitrios
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Late Bronze Age town laid out on a grid, excavated by the Vasilikos Valley Project in 1979–98. Its centre was Building X, an ashlar administrative building with cedar beams whose storerooms held jars for over 50,000 litres of olive oil; rich tombs beside it show a ruling elite tied into Aegean and Egyptian trade. Its clay matches the Alashiya letters sent to Egypt.

finds.t: Monumental tripartite ashlar building with a great pithos hall, the best-preserved Late Cypriot administrative centre.
432 g of gold jewellery, including two rings with Cypro-Minoan signs, buried with a young woman: the second-richest Late Bronze Age gold group on the island.

finds.n: The pithos hall of Building X
finds.t: Rows of giant storage jars sunk into the floor of the north wing with a combined capacity of more than 50,000 litres of olive oil. That is collection from a whole valley, not one estate's harvest, and it is the clearest evidence for Cypriot regional administration before the Iron Age.
Streets running north to south and east to west, the central one traceable for over 150 metres, with wells at intervals. A town laid out on a plan rather than one that grew.

finds.n: Cypro-Minoan inscriptions and bronze writing styli
finds.t: Inscribed objects together with the metal styli used to cut the signs, from inside Building X: the working tools of an administration whose records nobody can now read.

finds.n: The clay of the Alashiya letters
finds.t: Petrographic analysis published in 2003 matched the clay of letters sent by the king of Alashiya to Egypt and Ugarit to the geology around Kalavasos and Alassa rather than to Enkomi. It is the strongest physical argument yet about where Alashiya's king actually sat, and it has not settled the question.
finds.w: Letters in Berlin, London and Cairo; analysis published 2003

finds.t: The building burned and the town was abandoned. The fire baked its thick plaster floors, which is why they survive well enough to walk on, and the excavators found the storerooms still holding their jars.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Golgoi
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A sanctuary town of the Mesaoria plain, said to have been founded by Golgos from Sikyon, at its peak in the fourth century BCE and occupied into Early Christian times. Its limestone workshops produced thousands of votive statues for the sanctuary at Ayios Photios, plundered by Duthoit in 1862 and above all by Cesnola in 1870, whose haul became the core of the Metropolitan Museum's Cypriot collection. Since 1990 Davidson College has excavated a rural sanctuary at nearby Malloura.

finds.t: Over-life-size gods, priests and worshippers, and Hellenistic votive reliefs with syllabic inscriptions.
finds.w: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

finds.t: A limestone coffin carved with a hunt on one side and a banquet of four couches on the other.
finds.w: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

finds.t: Limestone and terracotta offerings from the sanctuary.
finds.w: Larnaca District Museum; Kallinikeio Municipal Museum, Athienou

finds.t: Edmond Duthoit, working for the French mission, took between 150 and 200 sculpted heads from the votive deposits eight years before Cesnola arrived. Golgoi was being emptied by two nations at once.

A limestone statue of a bearded man in a wreath cradling a dove, among the best known of Cesnola's Golgoi figures and one of the images that defined 'Cypriot sculpture' for American visitors. The dove is Aphrodite's bird, offered to a god the inscriptions call Apollo.
finds.w: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

finds.t: Statue bases and reliefs inscribed in the Cypriot syllabary naming the dedicants and, usually, Apollo. They are what identifies the god of the sanctuary, since Golgoi's most famous divine name, Aphrodite Golgia, belongs to shrines elsewhere.
finds.w: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Terracotta riders and limestone votaries from the rural sanctuary two kilometres away, excavated stratigraphically by the Athienou Archaeological Project since 1990. Malloura is the control that shows what was lost at Golgoi itself.
finds.w: Kallinikeio Municipal Museum, Athienou; Larnaca District Museum

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayia Irini
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A rural open-air sanctuary founded in the twelfth century BCE and used until the early fifth, found by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition in 1929 after the village priest turned up fragments in his field. Around a sacred stone and altar stood about 2,000 terracotta figures, most of the seventh and sixth centuries BCE: warriors, charioteers, bulls and minotaur-like creatures, the largest such group from the ancient Mediterranean. Half went to Sweden in 1931.

finds.t: About 2,000 clay votaries, the figure the Swedish excavators published, from a few centimetres to life size, set in a semicircle around the altar.

finds.n: Bull figurines and the sacred stone
finds.t: Clay bulls and the aniconic cult stone at the heart of the shrine.

finds.n: The temenos and its seven periods
finds.t: Erik Sjöqvist dug the whole enclosure in 1929 and separated seven phases of use, of which periods four to six, about 700 to 500 BCE, were the busiest. The walled court with its altar was never roofed: this was an open-air shrine to the end.

Clay men wearing bull masks, long labelled minotaurs, standing among the warriors and charioteers. They are usually read as priests or dancers in costume, which would make them the only surviving picture of Cypriot ritual performance.

Model two-horse and four-horse chariots with crews of driver and warrior, standing in the outer ranks of the semicircle. Taken with the shields and swords, they suggest a god who was asked for victory as well as fertility.

The Medelhavsmuseet displays its half of the figures in the concentric semicircle in which they were found, one of the few museum installations anywhere that reproduces an excavated arrangement. A full restudy of the sanctuary was published in 2025.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Chytroi
SETTLEMENTS.desc: An inland city-kingdom at the great spring of Kythrea, listed on Esarhaddon's prism in 673 BCE and prosperous in Classical, Hellenistic and Roman times, when its water was carried by aqueduct across the plain to Salamis. Ancient authors mention a gymnasium and shrines of Artemis, Hermes and Herakles. Sacked by Arab raiders in 912 and abandoned; the site is largely unexcavated.

finds.t: A 2.08 m nude bronze emperor found by chance in 1928, the largest bronze statue from Cyprus.
Channel and arches carrying Kythrea's spring water some 50 km to Salamis-Constantia.
finds.w: In situ, fragments near Kythrea and Salamis

finds.t: A country shrine a few kilometres from Kythrea, excavated by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, which produced large groups of limestone and terracotta votives. Voni is one of the inland sanctuaries where limestone sculpture stayed in fashion after the coast turned to marble.
Named as Pilagura on Esarhaddon's prism, the earliest mention of the kingdom and one of the ten Cypriot kings recorded there. Nothing else is known of him.
finds.w: Prism in the British Museum, London

finds.t: The Kefalovryso, the largest spring on the island, which is the whole reason a kingdom sat here in a dry plain. It ran until heavy pumping dried it in the twentieth century.

Chytroi is known from texts, from its aqueduct and from stray finds; the city itself has never been systematically dug, and lies under the modern village and its gardens. It is the least investigated of the ten kingdoms.

The Life of Demetrianos, a Cypriot text written not long after his death, says that when raiders carried off the people of his diocese the old bishop followed them to the caliph's court and argued them free. The raid is usually identified with the one that wrecked Chytroi in 912. The Life is the only source for the embassy, and it is exactly the kind of story the condominium centuries produced.
finds.w: Text edited from a Constantinople manuscript; the saint is kept on 6 November

finds.t: One of the fourteen sees of Byzantine Cyprus, held by Eustathios and then by his priest Demetrianos, who succeeded him. The Latins cut the fourteen Orthodox sees to four after 1191 and Chytroi vanished from the list.

The strongest spring on the island fed a chain of watermills down the Kythrea valley and made the place worth a kingdom, an aqueduct and a raid. It failed in the later twentieth century as boreholes dropped the water table.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Palace of Vouni
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Hill west of Soli, Morphou bay
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A hilltop palace of the Persian period, excavated by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition in 1928–29. Built around 500 BCE on an Oriental plan around a great court and cistern, it was remodelled in Greek fashion in the fifth century and burned around 380 BCE, never to be rebuilt. Its excavator Einar Gjerstad thought pro-Persian Marion built it to watch Greek Soli below.

finds.t: Gold and silver bracelets with animal-head ends in Persian style, silver bowls and 248 silver coins hidden in a jar under a stair as the palace burned.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; some finds in the Medelhavsmuseet, Stockholm

finds.t: A 137-room complex around a central court with a deep cistern and a carved stone windlass stand.

finds.n: Temple of Athena on the summit
finds.p: First half of the 5th century BCE
finds.t: A sanctuary above the palace, identified as Athena's from inscribed bronze bowls and sculptural fragments, with a square single-roomed shrine and a block of adjoining rooms. A Greek goddess on the hill above a palace built on an oriental plan is the puzzle of the site.
A limestone head crowned with a diadem carved in relief, the best-known sculpture from the site. It is Cypriot work under strong Ionian influence.
A standing goddess in Ionian Greek style, unusually large for a Cypriot hilltop shrine. Whether she is Persephone or a local goddess given a Greek name is not settled.

finds.n: The Greek remodelling of the palace
finds.t: The original plan, rooms around a great court with a cistern in the eastern manner, was rebuilt so that a visitor entered through a columned porch into a hall, in the Greek fashion. The rebuild is usually read as a change of dynasty, and dated to the aftermath of the Greek fleet's raid on Cyprus.
Limestone figures of both deities from the hilltop temple, Herakles in the lion skin with a club. The pairing is the same one the Phoenician kings used, where Herakles stood for Melqart.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Pyla-Kokkinokremos
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Plateau above Pyla, east of Larnaca
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A short-lived fortified settlement on a plateau above the bay of Larnaca, occupied for barely two generations around 1200 BCE and then abandoned with its valuables left behind. Dug by Dikaios in 1952, Karageorghis in the 1980s and 2010s, and a Belgian-Greek team since 2014, it is the twin of Maa-Palaeokastro in the debate over the newcomers of the Bronze Age collapse.

finds.t: Gold jewellery and a silver ingot hidden under a floor and never recovered by their owners.
Two inscribed clay tablets, rare outside Enkomi.

A continuous line of rooms built along the rim of the plateau so that their back walls form a defensive face. Whether this counts as a fortification or simply as terraced housing on a naturally strong site is one of the live arguments about the place.

Pottery from Mycenaean Greece, Minoan Crete, Nuragic Sardinia, Hittite Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt in one settlement occupied for barely two generations, a mixture unmatched anywhere else on the island at this date.

A well-cut shaft roughly three metres deep with cuttings in its walls for steps or beams. Sandy fill described as very like beach sand turned up in three sectors, which suggests the shore and its landing place were closer than the modern coastline implies.

finds.n: Copper alloy axe and metalworking debris
finds.t: A well-preserved axe found in 2023, with wire fragments and a broken bracelet, from a plateau with no water and no harbour of its own. Vasiliki Kassianidou's team has studied the metal; smiths worked here even so.

Ghent University and the Cyprus Institute have excavated here since 2014 under Joachim Bretschneider. The hoards of gold and silver hidden beneath the floors were never lifted, which is why the excavators think the people who buried them never came back.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Karpasia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The port town of the Karpas peninsula, with harbour moles still visible under the water. It became a bishopric in the fourth century, and the fifth-century basilica of Ayios Philon with its mosaic floors stands over the town. Abandoned after the Arab raid of 802, when its people moved inland to Rizokarpaso.

finds.t: An episcopal basilica with mosaic floors and a baptistery, later replaced by a small Byzantine church.
Two breakwaters of large blocks enclosing the ancient harbour.

Ancient writers said Karpasia was founded by the Phoenician king Pygmalion, that is Pumayyaton, a name borne by kings of Kition. The archaeology reaches back no further than the seventh century BCE, so the story is probably a later attempt to explain Phoenician-looking buildings.

Blocks dressed and laid in the manner of the Levantine coast, noted in the town's buildings and unusual this far north on Cyprus. It is the main physical support for the Phoenician connection in the sources.

Demetrios I of Macedon put his army ashore at Karpasia, took the town and marched on Salamis to fight Ptolemy's brother Menelaos. The harbour was chosen because it could take a fleet, which is what the moles under the water were for.
finds.w: Literary source; harbour submerged at Ayios Philon

finds.t: The town's masonry and house plans show Phoenician influence, and tradition made Pygmalion of Tyre its founder. Its first appearance in a text is in 399 BCE, and in 306 BCE the army of Demetrius Poliorcetes landed here and took Karpasia and neighbouring Ourania before marching on Salamis.

The town's first known bishop, whose commentary on the Song of Songs survives and is the earliest Cypriot biblical commentary we have. The basilica beside the harbour carries his name, and a later bishop, Hermolaus, sat at the Council of Chalcedon in 451.
finds.w: Manuscripts in European libraries; church in situ at Ayios Philon

finds.n: The small church inside the basilica
finds.t: When the fifth-century basilica of Ayios Philon fell, a small vaulted church was built inside its east end, reusing the old apse. Keeping the apse and shrinking the church around it is the standard Cypriot response to the raids, and the same thing happened at Kiti, Livadia and Soloi.
A baptistery with a cross-shaped font and mosaic floors on the south side of the basilica, part of the bishop's complex that made this small port a see.
The church the refugees built inland, over the tomb of a bishop Synesios. The town around it still holds the largest of the Greek Cypriot communities that stayed in the north after 1974.
The date usually given for the attack that ended the port. The harbour moles were left standing under the water, the town above was never reoccupied, and the fields over it have still not been dug.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kissonerga-Mylouthkia
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Kissonerga, Paphos district, on the sea cliff
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A coastal site eroding into the sea just south of Kissonerga, dug by Edgar Peltenburg's Lemba Archaeological Project between 1976 and 1996. Its earliest phase survives as almost nothing but wells: cylindrical shafts eight and seven metres deep, cut into bedrock with hand and footholds, among the oldest water wells known anywhere in the world. Nothing comparable is found on the Levantine mainland until much later, which suggests the settlers had to invent their own answer to a dry island. The wells were later filled with rubbish, animal carcasses and human bone, and that rubbish is now the richest single source we have for the first farmers of Cyprus.

finds.t: A cylindrical shaft at least 8 m deep cut into unweathered bedrock, with hand and footholds carved down the sides for climbing in and out. It is the only trace of the site's earliest occupation, and one of the two or three oldest water wells known from anywhere on earth. Specialists prefer 'among the earliest known' to 'the world's oldest', because the Cypriot wells and those at Shillourokambos overlap in date.
finds.w: In situ, backfilled; finds with the Department of Antiquities

finds.t: A hook cut from a slice of wild boar tusk, from the lowest fill of Well 116. It is the earliest fishing tackle known from Cyprus, and it came out of a well eight metres deep rather than off a beach.

The jumbled bones of six people recovered from the fills of two wells. In 2024 a team led from Oxford sequenced their genomes and found that these early Cypriots drew roughly 80 per cent of their ancestry from Aceramic Neolithic central Anatolia, around the Konya plain, and the rest from a genetically basal Levantine population: the first direct evidence of where the colonists came from.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities; samples analysed at Oxford

finds.n: Bony growths in the ear canals
finds.t: Several of the Mylouthkia skeletons carry external auditory exostoses, knots of bone that form in the ear canal after repeated immersion in cold water. The condition is common in modern divers and swimmers, and here it is read as evidence that some of these villagers habitually worked in the sea.

finds.n: Marine shell and fish bone from the wells
finds.t: Over 2,300 edible marine shells and hundreds of fish bones came out of the well fills, an unusually complete picture of a Neolithic coastal diet because the shafts were excavated and sieved with care.

finds.n: Sheep and goat carcasses in Well 133
finds.t: Whole and partial bodies of caprines were dropped down the well when it went out of use. They include some of the earliest sheep and goats on the island, animals that can only have arrived by boat.

Both wells produced stone vessels in quantity, hollowed from hard grey volcanic rock collected as river cobbles from the Troodos, together with debris from working picrolite, the blue-green stone of the Cypriot river beds.
finds.w: Paphos District Museum; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: A small hammered copper hook from the site's later Chalcolithic levels, often cited as the earliest metal object excavated on Cyprus. The claim competes with the copper chisel from Erimi-Pamboula, and which is genuinely older is not settled.
Disarticulated bones of several people at the base of a second well, mixed with animal bone. Whether this counts as burial, clearance or something else is still argued over.
Blades and flakes of volcanic glass with no Cypriot source, nearly all of them from Well 116. Small in quantity but decisive: the settlers kept in touch with the mainland they came from.

Two long ditches running side by side across the site, cut in the Chalcolithic. They have been read as an enclosure or even a defence, which would be unique for the period, and as drainage or quarrying, which would not.
Sheep, goat, cattle, pig, dog, wheat, barley and lentils, all of them non-native, all of them present from the start. Cyprus has no wild ancestors for any of them, so every one arrived on a boat.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kritou Marottou-Ais Giorkis
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Near Kritou Marottou, Paphos district, in the western Troodos foothills
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The one early Neolithic settlement on Cyprus that is not on or near the coast. It sits in the hills about 25 km from the sea, and Alan Simmons of the University of Nevada dug it over campaigns from 1997 to 2018. Everything about it is awkward for the standard story: the architecture is unlike anything else on the island, the cattle bones are among the earliest directly dated domesticates anywhere in the Near East, and 982 marine shells were carried all the way up from the coast. It is the main reason the colonisation of Cyprus is no longer told as a story of coastal beachheads.

finds.t: Roughly circular platforms of packed river cobbles, several metres across, with pits and caches of blades around them. They are unparalleled on Cyprus. Foundations for dwellings is the least strained reading, but the excavators concede other uses cannot be excluded.

Some of the earliest directly dated domestic cattle in the Near East, at a site 25 km inland and 500 m up. Cattle then disappear from the Cypriot record for thousands of years, which suggests the first herds could not be sustained without fresh animals shipped from the mainland.

Emmer, einkorn and barley, much of it in a partly processed state, together with plants that may have been medicinal. The archaeobotany showed island crops changing shape unusually fast, an accelerated evolution under isolation.

Vessels moulded from lime plaster, a mainland technique that does what pottery does and predates the first Cypriot pots by well over two thousand years. Its presence here is one of the arguments that contact with the mainland never stopped.
Sixty-six pieces of Cappadocian obsidian, brought across open sea and then 25 km uphill. Small beside the four thousand from Akanthou, but a great deal for a hill farm.

Two beads of orange-red carnelian, part of a group of only about fifty known from the whole island. Portable XRF shows at least two chemical groups, but the source, somewhere in Anatolia or the Caucasus, has still not been pinned down.

982 marine shells, 189 freshwater shells and nine fossils, catalogued by David Reese. The marine shells had to be carried some 25 km from the coast, which says something about how the uplands and the shore were used by the same people.

Concentrations of animal bone and ground stone read as the debris of communal eating, alongside caches of unused blades. Feasting at an upland site raises the possibility that Ais Giorkis was a gathering place as much as a farm.
finds.w: In situ; finds with the Department of Antiquities

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayia Varvara-Asprokremnos
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Between Ayia Varvara and Mathiati, Nicosia district
SETTLEMENTS.desc: One of only two places on Cyprus as old as the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A of the mainland, and the odd one of the pair: not a village but a working camp in the eastern Troodos foothills, where people made stone tools and ground red ochre. Carole McCartney's Elaborating Early Neolithic Cyprus project dug 203 square metres over five seasons up to 2013. The suggestion that its pigment was being produced partly for export back to the Levant turns the usual picture around, with Cyprus supplying the mainland rather than only receiving from it.

finds.t: A small complete human figure of picrolite, found in 2013 in a group of igneous stone objects and announced by teams from Toronto, Cornell and the University of Cyprus. It is the earliest complete anthropomorphic figurine known from the island, older by two thousand years than the stone figures of Khirokitia.

Flat stone tools found with the figurine, one of them thickly coated in red ochre residue, alongside worn blocks of the raw pigment. Ochre processing on this scale at so small a site is what prompted the idea that Asprokremnos was extracting a mineral commodity rather than simply farming.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Department of Antiquities

finds.t: A semi-subterranean building, the only substantial structure on the site. Everything else is hearths and thin camping traces, so the excavators read Asprokremnos as seasonal or periodic rather than a settled village.

Grooved stones for straightening arrow shafts, both cut with lattice patterns. The same designs appear in the Early Neolithic of the Near Eastern mainland, early evidence that Cyprus and the Levant shared a set of symbols and not just a tool kit.

Hunted pigs supply about 95 per cent of the animal bone at Asprokremnos and Klimonas alike. These were the descendants of boar shipped over by the earlier Epipalaeolithic visitors, and for five centuries they were the only large game on the island.
Large quantities of chipped stone waste showing on-site production of small blades and microliths, of a kind that ties the site to the mainland PPNA rather than to anything later on Cyprus.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Akanthou-Arkosykos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A ninth-millennium village on the north coast, and the place where Anatolian obsidian came ashore. Over four thousand pieces have been recorded here, more than every other Cypriot site put together, all of it finished bladelets from the Kömürcü-Kaletepe source in Cappadocia. Müge Sevketoglu ran rescue excavations from 2000 after building work began to destroy the site; less than five per cent of it has been dug. Its buildings had lime-plaster floors and painted plaster walls, and a broad ditch cut into bedrock runs across the excavated area.

finds.t: More than four thousand pieces of Cappadocian obsidian, of which 3,600 have been catalogued. Over 95 per cent are finished bladelets, with almost no core waste, so the blades were made at the quarry in Anatolia and shipped across as a product. By comparison Shillourokambos has about 430 pieces, Ais Giorkis 42 and the Mylouthkia wells 8.
finds.w: Excavation stores, Cyprus International University; analysed at Tübingen

finds.t: Six buildings of stone and mudbrick, round and rectilinear, with floors of fine lime plaster relaid many times over and fragments of painted wall plaster in the collapse layers. Making quicklime this early puts Akanthou alongside the great plaster-using sites of Anatolia and the Levant.
finds.w: In situ; samples with the excavation project

finds.t: A wide ditch with vertical sides cut into bedrock, running east to west across the whole excavated trench, with the buildings and the plaster surface respecting its line. It filled slowly with erosion and rubbish after the village was abandoned, and one collapsing wall fell into it.

finds.n: Disarticulated human bone in the ditch fills
finds.t: Teeth, skull and jaw fragments, vertebrae and the small bones of hands and feet, several from children, scattered through the ditch deposits. These are exactly the parts left behind when a body is dug up and moved after the flesh has gone. No graves have been found anywhere on the site.
Hake, dogfish, shark and tunny alongside smaller inshore fish, plus the remains of ten complete loggerhead turtles. Catching tunny and shark means going out well beyond the shore.

Two small hollow cups of blue-green picrolite, under 3 cm long, cut with hatched lines. Near-identical pieces come from Shillourokambos. They have been read, imaginatively, as models of boats, which would make them the oldest pictures of a vessel in the Mediterranean; the reading is not widely accepted.
Bricks laid in regular courses, averaging 0.33 by 0.20 by 0.10 m and bonded with white plaster or gypsum mortar, so consistent in size that they suggest a standardised way of making them.

Fallow deer make up 45 per cent of the identified bones, sheep and goat 27 per cent and pig 17 per cent, while cattle amount to barely 2 per cent. The sheep and goats were killed young, as herders kill them; the deer were taken at all ages, as hunters take them.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Cape Andreas-Kastros
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Zafer Burnu, tip of the Karpas peninsula
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A fishing hamlet clinging to a ledge on the steep flank of a limestone headland at the very tip of the Karpas, halfway between the plateau above and the sea below, in a position so awkward that it can only have been chosen for the water. Alain Le Brun's French mission dug it in three seasons between 1970 and 1973; the 1974 war ended the work and the site has since been badly damaged. Of all the Neolithic settlements on Cyprus this is the one that comes closest to being a genuine fishing village.

finds.t: Circular dwellings only 2.5 to 2.8 m across, with thin dry-stone walls, hearths inside and storage bins set at floor level, some grouped around shared courtyards. They are the smallest Neolithic houses known on the island, a third the diameter of the largest at Khirokitia.

Nearly four thousand identified fish bones. Tuna alone accounts for 36.5 per cent of the assemblage, alongside grouper, sea bass, sea bream and mullet. Tuna are large, fast, migratory fish; taking them needs skilled crews and specialised tackle, not a line off the rocks.
finds.w: Study collections, France; Department of Antiquities

finds.t: An array of hooks cut from bone together with perforated stone rings, generally taken for net sinkers. Together with the tuna they are the best direct evidence of Neolithic fishing gear from Cyprus.
Over 4,500 marine invertebrate remains, mostly dove shell, topshell and limpet, with some 350 crab remains and sea urchins. The shore was the household larder as much as the fields were.

Four pierced shells and one dentalium found with a body, the only ornaments from a grave at the site. Dentalium in burials links Kastros to a mortuary habit that runs from the Natufian of the Levant right through the Neolithic.

Shallow bowls and pots of local stone with grinding querns, the standard aceramic kit. Carbonised remains show einkorn, emmer and barley with lentils, and gathered wild pistachio, fig and olive, so this was a farming household as well as a fishing one.

A tenth of what the earlier villages handled. Across the Late Aceramic Neolithic the whole island yields about 57 pieces, against some 4,500 in the preceding centuries, a tenfold collapse in the obsidian trade whose cause is still argued.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kholetria-Ortos
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Kholetria, Paphos district, above the Xeros Potamos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A large village of the Khirokitia culture on a vine-covered plateau above the lower Xeros Potamos, spotted by the Canadian archaeologist Bill Fox during the Palaipaphos survey in the 1980s and tested by Alan Simmons in 1993 and 1996. Ploughing has taken away the buildings, so Ortos is known almost entirely from pits and the material in the soil. Even so it ranks with Khirokitia and Kalavasos-Tenta among the larger settlements of its day, which is a warning about how many equally big villages have been quietly erased by farming.

finds.t: A fist-sized head of grey diabase, 8.5 cm high, with chiselled brows, a flat vertical nose and a jutting chin, and diagonal lines engraved for what looks like a braided hairstyle. It is broken off just below the chin and was once part of a larger figure. Found on the surface in 1988.

Pebbles scored with grids of fine lines on one or both faces, matching examples from Khirokitia and from the earlier village at Shillourokambos. They have been read as pictures of fishing nets, as net weights, and as counters in a system of exchange; all three readings are still in play, and the same objects turn up in Levantine sites of the same date.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Department of Antiquities

finds.t: Shells carried some 9 km inland from the coast, a reminder that even the hill villages of the Late Aceramic Neolithic kept a working relationship with the sea.
Two, at a village of Khirokitia's size. Set beside the four thousand pieces at Akanthou a thousand years earlier, this is the clearest single measure of how far the Anatolian trade had fallen away.
Bowls, trays and basins hollowed from hard igneous rock, in a period with no pottery at all. The raw material is river cobble from the Troodos, and the Ortos Head is carved from the same diabase.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Department of Antiquities

finds.t: Simmons found pits, hearth bases and a dense artefact scatter, but no standing walls: the plough had gone through everything. The negative result is itself the find, and it is the reason Ortos is cited whenever anyone argues that the map of Neolithic Cyprus is badly incomplete.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kantou-Kouphovounos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Ceramic Neolithic village on a prominent hill 243 m above sea level on the west bank of the Kouris, about 5 km inland. It was the first Cypriot field project of the University of Athens, dug by Eleni Mantzourani from 1992 to 1999 and published in full in 2009 and 2019, which makes it one of the best documented villages of the Sotira culture. Its two floor burials are the only ones of their kind in the whole period.

finds.t: Two pits cut into the floor of an apparently abandoned building held an adult man and a baby of about nine months. In the Aceramic Neolithic burying the dead under house floors was the rule; in the Ceramic Neolithic the dead were normally taken outside the village, and these two are the only known exceptions, which may say something about who they were.
finds.w: In situ, conserved; skeletal material with the University of Athens project

finds.t: The adult male has an oval depression measuring 1 by 2 cm above the right eye socket, consistent with a blow from a blunt object. It is very nearly the only trace of interpersonal violence from Neolithic Cyprus, though the excavators are reluctant to make it evidence of unrest in what otherwise looks like a thoroughly egalitarian society.
finds.w: Study collection, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

finds.n: Marine shells at an inland village
finds.t: Thirty-five marine species, dominated by murex with over 120 fragments, cockle with 97 and oyster with 31, along with 23 crab fragments and two sea urchins. All of it was carried up from a coast 5 km away, and murex in that quantity raises the question of whether the shells were food, dye or ornament.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities; study collections, University of Athens

finds.t: A group of teeth found north of Building 1 in the western sector, from at least one further adult. Scattered teeth without a grave are the usual signature of a body that has been dug up and moved, a practice better attested at Akanthou two thousand years earlier.

The village lies in the southern zone where the combed style dominates, its red slip dragged into wavy bands with a multi-toothed tool, but it also holds painted Red-on-White of the sort commoner in the north and east.
finds.w: Limassol District Archaeological Museum; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Free-standing single-roomed buildings, sub-rectangular with rounded corners, on stone footings under mudbrick, arranged along the summit and the western and southern slopes. The plan is close to Sotira-Teppes, one of several signs that the Ceramic Neolithic was culturally uniform even where its pottery was not.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Paralimni-Nissia
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Protaras, Famagusta district, on the shore
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Ceramic Neolithic village on a low hillock right on the shore beside a natural harbour, excavated for the Department of Antiquities by Pavlos Flourentzos between 1995 and 2000. Around forty round and sub-rectangular houses stood on 3,250 square metres inside a horseshoe-shaped wall with two gates. If any Cypriot Neolithic site deserves to be called a fishing village it is this one, and yet three quarters of its meat came from hunted deer. An underwater survey published in 2025 has traced five drowned shorelines offshore, so how close to the water the village actually sat is now being reconsidered.

finds.t: A curved wall around the settlement with a main gate and a second on the south side, an unusual piece of communal building for the Ceramic Neolithic, when most villages were simply clusters of free-standing houses.
Not more than forty circular and sub-rectangular buildings, exposed at a depth of only 20 to 30 cm around a central plateau. The shallowness is why the site was so easily found and is so vulnerable.
A small figure carved in the shape of a fish, among the most distinctive small finds from the site and a rarity in a period when figurine-making had largely stopped on Cyprus.
finds.w: Famagusta district collections, Department of Antiquities

finds.t: Hooks cut from stone together with perforated and grooved stones described in the excavation report as loom weights. They are almost certainly net sinkers instead: the earliest genuine loom weights on Cyprus are a thousand years later.

Sixteen mollusc species with over 950 individuals, but only nine fish bones from seven deposits and two crab claws. The imbalance is a reminder that flotation and water-sieving were not used consistently, and that fish are almost certainly under-counted.

Some 77 per cent of the mammal bones are Mesopotamian fallow deer, which supplied roughly 90 per cent of the meat. A coastal village next to a harbour was living mainly by hunting an animal its ancestors had shipped to the island for exactly that purpose.

Bathymetric survey, geomorphology and diving off Nissia have identified five possible palaeocoastlines, published in 2025. The work matters beyond this one site: it offers a way of telling how far the Neolithic shore lay from villages that today sit at the water's edge.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Petra tou Limniti
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The only Neolithic settlement in Cyprus on an offshore island: a small rocky islet a few hundred metres out from the coast at Limnitis. The Swedish Cyprus Expedition dug it in 1929, which makes it the first aceramic site ever excavated on the island and the reason the period was recognised at all. In the Neolithic the sea stood lower and the rock may still have been attached to the shore, so whether these people were islanders within an island is genuinely open.

finds.n: Round stone houses on the summit
finds.t: Circular dry-stone buildings crowded onto the top of the rock, of the same family as those at Khirokitia and Cape Andreas-Kastros. The whole settlement is smaller than a single Khirokitia courtyard.
Vessels hollowed from andesite and diabase, carried out to the islet ready-made, since the rock itself is limestone and the igneous cobbles come from Troodos rivers well to the south.

One flake, the smallest obsidian count from any excavated aceramic site on Cyprus. It is a useful corrective: even a settlement out in the water was barely touched by the Anatolian trade by this date.

finds.n: Twelve marine shells and 25 fish bones
finds.t: The recorded totals from a site surrounded by sea. The figures say far more about 1929 excavation methods, which involved no sieving, than about what the inhabitants ate, and Petra tou Limniti is regularly cited as a site that would repay re-excavation.
Blades and flakes of local Lefkara chert with grinding stones, the ordinary equipment of a farming household, which is the point: people were growing and grinding grain on a rock in the sea.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Vretsia-Roudias
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Near Vretsia, Paphos district, upper Xeros valley
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A hunters' camp high in the western Troodos, excavated by Nikolaos Efstratiou of Thessaloniki from 2011 and still under study. It matters for two reasons. It shows that the earliest Cypriots did not cling to the coast but went up into the mountains and adapted to them, shedding their maritime habits; and it helps fill the long blank in the record between the rock shelter at Aetokremnos and the first villages. Occupation was intermittent, with a later Aceramic Neolithic phase on top of the Epipalaeolithic one.

finds.t: A large built stone platform with at least three construction phases of different dates, closely resembling features at Ayia Varvara-Asprokremnos. What it was for is unresolved; that two upland sites hundreds of years apart built the same thing is the interesting part.

Large ground stone tools together with fragments of possible stone vessels, found in the earliest levels. Heavy equipment of this sort is not what one expects from a mobile hunting camp, and it is part of why the site is being read as more than a stopping place.
A small number of beads, the ornaments of people who were 25 km from the nearest coast and had left the shell-bead habit of the Aetokremnos generation behind them.

Blades, bladelets and microliths of a technology that parallels the Natufian of the Levantine mainland, the same industry as at Aetokremnos and the basis for dating the camp to around twelve thousand years ago.

Fallow deer with sheep and goat from the upper levels, published in 2023. They show the Troodos being worked by the later farming villages as well, presumably as summer grazing and hunting ground, which is a use of the mountains almost invisible elsewhere in the record.
finds.w: Study collections, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

finds.t: Systematic flotation of the deeper layers for charcoal and seeds, run by Maria Ntinou, aimed at reconstructing what the Troodos woodland looked like when the first Cypriots walked into it. Results are still coming out.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kalavasos-Kokkinoyia and Pamboules
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Kalavasos, Larnaca district, in the Vasilikos valley
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Two adjacent Ceramic Neolithic sites in the Vasilikos valley, downstream from Kalavasos-Tenta, first dug by Porphyrios Dikaios in the 1940s as Kalavasos Site A and Site B and reinvestigated by Joanne Clarke. Instead of building houses, the people here cut chambers and pits into the soft local limestone called havara and linked them together. Nothing else on Cyprus at this date looks like it, and the practice reappears in the Early Chalcolithic at nearby Kalavasos-Ayious.

finds.t: Chambers and pits cut into the havara bedrock and connected to one another, with post-holes in some suggesting roofed structures standing over them. Whether these were dwellings, stores or something else is not resolved, and it is the central puzzle of the site.

Large sea-snail shells found in Chambers 105 and 221. Because triton shells are useless as food at that size and turn up in special places elsewhere in the Mediterranean, they have been read as deliberate ritual deposits marking particular chambers.

finds.n: Obsidian: two blades and a bladelet
finds.t: Three pieces, the largest Ceramic Neolithic obsidian find on the island. Carole McCartney called what remained of the Anatolian traffic by this date an infrequent trinket trade, and this is the whole of it at one village.

A sandstone pebble cut with a grid of lines, of exactly the type otherwise confined to the earlier aceramic villages at Khirokitia and Ortos. It was picked up on the surface, and it is the only hint that there might be an older phase here, which nothing else supports.

finds.n: A burial and the remains of an earlier one
finds.t: One intact interment together with fragments of a previous burial disturbed by it. Ceramic Neolithic burials are scarce across the whole island, so even two counts. Dikaios also mentions a burial of uncertain date at nearby Pamboules.
Kokkinoyia is one of the southern sites on which the definition of the combed style rests, the red slip dragged into wavy bands with a toothed tool while still wet.
finds.w: Larnaca District Archaeological Museum; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Mostly limpets, collected over many seasons of survey and excavation. A very small total for a site 4 km from the sea, and further evidence that the Ceramic Neolithic villages of the interior had largely turned their backs on the shore.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Chlorakas-Palloures
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Chalcolithic village of about four hectares on the coastal shelf north of Paphos, half destroyed by a 1970s land consolidation scheme that drove roads straight through it and then scheduled for building. The Department of Antiquities asked Leiden University to rescue what was left, and Bleda During's team has dug there with the University of Cyprus since 2015. The results were startling enough that the state bought the land outright and invited the excavators to stay.

finds.t: A small, heavy blade 7.5 cm long weighing 119 grams, 99.5 per cent copper with a trace of tin. It is the only copper axe from a securely dated Chalcolithic context on Cyprus, has no Cypriot parallels, and matches flat axes from Horoztepe, Demircihuyuk and Thermi, so it was probably imported ready-made or cast from imported metal.

finds.n: The buried jar and its contents
finds.t: The axe was inside a large storage jar sunk into a lime-plaster surface, together with a broad basalt stone axe 12.7 cm long, four delicate fish hooks cut from pig tusk and a partly unrolled copper spiral. The excavators cannot decide between a hoard stashed for safekeeping and a deliberate ritual deposit, and lean towards the second.

A roundhouse about eight metres across, its wall standing four courses high on a platform cut level into the bedrock, and one of the largest Chalcolithic buildings known. A flimsier successor, Building 6, was built partly from its robbed stones.

A house that burned down while stacked full of pots, stone tools and other combustible material. Its layer-by-layer study, published in 2022, is one of the few detailed accounts of how these fires actually happened.
A stone pestle 47 cm long, found with five other ground stone tools on a floor surface. Grinding at this scale suggests processing for more than one household.
A strip of copper about 4 cm long and half a centimetre wide, coiled and partly unrolled, with a close parallel in the shaft graves at Souskiou.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kissonerga-Skalia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Bronze Age settlement barely a hundred metres from the Chalcolithic village at Mosphilia, dug since 2007 by Lindy Crewe for the Cyprus American Archaeological Research Institute. Occupied for some eight centuries, it covers exactly the stretch that western Cyprus is otherwise almost blank for: from the Philia horizon through to the end of the Middle Bronze Age. Its best-known feature is a domed mud-plaster structure argued to be a malting kiln.

finds.t: A domed mud-plaster chamber whose shape suits drying malt or curing malt cakes rather than firing pots or baking bread. A replica built by the site's field school was used to brew beer successfully, which supports the reading without proving it.
About 1,600 square metres of planned building that required serious earthmoving and terracing, then went out of use after perhaps one or two generations.
Sets of tiny vessels deposited where one building phase gave way to the next, read as the remains of communal drinking at moments of rebuilding.

finds.n: Plain White pithoi from eastern Cyprus
finds.t: Big storage jars whose fabric belongs to the far side of the island, the clearest evidence yet that the west was inside an inter-island exchange network before the Late Bronze Age.

finds.n: Deeply Incised and Red Polished wares
finds.t: Locally made pottery covering the whole span of the village, including the deeply incised style that is a western regional signature.
finds.w: Paphos District Museum; Department of Antiquities, Cyprus

SETTLEMENTS.name: Politiko-Troullia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: An Early and Middle Bronze Age village on a terrace between two streams in the Troodos foothills, at the exact seam between the grain land of the Mesaoria and the copper-bearing pillow lavas. Steven Falconer and Patricia Fall have dug it since 2004, and twenty-five radiocarbon dates put its six occupation phases between about 2050 and 1850 BCE. It is the clearest picture available of ordinary households that mined and smelted their own copper.

finds.t: The largest stone plank figure excavated on Cyprus, recovered not from a tomb but from an open public space in the middle of the village, which is why it matters: it puts these figures into communal life rather than the grave.
Copper ore, slag and casting debris in ordinary courtyards, with the blades, chisels and axe-heads that came out of them. Metallurgy here was domestic work, not a separate industry.
A well inside the settlement, giving the villagers drinking water without leaving the built-up area.
Concentrations of Mesopotamian fallow deer bone in courtyards alongside sheep, goat, pig and cattle, read as communal feasting on hunted rather than herded meat.
Flat clay figures with incised faces and ornament, found across the site in patterns that let the excavators map where they were actually used.
Six stratified phases of rectangular courtyard houses linked by lanes, rebuilt on the same lines for two hundred years.
Charred olive and grape remains beside charcoal from surviving woodland, which was the fuel that made the smelting possible.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ambelikou-Aletri
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A small industrial hamlet west of Ambelikou village, in the northern Troodos foothills beside Skouriotissa, one of the richest orebodies on the island. In 1942 modern miners broke into an ancient shaft and found pottery of about 2000 BCE in it, which brought Porphyrios Dikaios to the spot. Ambelikou remains the earliest place on Cyprus where copper mining itself, rather than the copper, can be proved, and it also produced a potter's workshop abandoned mid-job.

finds.t: A shaft found during twentieth-century mining, containing Middle Bronze Age pots left by the men who dug it. This is the oldest direct evidence for copper mining on Cyprus, as against copper objects, which are older.
finds.w: In situ (inaccessible); pottery in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: A crucible, a mould and slag from the settlement itself, so the ore was being smelted and cast within sight of the mine rather than carried away raw.
A workshop abandoned suddenly with its installations in place and roughly four dozen jugs still stacked from the last kiln load, a rare snapshot of a craft interrupted.
Broken ore awaiting the furnace and the waste left after it, the industrial rubbish that lets metallurgists reconstruct the process.
Heavy hammers and picks of the kind used to break ore out of a gallery by hand and firesetting.

finds.n: Red Polished and White Painted pottery
finds.t: The domestic pottery of the miners, which is what dates the whole operation to the very start of the Middle Bronze Age.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Deneia (Kafkalla)
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The largest Bronze Age burial ground known on Cyprus, spread over about six hectares of hard limestone crust on the south side of the Ovgos valley. It is also the most comprehensively robbed. When David Frankel and Jennifer Webb surveyed it in 2003 and 2004 they mapped 1,286 pillaged tombs, and argued that even a cemetery this badly damaged still carries readable information about population and wealth, and should not be written off to the bulldozer.

finds.t: The survey's central figure, and the reason so many unprovenanced Cypriot Bronze Age pots in world collections are labelled simply 'Deneia'. Tomb architecture and the sherds left behind still gave a curve of rising population and rising funerary spending through the Bronze Age.
Chambers entered down a sloping passage cut into the kafkalla, each holding several burials, the standard form of the island-wide extramural cemetery tradition.

finds.n: Red Polished and Black Polished vessels
finds.t: Burnished jugs, bowls and bottles, many of them decorated with incised lattice and zigzag, published as tomb groups by Frankel and Webb in 2007.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; and in private and public collections worldwide through the antiquities trade

finds.t: Pouring vessels modelled as animals or given animal spouts and horns, a favourite of the Red Polished potters and of collectors.
Tanged blades from the tombs, the standard male grave gift and a reminder that the valley sat on the route from the mines to the north coast.
A tomb recorded by Sophocles Hadjisavvas in 1985 showing that burial here continued long after the Middle Bronze Age peak.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Vasilia-Kafkallia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A north-coast cemetery of tombs cut into soft gypsum, dug by James Stewart in 1955. Its material is unlike anything at other Philia-phase sites and includes weapons that were made outside Cyprus, which is why the site sits at the centre of the argument about whether the Philia horizon means Anatolian migrants or only Anatolian fashions. Stewart thought the Philia style survived at Vasilia long after it had ended elsewhere, a view still contested.

finds.t: Nine metal objects hidden beneath the plaster lining of a tomb passage, one of the largest metal groups of its date on the island and evidently placed there deliberately rather than dropped.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Nicholson Museum, University of Sydney

finds.t: A rat-tang spearhead and a sword whose forms have no Cypriot ancestry, and whose lead isotope ratios point to copper from the central Taurus mountains. The likeliest reading is that both arrived as finished weapons.
A hoop of metal of a type used as portable value in Anatolia and the Cyclades, and further evidence that the north coast was plugged into a mainland metals trade.
The distinctive jugs and bowls of the Philia horizon, with their long cutaway spouts, mostly made on the island but shaped to Anatolian taste.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Nicholson Museum, University of Sydney

finds.t: Tombs whose contents span much of the prehistoric Bronze Age, which makes them hard to date and is the root of the long dispute over how late the Philia style lasted here.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Psematismenos-Trelloukkas
SETTLEMENTS.desc: An Early Bronze Age cemetery near the south coast, found in advance of building and excavated in a single rescue campaign in 2008 by Giorgos Georgiou for the Department of Antiquities with Jennifer Webb and David Frankel of Melbourne. It was published in full in 2011, which makes it rare and valuable: an early cemetery dug complete, and therefore the yardstick against which plundered cemeteries such as Deneia have to be measured.

finds.t: Every grave in the excavated area recorded, with its position, form and contents, at a period otherwise known almost entirely from robbed tombs and museum purchases.

Graves holding several people rather than one, including a group large enough to be called a mass burial. Psematismenos is a key data point for the shift from single to collective burial in the early Bronze Age.
The regional Early Cypriot fabric of this coastline, whose tight dating here helps anchor the sequence for the whole south.
finds.w: Larnaca District Archaeological Museum; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.n: The human and animal bone reports
finds.t: Kirsi Lorentz's study of the skeletons and Paul Croft's of the animal bone, giving age, sex and health for a whole burying community rather than a few showpiece graves.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Pyrgos-Mavroraki
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Not a village but an industrial quarter, now hemmed in by the villas of modern Pyrgos, excavated from 1998 by Maria Rosaria Belgiorno for Italy's National Research Council. Copper smelting, olive pressing, weaving, wine and perfumed oil were all carried on in one complex, with the olive oil apparently doubling as furnace fuel. An earthquake flattened it around 1850 BCE and thereby preserved the equipment where it stood.

finds.t: A press hall with funnels, maceration juglets, small perfume bottles and amphorae found in place, excavated between 2000 and 2003 and described by its excavator as the oldest perfume production site in the world. The superlative is contested; the installation is not.
finds.w: In situ, Pyrgos-Mavroraki; finds in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: A vessel identified as distillation apparatus. If the reading holds it is among the earliest distillation equipment anywhere, which is exactly why other specialists want a second explanation for the shape.

Chemical and pollen analysis identified rosemary, lavender, marjoram and myrtle steeped in olive and almond oil, matching methods later described by Theophrastus, Pliny and Dioscorides. Working replicas of the fragrances have been made from the results.
finds.w: Reconstructions shown at Musei Capitolini, Rome (2007), Officina Profumo Santa Maria Novella, Florence (2008) and the Pierides Museum, Larnaca (2009–2010)

finds.t: Furnaces, slag and casting waste in the same complex as the presses, with evidence that olive oil was burnt as fuel. Copper and cosmetics were run as one business.
Presses, vats and storage jars for oil and wine, the agricultural half of the operation that supplied both the perfumers and the smiths.
Large quantities of molluscs that were not eaten, studied as raw material for dye, ornament or lime rather than as food waste.
Collapsed walls and roofs that buried the workshops with their tools still in position, which is the only reason so fragile an industry can be reconstructed at all.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kalavasos-Laroumena
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A fifteen-hectare promontory just north-west of Kalavasos, next to the thirty-five-hectare terrace of Arkhangelos, both thick with Middle Bronze Age surface finds. The Kalavasos-Laroumena and Arkhangelos Archaeological Research Project began surveying in 2022 and digging in 2023 to fill the one gap in a valley otherwise excavated end to end, the centuries between the Chalcolithic villages and the Late Bronze Age town at Ayios Dhimitrios downstream.

finds.t: The excavators found a building wall running under a modern terrace wall, which suggests the hillside was first cut into terraces to carry houses rather than crops.
Three walls forming a small room packed with thick ash and charcoal, the first securely dated Middle Bronze Age architecture from the site.
Pieces of large storage jars, which the project reads as evidence of families competing in surplus and display, a habit that leads towards the state society of the Late Bronze Age.
Pottery of the late Chalcolithic, Early, Middle and Late Bronze Age and the Iron Age in the same soil, showing people returned to this promontory again and again.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Episkopi-Phaneromeni
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A settlement and cemetery on the ridge less than a kilometre east of Episkopi, above the mouth of the Kouris. J.R. Carpenter and then Stuart Swiny dug it for Kent State University between 1975 and 1978, with a survey of the surrounding country. Because the village runs from the Early Bronze Age through to the very start of the Late Bronze Age and then stops, it is the standard case study for how a southern farming community met, and did not survive, the changes of about 1600 BCE.

finds.t: Agglomerated rooms and courtyards of the Middle Cypriot III and Late Cypriot IA village, among the very few settlements of that transitional moment ever properly excavated in southern Cyprus.
Earlier buildings on the same ridge, so that the two areas together give an Early and Middle Bronze Age sequence in one place.
Rock-cut tombs with Red Polished and White Painted grave goods belonging to the same community as the houses, which is unusual: settlement and cemetery are rarely both available.
finds.w: Kourion Museum, Episkopi; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: The village was given up in Late Cypriot IA, and the reasons, whether coastal insecurity, drought or the pull of new towns, are still argued.
The grinding equipment and spindle whorls of an ordinary household economy, published as a full assemblage rather than as selected pieces.
Swiny's walk over south-west Cyprus around the excavation, which produced the first real map of Bronze Age settlement in the region and is still cited.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayios Sozomenos
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A cluster of fortified sites on the plateau above the meeting of the Alykos and Yialias rivers in the middle of the Mesaoria, built and given up inside about a century and a half around 1750 to 1600 BCE. Barsak, on the cliff edge, had a double circuit wall with a ditch outside it; Nikolidhes, two kilometres to the south-west, was ringed by a wall some 900 metres long with a rectangular tower. Einar Gjerstad dug at Glyka Vrysi in 1924, Hector Catling surveyed the group in the 1950s, and Despina Pilides has excavated here in recent years. Whether these works were raised against raiders from the sea or against each other is the central unresolved question of the period.

finds.t: A double circuit wall with a deep ditch cut outside it, contemporary with the first phase of the settlement at Dzirpoulos and then given up.
An enclosure wall some 920 metres long and over three metres thick in places, built of squared blocks with a rubble core, with substantial walls running inwards to divide the interior.
A tower fifteen metres by seven and a half, of large dressed blocks laid flat, standing clear of the main wall and added later. Somebody decided the fort was not strong enough.
Signs painted and incised on sherds and on storage jars, among the earliest writing on the island and a surprise from a supposedly rural fort.

finds.n: Copper pendant and workshop debris from Dzirpoulos
finds.t: Metalworking areas and a copper pendant from the valley settlement, announced in 2022, which tie the forts to the business of moving copper out of the foothills.
A deep ditch quarried out of the plateau edge in front of the Barsak wall, the plainest statement of intent among all the Cypriot forts: this was built against people.

Two concentric walls, each about two metres thick, along the top of cliffs 40 to 50 metres high, with a deep ditch cut outside them. It is the most heavily defended of the group and commands the whole confluence.

A wall roughly 900 metres in circuit with a rectangular tower about 15 by 7.5 metres, enclosing far more ground than the population is likely to have needed, which suggests refuge for people and animals from a wider district.
Two conjoined walled areas on the plateau containing ordinary domestic buildings, showing that some of these places were lived in rather than manned only in emergencies.
A fortified post at the foot of the plateau beside fresh water, dug by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition under Einar Gjerstad in 1924, the first of the group to be investigated.
finds.w: In situ; finds in Medelhavsmuseet, Stockholm

finds.t: Levantine transport jars and Late Helladic pottery from the settlement areas at Tzirpoulos and Ampelia. Inland forts in the middle of the plain were nonetheless plugged into the sea trade.
Small imported prestige objects from the settlements, the kind of thing that in this period starts to separate some households from others and gives the forts their point.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Nitovikla
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A square fortress of cyclopean masonry on a hill above the south coast of the Karpass, with towers at three corners and flanking the gate and a cistern in its courtyard. The Swedish Cyprus Expedition dug it in 1929 and published it in 1935; tombs nearby date to about 1725 to 1600 BCE. It belongs to a group of forts thrown up as Cyprus turned from a society of villages into one with copper worth defending. The usual reading is that they guarded the routes from the mines to the coast, but whether they watched the sea, the roads or each other is still argued.

finds.t: Walls of huge unworked blocks on a square plan, with corner towers and a gate passage flanked by two more, a design without Cypriot precedent and with Levantine and Anatolian relatives.
A cut cistern in the internal courtyard, which is what allowed the garrison to sit out a siege on a waterless hilltop.
Destruction layers between building phases. Whether they mean warfare, earthquake or accident is not settled, but the fort was twice thought worth rebuilding.
Tombs found by the Swedish team near the fort, which supplied the pottery that dates its foundation.
Photographs, plans and finds from Erik Sjoqvist's season, part of the great division of material between Nicosia and Stockholm that still governs where Cypriot antiquities sit.
The fort's whole logic is visible from it: the plateau routes inland on one side, the sea approach on the other. Whatever it was watching for could come from either.
