A square enclosure built of huge unworked blocks, the earliest monumental defensive architecture on Cyprus. Nothing on the island before this needed walls of this kind.

Towers at three corners and a pair guarding the entrance, a scheme with Levantine and Anatolian parallels rather than Cypriot ones, which is part of why the forts are read as a response to something from outside.

Chamber tombs on the slopes below, excavated in 1929, with Middle Cypriot pottery that supplies the fort's date. The Swedish expedition's Cypriot material forms the core of the Medelhavsmuseet's collection in Stockholm.

The fort looks out over the shortest crossing between Cyprus and the Cilician and Syrian coasts. It has not been excavated again since 1929 and lies today in the north, so almost everything known about it rests on one season's work.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Toumba tou Skourou
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A mound of collapsed mudbrick on the west side of the Ovgos river, on what was then the shore of Morphou bay. Emily Vermeule dug it for Harvard and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, with Florence Wolsky, in 1971 to 1973; the events of 1974 ended the work and the team left the island for good. Under the mound lay a potters' quarter with kilns and clay-working floors, and rich rock-cut tombs whose Cretan, Egyptian and Levantine imports have made the site one of the fixed points for tying the Cypriot Bronze Age sequence to the Aegean one.

finds.t: Aegean pots, Egyptian bronze razors, imported seals, ostrich eggs and objects of faience, ivory, silver, gold, carnelian, amethyst and rock crystal from a handful of chamber tombs. Nothing earlier on Cyprus is so international.
Fine eggshell-thin Cretan pottery, among the earliest Minoan imports on the island. Which mound and context individual pieces came from is not always clear from the record.

Locally made cups whose handles copy Minoan shapes, a potter's own answer to the imports arriving in the harbour. They are the reason the site is discussed in every account of Cretan influence on Cyprus.
Working areas, clay preparation basins and firing installations on the mounds, which gave Vermeule's final report its subtitle and make this the best-known Bronze Age pottery workshop on the island.

finds.n: White Painted and Proto White Slip pottery
finds.t: The local sequence across the Middle to Late Bronze Age join, which is what allows the imports to be dated against Cypriot and Aegean chronologies.
The site's name means the mound of the slag heap, and the mounds themselves are made of collapsed and rebuilt mudbrick, metres deep. Vermeule spent two years working down through them.

A tell of decayed mudbrick that Vermeule's first report called the mound of darkness, on the edge of what is now the town of Guzelyurt. The shore it once stood on has moved: the Ovgos delta silted the bay out, and the site is well inland today.

Multi-chamber rock-cut tombs holding hundreds of vessels, dug into the settlement's own ground. Their contents were published in 1990 with roughly 2,000 photographs and drawings, which is why the site remains usable evidence despite the excavation being cut short.

Cretan pottery in the tombs, closely datable within the Late Minoan sequence, which lets Cypriot phases be pinned against Aegean ones. Vermeule's stratified groups are still cited in arguments about absolute Bronze Age chronology.

Scarabs and imported juglets from Egypt and the Syro-Palestinian coast. Vermeule described the site as the meeting of three foreign strands, Levantine, Egyptian and Minoan, laid over an entirely Cypriot industry.

Work stopped mid-season and was never resumed; the trenches were left as they were and the site now lies inside a modern town in the north. Vermeule published a preliminary account in 1974 and the full report only in 1990.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Maroni-Vournes
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A Late Bronze Age town in the lower Maroni valley about 500 metres from the sea, with a coastal twin at Maroni-Tsaroukkas and an open anchorage offshore; taken together the localities cover something like 35 hectares. The British Museum opened tombs here in 1897, Gerald Cadogan excavated the settlement for the University of Cincinnati between 1982 and 1989, and Sturt Manning worked on the coastal site and its seabed in the 1990s. Its centre was an ashlar building given over to pressing and storing olive oil on a scale far beyond any household's needs, abandoned around 1200 BCE and then reoccupied as a sanctuary in the Iron Age.

finds.t: A tripartite building roughly 30.5 by 21 metres, built partly of large finely cut and closely fitted blocks, with pressing installations and storerooms for olive oil. It is one of a small group of monumental buildings, with Kalavasos and Alassa, that mark the appearance of something like regional administration on Cyprus.

A four-aisled hall separated from the Ashlar Building by a street 4.5 metres wide, of a plan with no close parallel on the island. Whether it was a store, a workshop or a hall of assembly is unsettled; Jan Driessen has argued for reading the whole complex as a seat of power.

Four short texts in the island's undeciphered Bronze Age script, published together in 2016 by Cadogan, Driessen and Silvia Ferrara. They put Maroni among the handful of Cypriot places whose officials wrote things down.
finds.w: Department of Antiquities, Cyprus (exact museum unconfirmed)

finds.n: Stone anchors on the seabed off Tsaroukkas
finds.t: Dozens of pierced stone anchors and large carved sandstone blocks lie in shallow water off the coastal site, first recorded in the 1990s and re-surveyed for a 2022 study of the coastscape. They mark a working roadstead rather than a built harbour: ships anchored off and lightered their cargo ashore.
A pottery model of a vessel from one of the 26 tombs the British Museum emptied at the coastal site in 1897, a rare Cypriot picture of the ships that carried the island's copper.
A hollow pouring vessel in the form of a bull, of a class used to pour liquid offerings, from the Tsaroukkas cemetery. The tombs also gave up Mycenaean vases and gold and faience earrings.

finds.n: The Iron Age sanctuary in the ruins
finds.t: The ashlar building was not left to decay after 1200 BCE. By at least the seventh century BCE people were making offerings among its standing walls, one of the clearest Cypriot cases of a Bronze Age ruin becoming holy ground.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Alassa-Paliotaverna and Pano Mandilaris
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Two localities on a triangular plateau in the Troodos foothills, unknown to archaeology until a salvage survey in 1983 ahead of the Kouris dam. Sophocles Hadjisavvas dug them from 1984 to 2000 and published the final report in 2017. Paliotaverna, on the upper plateau, held a group of three monumental ashlar buildings, the largest a great pi-shaped complex; Pano Mandilaris, 250 metres to the south-east, was a crowded residential quarter with metalworking going on among the houses. Petrographic work on the clay of the Alashiya letters points to this stretch of the south coast rather than to Enkomi, which makes Alassa one of the candidates for where the king of Alashiya actually sat.

finds.t: A pi-shaped complex of about 1,410 square metres built largely of finely cut ashlar blocks, one of the largest Late Bronze Age buildings known on the island. Ashlar masonry on Cyprus is almost always a sign of high status, and this is its fullest display outside Enkomi.

finds.n: Pithoi with relief friezes and seal impressions
finds.t: Some 200 fragments of giant storage jars decorated with raised bands and with friezes rolled on by cylinder seals, the great majority of all such vessels known from Cyprus. The impressions are usually read as marking whose stores the contents were, or which occasions they were kept for.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Limassol District Museum

finds.t: A treading floor and vat inside one of the ashlar buildings, so far the only Late Bronze Age wine press found on Cyprus. Its neighbours at Kalavasos and Maroni pressed olive oil; Alassa also made wine.

Furnace fragments, slag and crucibles set among ordinary houses and small domestic shrines. Metalworking here was neighbourhood work carried on beside cooking and cult, not something shut away in a palace quarter.
Two imported Greek oil jars from Pano Mandilaris, the standard container for perfumed oil moving around the eastern Mediterranean, found in a residential quarter rather than in an elite building.

The dam that prompted the rescue excavation now fills the valley below. The old village was moved uphill and the ancient buildings survive above the waterline, which is why a visitor can still walk the ashlar walls.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Apliki-Karamallos
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Apliki mine, Solea district, Nicosia district
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A miners' village on the north-western flank of the Troodos, in the Solea copper district beside Skouriotissa and Mavrovouni. It came to light in 1938 when the Cyprus Mines Corporation began to open the Apliki orebody, and Joan du Plat Taylor was asked to dig it in haste in 1938 and 1939. Lead isotope analysis has since matched almost every oxhide ingot yet tested, on Cyprus and abroad, to ores of this district and above all to Apliki, which makes this small and short-lived settlement the source of the metal the Bronze Age world was buying. Most of it has been eaten by modern open-cast mining; Taylor's notebooks were finally published in full in 2012.

finds.n: The L-shaped building of Area A
finds.t: A multi-room house on a rock terrace with storage vessels set into its floors, the only dwelling of Late Bronze Age Cypriot copper miners ever excavated. The jars are usually read as rations and supplies issued to a workforce rather than as a family's own stores.
finds.w: Destroyed by modern mining; recorded in du Plat Taylor's plans

finds.t: The settlement sat on terraces of its own waste. Smelting was done at the mine head, where the fuel and the ore were, and the metal then travelled to the coast as ingots rather than as rock.

finds.n: Ivory cylinder, steatite cylinder seal and gold earring
finds.t: Small valuables from the houses. Even a company village at the pit head had objects worth keeping, and a seal implies somebody there had to authorise something.

The ship wrecked off Uluburun in Turkey carried 354 oxhide ingots, about ten tonnes of copper, with roughly a tonne of tin and nine Cypriot storage jars packed with pottery, oil or pomegranates. The lead isotopes of the copper point back to the Solea mines. Excavated by the Institute of Nautical Archaeology from 1984 to 1994.
finds.w: Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, Turkey

finds.t: Copper cast in slabs the shape of a stretched hide, with a handhold at each corner and weighing around 30 kg, has been found from Sardinia to Anatolia and inland into Bulgaria. Every analysed ingot of fourteenth-century date or later is isotopically Cypriot, which is as close as archaeology comes to a trademark.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Bodrum Museum; National Archaeological Museum, Cagliari

finds.t: This district produced more than four-fifths of the copper concentrate Cyprus exported in modern times. The pit that revealed the Bronze Age village is also what destroyed it, and the working landscape of terraces and red spoil is what a visitor sees.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Myrtou-Pigadhes
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A sanctuary in the hills south of Myrtou, used from about 1650 BCE to the end of the Bronze Age and excavated in 1949 and 1950 by Joan du Plat Taylor and Veronica Seton-Williams for the Department of Antiquities. Its courtyard holds a stepped altar of dressed stone crowned with carved horns, the Cretan sign of sanctity known as horns of consecration, rebuilt on the spot by the excavators. The wells that give the place its name, pigadhes, supplied the rites. Bones of sheep, goat and deer, hearths and a mass of drinking vessels point to sacrifice and feasting in the open rather than to a temple with a resident priesthood.

finds.t: A stepped block-built altar in the west court, re-erected by the excavators with a pair of stone horns on top. It is the largest and best preserved of its kind on Cyprus and the plainest borrowing of Minoan religious symbolism on the island; what stands today is a reconstruction, and its exact original height is not certain.

finds.n: The wells and the west court
finds.t: Rock-cut wells and a paved court with hearths for burnt offerings, built and rebuilt over some six centuries. The sanctuary began as a modest platform and was monumentalised in stages.
Small clay bulls and human figures left as offerings, part of a Cypriot cult of the bull that runs from the Vounous models of the third millennium to the Enkomi Horned God.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Ashmolean Museum, Oxford

finds.t: Bones of sheep, goat and deer with shells and quantities of eating and drinking vessels, the residue of communal meals. Cypriot Bronze Age religion is legible mostly through what was eaten at it.
Aegean stirrup jars and fine ware among the offerings, showing that even an inland country sanctuary in the north received goods from the sea trade.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Ashmolean Museum, Oxford

finds.t: Metal tools from the sanctuary deposits, likely used in butchering the sacrifices, alongside the copper that paid for everything else on the island.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Episkopi-Bamboula
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The Late Bronze Age town of the lower Kouris valley, on a low hill by Episkopi a short way inland from the sea, excavated by the University of Pennsylvania Museum from 1934 under Bertram Hill, George McFadden and John Franklin Daniel. Six hectares of planned housing with streets and wells, an outer town and a fortified inner town on the hill, and the dead buried among the living in single-chamber tombs. Its seals and writing tools give the best stratified sequence for Cypriot administration and for the island's earliest writing; it was never sacked, but drifted into abandonment by the later twelfth century BCE, and the population later gathered on the cliff at Kourion above.

finds.n: Bamboula hill and its circuit wall
finds.t: A fortification wall thrown round the inner town in the thirteenth century BCE, with the open outer town spreading beyond it. The hill is the visible remnant of a place that once functioned as the harbour arm of an inland polity, probably centred at Alassa.
Rectangular dwellings of five or six rooms on stone footings with mudbrick above, each a distinct household unit on a laid-out street grid rather than an organic huddle.

finds.n: Cylinder seals and bronze writing styli
finds.t: Seals used both as administrative devices and as personal ornaments, found with the metal styli used to cut Cypro-Minoan signs into clay. Because they come from a stratified settlement rather than from looted tombs, they underpin the dating of Cypriot seals and of the script.
finds.w: Penn Museum, Philadelphia; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Hoop earrings finished with the head of a bull, a characteristic Cypriot type, from the intramural tombs. The bull runs through Cypriot Bronze Age imagery from ploughing models to the Horned God.
finds.w: Penn Museum, Philadelphia; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.n: Hippopotamus tusks, an ostrich egg and a glass pomegranate
finds.t: Exotica from the tombs: raw ivory from the Nile, an ostrich egg, and a small pomegranate of glass, along with faience beads, alabaster and Egyptian scarabs. A short list of one tomb group maps most of the eastern Mediterranean.
finds.w: Penn Museum, Philadelphia; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.n: Mycenaean and Red Lustrous Wheelmade pottery
finds.t: Greek drinking and oil vessels alongside the hard, thin-walled red spindle bottles traded all over the Levant, whose place of manufacture, Cyprus or Anatolia, is still disputed.
finds.w: Penn Museum, Philadelphia; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

SETTLEMENTS.name: Salamis, the Royal Necropolis
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A cemetery of some seven square kilometres west of the city, where nine great built chamber tombs of the late eighth to early sixth centuries BCE were approached by long ramps. Horses in harness were killed at the ramp mouth and left where they fell, sometimes still yoked to a chariot or a hearse, and the burials were furnished with ivory furniture, bronze cauldrons, jars of oil and honey and imported Levantine and Greek pottery. Vassos Karageorghis and Porphyrios Dikaios began systematic excavation in 1957; every chamber had already been robbed, so almost everything known comes from the ramps and the forecourts. The resemblance to the funeral of Patroklos in the Iliad has been argued over ever since, some reading it as living Homeric practice and others as eighth-century kings deliberately staging an ancestral past.

finds.t: The richest of the tombs, used twice within a few years. Two horses lay in the ramp with the impressions of a chariot and a hearse in the soil beside them, along with bronze harness, iron bits and a yoke.
finds.w: In situ; contents in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.n: Ivory throne and bed from Tomb 79
finds.t: Furniture of wood faced with carved ivory plaques, some inlaid with blue glass and gold leaf, in a Phoenician and Egyptianising manner. A throne of the same kind is what Homer's Penelope sits on, and the parallel has kept the tomb in the literature for seventy years.

finds.n: Bronze horse trappings with blinkers and frontlets
finds.t: Embossed bronze blinkers and forehead plates showing a lion attacking a bull and a sphinx before a sacred tree, made for the sacrificed teams. The nearest parallels come from Assyrian sites, and whether they were imported or made on the island is still argued.

One of only two tombs in the necropolis covered by an earth tumulus. Its iron weapons include a sword with silver rivets in the hilt, a large spearhead and arrowheads, an armoury rather than a set of ornaments.
finds.w: In situ; weapons in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Rows of large storage jars stacked in the forecourts, some with the residue of olive oil and honey still detectable. They are the physical trace of the funeral feast and of offerings poured for the dead.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; some in situ

finds.t: A crowded field of small rock-cut tombs cut into the soft limestone a little south of the royal tombs, reached by steep stepped passages, used by ordinary Salaminians for four centuries. Many held cremations in jars, and the contrast with the ramped tombs is the clearest picture of social rank the island offers.

A mound over a mudbrick platform on which clay heads and torsos of near life size stood among burnt offerings, but with no burial beneath. It is usually read as an empty memorial to Nikokreon, the last king of Salamis, whose family killed themselves in the palace around 311 BCE, though the identification rests on argument rather than an inscription.
finds.w: In situ; clay figures in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

SETTLEMENTS.name: Palaepaphos-Skales
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The main cemetery of Palaepaphos at the moment the Bronze Age ended and the Iron Age began, about a kilometre south-east of the town. Bulldozing for farmland exposed the tombs, and more than fifty chamber graves were dug in the winter and spring of 1979 under Vassos Karageorghis, with further rescue work down to 2011. The dead were laid in chambers reached by long sloping passages, with bronze bowls, gold and faience jewellery, iron weapons and the roasting spits that mark a meat-eating warrior elite. Because one of those spits carries a Greek name in the local syllabary, Skales is the single site most often cited for the arrival of Greek speakers on Cyprus.

finds.t: A chamber tomb holding three bronze roasting spits, one of them inscribed in the syllabary with the genitive of a Greek personal name, Opheltas. The tomb is the find context for the earliest Greek text from the island, and the reading of the last sign is still discussed.
finds.w: In situ (backfilled); contents in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: Knives with iron blades riveted into bronze or ivory handles, among the earliest worked iron on Cyprus. They show local smiths mastering the new metal while the old one was still the prestige material.
The first pottery of the Iron Age, decorated with Aegean-derived motifs but made in Cypriot shapes, in quantity here for the first time. Skales gave the type its stratigraphic anchor.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Kouklia Local Museum

finds.t: Gold spiral earrings, embossed sheet-gold mouthpieces and diadems, and faience and glass beads of Egyptian and Levantine type. They show that Paphos was still trading east while the Aegean palaces were in ruins.

A minority of the dead were burned and their bones gathered into jars, a practice new to Cyprus at this date. Recent osteological work on the cremated bone is being used to test whether the rite marks incomers or a new fashion among locals.
finds.w: Studied material with the Department of Antiquities, Cyprus

finds.t: One of the later-excavated graves, unusually well furnished with bronze vessels and weapons and published in 2021. Its contents strengthened the case that a small hereditary elite at Paphos survived the Bronze Age collapse intact.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kourion-Kaloriziki
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The cemetery on the saddle below the Kourion bluff, and for a long time the only real evidence for the early history of the kingdom, since the Iron Age town itself has never been found. The University of Pennsylvania Museum expedition dug here in the 1930s, and its tombs run from the eleventh century BCE to Classical times, with the Cypro-Geometric graves the richest. Their bronze vessels and Aegean-style pottery were once read as the graves of Argive founders arriving after the Trojan War; the current reading is more cautious, and speaks of local elites who chose Aegean things.

finds.t: A short gold staff whose head is a globe of cloisonné enamel surmounted by two falcons, about 16 cm long. The enamelling has no Aegean parallel and looks Egyptian in technique, and it is one of the earliest true enamels anywhere; it is usually called royal, though the tomb was disturbed and the claim cannot be proved.

finds.p: First half of the 11th century BCE
finds.t: A shaft grave holding a cremation in a bronze vessel, two bronze rod tripod stands, the remains of a shield and the gold sceptre. Once described as the tomb of the Achaean founder of Kourion, it is now more often read as the grave of a Cypriot or Phoenician notable.
finds.w: In situ (backfilled); contents in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia, and the Penn Museum, Philadelphia

finds.t: Openwork stands of cast bronze rods made to carry a bowl, a Cypriot speciality of the very end of the Bronze Age. Examples travelled to Crete and the Greek mainland, and they are the clearest sign that Cypriot smiths were still exporting skill after the palaces fell.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Penn Museum, Philadelphia

finds.t: Rock-cut chambers entered from short passages, reused over generations, with painted pottery, iron weapons and imported Levantine flasks. Their gold and silver point to a community growing steadily richer on the copper and timber of the Kouris valley.
Painted cups and jugs from Euboea, Attica and the East Greek islands, in higher proportion here than at any other Cypriot cemetery of the period. Kourion looked west while Kition looked east.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; Penn Museum, Philadelphia

SETTLEMENTS.name: Meniko-Litharkes
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A small country sanctuary on the northern approaches to the Troodos, near the copper ground of Mitsero, excavated by the Department of Antiquities under Vassos Karageorghis in the early 1970s and published with a second shrine in 1977. It matters because the deity worshipped in it was not Greek: the cult statuary is of the Phoenician Baal Hamman, the bearded god enthroned between rams, in a village well inland from Phoenician Kition. Meniko is the standard evidence that Phoenician religion reached the Cypriot countryside and not only the coastal city, probably along the road to the mines.

finds.n: Limestone statue of an enthroned bearded god
finds.t: A seated male figure with a long squared beard on a throne whose arms end in rams' heads, the standard image of Baal Hamman. No inscription names him, so the identification rests on the iconography, which is why some prefer the neutral 'enthroned god'.

A companion figure of the same god at smaller scale, found in the same rooms. Two images of one deity in one small shrine is unusual and has been read as an old statue kept in service beside its replacement.
A block cut with a shallow burning hollow, of the type used for aromatics in Phoenician cult. Burnt residue on such altars is the plainest surviving trace of what actually happened in these shrines.

A modest rectangular structure of rubble and mudbrick with a court and inner rooms, not a temple in the Greek sense but a walled house for the god and his offerings. It went out of use around the end of the Archaic period and was not rebuilt.
finds.w: In situ, Meniko (unroofed and largely reburied)

finds.t: Mould-made and handmade clay figures, including horse-and-rider groups and bulls, left by ordinary visitors. They are the same repertoire found at Greek-dedicated shrines on the island, which is the point: the offerings were Cypriot even when the god was not.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kafizin
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Conical hill south-east of Nicosia, near Aglantzia
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A cave shrine to a Nymph on a conical hill south-east of Nicosia, dug in 1939 and again between 1949 and 1955 and published by Terence Mitford in 1980. It produced some 310 inscribed pots and terracottas, of which 269 were dedicated by one man: Onesagoras son of Philounios, a barber who gave himself the title dekatephoros, tithe-bringer. The dedications are dated between 225 and 218 BCE and many are written out twice, once in the Cypriot syllabary and once in the Greek alphabet, which pushed the survival of the old script down to the end of the third century BCE. It is the best evidence anywhere for how an ordinary Cypriot under the Ptolemies actually spoke to a god.

finds.t: About 310 pots, of which 269 were dedicated by Onesagoras, inscribed before and after firing with dates, quantities and addresses to the Nymph. They read like a working ledger crossed with prayer, and they carry precise regnal dates, which is why the group anchors so much Cypriot chronology.

finds.n: Syllabic and alphabetic texts side by side
finds.t: Some vessels carry the Cypriot syllabary, some the Greek alphabet, and some both, occasionally mixing the two in one word. Nowhere else can the retreat of the syllabary be watched at this resolution.

finds.n: The cave and the conical hill
finds.t: A rock cavity on a steep isolated cone, called simply 'the conical hill' in the inscriptions themselves, a phrase attested at no other Cypriot site. The hill is a landmark from the Mesaoria and needs no signpost.

Onesagoras styles himself tithe-bearer, apparently a man who brought a tenth of a crop or a trade to the goddess. Whether this was a priesthood, a tax office or a private vow he invented for himself is still argued.
finds.w: Texts in the Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: A smaller group of pots names other dedicants, among them relatives and men described as fellow workers, so the shrine was not a one-man affair. The names are a rare census of ordinary Hellenistic Cypriots.

269 of the roughly 310 inscribed vessels from the shrine were given by a single barber, an intensity of devotion that has led scholars to call him a nympholept, a man seized by the Nymph. No other Greek sanctuary has anything comparable from one hand.

Texts written in both the Cypriot syllabary and the Greek alphabet on the same vessel. They are the latest securely dated syllabic writing on the island and they killed the older view that the script died out with the city-kingdoms.

finds.n: The Nymph of the conical hill
finds.t: The goddess is addressed as dwelling in the conical hill itself and given epithets such as mountain-ranging and sister. She has no name, no temple and no statue: the hill is the cult.
The texts are full of rare or otherwise unknown words whose meanings are still argued over, which is why a small rural shrine has a bibliography out of all proportion to its size.
Alongside ordinary jugs the shrine produced ceramic and terracotta objects of shapes not found elsewhere, apparently made for the cult rather than adapted from household ware.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Arsos, sanctuary of Aphrodite
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Arsos (Yiğitler), Larnaca district, now in the north
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A rural sanctuary of Aphrodite in the eastern Mesaoria, known from inscriptions that call the goddess Golgia, the Aphrodite of Golgoi, so the shrine belonged to a cult network rather than standing alone. Its votive deposit was unusual for containing mostly female statues, which makes it the best single source for how Cypriot sculptors handled women, from stiff Archaic figures in heavy jewellery to softened Hellenistic types. The finds were dispersed in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and the shrine has never been properly excavated or securely located on the ground.

finds.t: Standing women in long chitons with earrings, necklaces and flower-held-to-the-breast gestures, a series long enough to trace three centuries of changing style. They are the counterweight to the male votaries that dominate almost every other Cypriot sanctuary.
finds.w: Cyprus Museum, Nicosia; British Museum, London; other European collections

finds.t: Inscriptions naming the goddess as Golgia, the epithet that ties Arsos to the great sanctuary town of Golgoi some twelve kilometres west. They are the reason the site is identified as Aphrodite's at all.
Mould-made clay figures of women, some holding infants or tambourines, cheap versions of the stone votaries. They show who was actually paying: villagers, not kings.

Limestone heads with the almond eyes and pressed smile borrowed from East Greek sculpture, wearing wreaths and diadems. Arsos is one of the sites used to date the moment Cypriot carvers turned from Egyptian to Ionian models.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Achna, rural sanctuary
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Achna (Düzce), between Larnaca and Famagusta, now in the north
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A country shrine in the plain between Kition and Salamis, usually said to be Artemis's, emptied in 1882 by Max Ohnefalsch-Richter working for the British Museum. More than a thousand stone and terracotta figures came out of it, and almost nothing was recorded about where any of them lay, so Achna has become the standard example of how much Cypriot archaeology was lost while it was being collected. The finds were divided between sponsors and are now spread across the British Museum, the Louvre, the Pierides Museum and the Cyprus Museum.

finds.t: Over a thousand limestone and terracotta figures dug out in a single season of 1882. The sheer number shows a shrine used continuously for four centuries, but with no plan and no stratigraphy nothing can be said about how the cult worked.
finds.w: British Museum, London; Louvre, Paris; Pierides Museum, Larnaca; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: A clay female figure about 40 cm high, pressed from a mould with the hands to the breasts in the Levantine Astarte pose. Mass production of this kind put a goddess within reach of anyone who could pay a potter.

Male figures in the pleated kilt and double crown borrowed from Egypt, a fashion that swept Cypriot sculpture while the island paid tribute to the Saite pharaohs. Achna supplied a large part of the series now in London and Paris.
Small clay riders on stiff-legged horses, a type found at almost every Cypriot country shrine and probably a soldier's or a traveller's offering. Achna produced them in quantity.
finds.w: British Museum, London; Cyprus Museum, Nicosia

finds.t: The sanctuary itself has never been relocated on the ground; the village was abandoned in 1974 and no modern survey has fixed the temenos. It is the clearest case on the island of a major site known only from its objects.
finds.w: Site location unrecorded, Achna village lands

SETTLEMENTS.name: Agios Georgios-Pegeia (Cape Drepanon)
SETTLEMENTS.desc: An unwalled town spread over the neck and southern slope of Cape Drepanon, busy in the Roman period and at its height under Justinian, when three basilicas and a bath house stood on the headland. Its position at the island's north-west corner made it a natural call for ships carrying Egyptian grain to Constantinople, and the sherd dumps show it shipped wine of its own as well. The Department of Antiquities dug the churches between 1952 and 1955; the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki from 1992 and the Greek Archaeological Expedition since 1999 have worked on the settlement itself, which turned what had looked like a pilgrimage complex into a proper town.

finds.t: The largest of the three churches, three-aisled with a baptistery against its west end, standing on the neck of the cape where the main street ran. Its floors are laid with mosaic panels of geometric patterns and animals.
A three-aisled church lower down the southern slope, close to the shore and the anchorage that the town used.

finds.n: Basilica C, with its oil press and hostel
finds.t: The smallest church, with a range of working buildings attached: an oil press and a block the excavators read as lodging for travellers. It is the clearest sign that the cape served people passing through.
A small bath complex beside Basilica A, generous for a settlement of this size and one of the reasons the site is read as a watering and victualling stop for shipping.

finds.n: Rock-cut necropolis on the cliff edge
finds.t: Chamber tombs cut into the soft rock along the cliff, with a further cemetery inland in the Meletis forest above the cape.

More than 700 kg of amphora sherds recorded under Stella Demesticha of the University of Cyprus, dominated by Late Roman 1 jars made near Paphos and in Cilicia, with Gaza and Palestinian imports among them. It is one of the plainest pictures anywhere of what a Cypriot port actually handled.
finds.w: Study collection, University of Cyprus and site store

finds.t: A small vaulted chapel raised over part of the abandoned town, the reason the cape still carries the saint's name and still draws pilgrims on his feast day.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Yeronisos
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Islet off Cape Drepanon, Pegeia, Paphos district
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A flat-topped islet of about 2.6 hectares rising some 21 m out of the sea a short way off Cape Drepanon, its name meaning Holy Island. Sophocles Hadjisavvas began digging in 1982 when a hotel was proposed for it, and Joan Breton Connelly of New York University has directed the excavation since 1990. In the last decades of Ptolemaic rule, under Cleopatra VII, a striking amount of money went into turning the rock into a sanctuary of Apollo with its own kitchens, stores and lookout; it was abandoned after an earthquake around the turn of the era. Chalcolithic remains lie beneath the Hellenistic buildings and a Byzantine reservoir and animal shelters above them.

finds.t: A potsherd inscribed with the god's name, and the only object that actually names the divinity of Holy Island. The identification of the sanctuary rests on this sherd and on amulets that match ones from Apollo shrines elsewhere on Cyprus.
The only Ptolemaic ostraka found on Cyprus, written in Greek and concerned with the running of the sanctuary and its stores. Ostraka of this kind are common in Egypt and almost unknown on the island.
A slab pierced with a row of holes for a peg to be shifted along through the days of the month, a working calendar of a kind rare anywhere in the Greek world.

Small pierced amulets shaped rather like miniature loom weights, cut with a mixture of old Cypriot and Ptolemaic Egyptian motifs. Twenty-five years of digging have produced a whole series, and they are the strongest argument for what kind of cult was practised here.
A paved circle in the middle of the island that Connelly reads as a dance floor used in rites of passage for boys. That is an interpretation and not a certainty, and other readings are possible.

A complex of rooms for preparing, distributing and storing food, built along the island's southern edge in the final years of Ptolemaic rule; in one room the plaster of the ground floor is still on the wall.

Stone tools from the island's first occupation, many found in the Hellenistic food-preparation area where they appear to have been picked up and put back to work three and a half thousand years later.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Akrotiri-Katalymata ton Plakoton
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Akrotiri peninsula, Limassol district (Western Sovereign Base Area)
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A church complex about 100 m long standing on its own in the western forest of the Akrotiri peninsula, surveyed from 2007 and excavated by Eleni Procopiou for the Department of Antiquities. Its main church is a three-aisled basilica 36 m wide and 29 m long crossed by a transverse aisle, a transept plan otherwise unknown on Cyprus and rare in the eastern Mediterranean. Pottery and inscriptions place its building in the first years of the reign of Heraclius, about 616 to 619, and its destruction shortly before the middle of the seventh century. Why so grand and so unusual a building was raised on an empty headland is still argued over.

finds.t: A three-aisled church 36 m by 29 m with a transverse aisle crossing the nave in front of the sanctuary. No other transept basilica is known on Cyprus, which is why the building is read as the work of masons and patrons from outside the island.
A narthex with three aisled branches forming a T, doubling as a martyrium. The plan implies relics or venerated burials, though whose is unknown.
Cut-marble and mosaic paving of high quality, uncovered in 2018, carrying Christian inscriptions of the reign of Heraclius including the plea 'My Lord, help those who honour thy name'.

A second sanctuary within the same 100 m complex, only partly dug. The pair make the site far more than a village church, and Procopiou has connected it with clergy fleeing the Persian conquest of Syria and Palestine, a reading that is not settled.
A carved stele from the martyrium recently read as setting Alexander the Great beside the emperor Heraclius. The reading is new and contested and should be treated as a proposal rather than a fact.
finds.w: Reported from the site; publication in progress

finds.t: The complex was wrecked and abandoned shortly before the middle of the seventh century, in the years of the first Arab raids, and never rebuilt or robbed for stone, which is why so much of its floor survives.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Akrotiri-Dreamer's Bay
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A line of stone warehouses along the shore of a small bay at the southernmost point of Cyprus, with a masonry breakwater now under water and quarries on the cliffs behind. John Leonard and Stella Demesticha surveyed it from 2000; Simon James of the University of Leicester, with Vicki Score as field director, has excavated since 2015. The digging killed the old idea of a lost port town: geophysics and trenching found no houses behind the warehouses, so the harbour was worked by people living in the villages across the middle of the peninsula and probably by Kourion. Lying inside a military base has left it one of the best preserved ancient ports in the Mediterranean.

finds.t: Long stone buildings sharing a single alignment, several with internal partitions and walled yards, laid out in one short planned episode rather than growing piecemeal. Burnt deposits in some of them suggest workshops as well as stores.
A masonry mole now beneath the water of the bay, along with scattered stone columns. How it joined the buildings on shore has still to be worked out.

Quarries cut into the marine conglomerate above the bay for squared building blocks and millstones, with ceramic water channels and small buildings beside them. Exporting stone appears to have been the port's industrial reason for existing.

Most of the warehouses were brought down by an earthquake, part of the same run of shocks that ruined Kourion a few years later. Near the harbour, in the excavators' Area 4, some buildings were put back up later in the fourth century.

Surface survey, trial trenches and geophysics over the ground behind the warehouses found no residential quarter at all, overturning the assumption that a town stood here. It is a useful reminder of how easily a row of buildings gets read as a city.

A broad spread of ancient material on the seabed off the bay, reported as covering some 130,000 square metres. Whether it is a single large wreck or an anchorage littered with jettisoned and lost cargo is not settled.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Pyla-Koutsopetria
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A hundred-hectare stretch of coast about 10 km east of Larnaca and much the same distance from ancient Kition, surveyed intensively since 2003 by William Caraher, R. Scott Moore and David Pettegrew. The ground carries an Iron Age sanctuary, a Classical and Hellenistic fortification on the Vigla ridge, a Late Roman town beside a bay that has since silted solid, and a coastal battery of the Venetian or Ottoman period. Its interest is method as much as material: the project published its survey data openly through Open Context, and it puts on the map a substantial Cypriot coastal settlement that no ancient author names.

finds.n: The fortification on the Vigla ridge
finds.t: Defensive walls excavated on the coastal ridge, the second time in a thousand years that people fortified this bay after Late Bronze Age Kokkinokremos a short way west. The repetition suggests the embayment itself was the strategic asset.
Geomorphological work identified a natural bay behind the present beach, now completely filled in, which would have served as the harbour for everyone living in the Pyla area.

A dense spread of building material, tile and pottery marking a substantial settlement that was the largest phase of occupation on the site. Only a small part has been excavated; almost everything known comes from survey.
Quantities of Late Roman 1 amphora sherds, the standard Cypriot and Cilician wine and oil jar of the period, showing the place was shipping out as well as consuming.
finds.w: Study collection; data published on Open Context

finds.t: Votive terracottas and other sanctuary debris from the earliest phase of the microregion, the beginning of a sequence that runs almost unbroken to the seventh century CE.
A small gun position beside the shore, the last military use of a bay that had been fortified twice already in antiquity.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Kalavasos-Kopetra
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The most thoroughly published Late Roman village on Cyprus, dug in the Vasilikos valley by Marcus Rautman and Murray McClellan and published in 2003. Three basilicas of the sixth and early seventh centuries stood in a settlement of a few hundred people, along with houses, storerooms and pressing installations. Its pottery, tested by neutron activation, was mostly made from the valley's own clays, while the amphora kilns at Zygi-Petrini a few kilometres away were turning out the standard export jar of the eastern Mediterranean. Kopetra matters because it shows the Cypriot countryside was not a backwater but wired into the economy of the late empire.

finds.t: Three churches for one modest village, all elaborately decorated, in the excavation areas the team called Kopetra, Sirmata and Spilios. Nobody has a wholly satisfying explanation for why a settlement this size needed three.
Pressing installations and storage rooms for oil and wine, the machinery of the surplus that paid for the churches.
Rubble-built rooms and courtyards of ordinary domestic use, the sort of evidence that almost never gets published in full for a Cypriot rural site.

Neutron activation analysis of the coarse and cooking wares matched most of them to clays from the Vasilikos valley itself, while the fine wares and amphorae came in from further afield. It is one of the earliest applications of the technique to a Cypriot rural assemblage.
Coins running from the fourth century and stopping early in the seventh, which is how the village's end is dated. The same terminal date turns up at Maroni-Petrera and across the south coast.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Maroni-Petrera
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A small rural church a little inland from the south coast, in what was probably the territory of Amathus. A bulldozer went through it in 1991, and Sturt Manning's Maroni Valley survey recorded and salvaged what was left between 1990 and 1997. Two churches were found, one succeeding the other on the same spot: a nearly square building of the early to mid fifth century, replaced around 500 by a larger one with a polygonal apse. Modest as it is, it is one of the very few rural churches on the island to have been properly excavated and published.

finds.t: An almost square church with large apses projecting from the east wall. The publication describes it as three-aisled, but its original arrangement seems to have been twin-aisled, which would be unusual in Early Christian architecture on Cyprus and has not been explained.

A larger three-aisled replacement with an apse polygonal on the outside, a surprisingly deep narthex later subdivided, and a separate chapel alongside. Both the external polygonal apse and the deep narthex are uncommon on the island.
One of several graves at the site, this one inside the apse itself, the most honoured position in a church and normally reserved for a founder or a cleric.
Tiles stamped with raised patterns, part of an assemblage of worked stone, glass and metal that lets the church be dated and its building materials sourced.
A cut and lined cistern beside the church, with a nearby building of uncertain function that produced the same range of dates.
Coins of the first half of the seventh century are the latest things on the site, putting its abandonment in the generation of the Arab raids.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Panayia Ematousa
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A rural site beside the chapel of Panayia Ematousa north of Aradippou, excavated by the University of Copenhagen between 1991 and 1999 as part of the teaching programme in classical archaeology and published in two volumes by the Danish Institute at Athens. Four periods of activity were found: Archaic to Early Classical, Hellenistic, Early Roman and Late Roman. Almost everything known about Hellenistic and Early Roman Cyprus comes from cities, so a farming settlement of those centuries dug and published in full is out of proportion to its size in importance.

finds.t: Four distinct phases of use separated in the stratigraphy, running from the Archaic and Early Classical periods through the Hellenistic and Early Roman to a Late Roman occupation. The sequence, not any single object, is what the site is famous for.

finds.n: Hellenistic and Early Roman fine wares
finds.t: Imported table pottery studied by John Lund, which shows which Mediterranean markets an ordinary Cypriot farming household was tied into, and when those ties shifted.
Querns, stone tools, cooking pots and loomweights: the ordinary furniture of rural life, and the reason the excavation can say something about work rather than just about dates.
The final occupation, contemporary with Kopetra, Maroni-Petrera and Pyla-Koutsopetria, and part of the same picture of a countryside busier in late antiquity than at any time since the Bronze Age.
The small church that gives the site its name and still stands beside it; the excavation trenches lie in the fields around it.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Aphendrika (Ourania)
SETTLEMENTS.desc: Strabo names Ourania among the towns of the Karpas, and in 306 BCE the troops of Demetrius Poliorcetes landed at neighbouring Karpasia and took both towns before marching on Salamis. What a visitor sees now is later: three ruined churches in a row, a citadel cut into the living rock on the hill behind, rock-cut tombs, and the silted harbour below. Nothing at Aphendrika has been excavated to modern standards, which is why the dates given for its churches vary widely from one account to the next, and it sits in the occupied north with no prospect of work soon.

finds.p: Byzantine, with a later chapel inserted
finds.t: The largest of the three churches, a ruined basilica into which a smaller vaulted chapel was later built, a common Cypriot economy when a congregation shrank.
A domed church of ashlar masonry standing next to the Chrysiotissa, with its vaults partly intact.
The third and smallest of the group, which gave the whole site its modern name. The three standing side by side are the reason the place is visited at all.
A fortified outcrop behind the churches with chambers, stairs and cisterns cut into the rock itself, the most likely core of the ancient town.
Chamber tombs cut into the rock around the site, the necropolis of Ourania. They have been robbed repeatedly and never recorded properly.
A small anchorage below the site, now largely silted, of the same family as the harbour moles still visible at Karpasia a few kilometres west.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Panagia Angeloktisti
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A domed church of the eleventh or twelfth century built over a fifth-century basilica whose apse was deliberately kept, because of what it held: a mosaic of the Virgin between two archangels, one of the finest pieces of early Byzantine wall mosaic anywhere. The name means 'built by angels'. A small dig under the floor in 1959 found graves cut into the older foundations and traces of two earlier building phases, a columned basilica and then a pier basilica. Whether the old apse was reused to save labour or out of reverence for the mosaic is still argued.

finds.n: The apse mosaic of the Virgin
finds.t: The Virgin stands on a footstool with the Christ Child on her left arm, flanked by Michael and Gabriel whose wings are worked in peacock feathers, all against a gold ground. The angels hold a sceptre and offer a globe surmounted by a cross. Scholars compare the modelling of the faces to San Vitale at Ravenna and the type to the apse of Saint Catherine's in Sinai.

The mosaic labels the Virgin 'Holy Mary' rather than Theotokos, Mother of God. The usage spread after the Council of Ephesus of 431 confirmed her title, and it is one small clue to how Cypriot churchmen read that council.

A jewelled frame in which pairs of ducks, beribboned parrots and stags drink from fountains. The parrot was a Persian sign of earthly power and the stag a reference to Psalm 42; the same imagery turns up on Bishop Agnellus's ambo at Ravenna and in churches in Macedonia and Dalmatia.

finds.p: 5th century CE, rebuilt in the 6th or 7th
finds.t: The timber-roofed basilica burned or collapsed in the seventh or eighth century, in the years of the Arab raids, but its apse was left standing and built into the small domed church that replaced it. The same trick was used at Panagia tis Kyras at Livadia.
Burials cut into the basilica's foundations, found in the 1959 excavation, showing the early church had also been a burial ground before the domed church went up.

finds.n: The Latin chapel on the south side
finds.p: Usually dated to the 14th or 15th century
finds.t: A small vaulted chapel, often called the chapel of Saints Cosmas and Damian, added against the south wall in the Frankish period; it carries armorial carving and is the clearest sign that Kiti kept a Latin as well as an Orthodox congregation.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Panagia Kanakaria
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A church of many periods beside the Famagusta road, whose central apse belonged to a fifth-century basilica and whose vaults and dome were raised over the old plan, probably in the eleventh century. Its sixth-century apse mosaic was one of only a handful of Byzantine wall mosaics anywhere to survive Iconoclasm. The priests left in 1976; by November 1979 word reached the Department of Antiquities that the church had been stripped and was being used to stable animals, and that the mosaic had been cut out of the wall with axes. Recovering four of the fragments through the American courts produced the leading modern judgment on buying looted antiquities.

finds.n: The apse mosaic of the Virgin enthroned
finds.t: The Virgin sat on a throne with the Christ Child on her lap, two archangels attending, and the twelve apostles in medallions ringed with acanthus around the arch. The handling is looser and more impressionistic than the mosaic at Kiti; the date is still argued, but most put it in the sixth century alongside the work at Ravenna.
finds.w: Byzantine Museum, Nicosia (recovered fragments); much of it still missing

finds.t: Four pieces about two feet square showing Christ, the bust of an attending archangel, the apostle Matthew and the apostle James. The Indiana dealer Peg Goldberg bought them for 1,080,000 dollars in cash in the free port area of Geneva airport on 7 July 1988, from the Munich-based dealer Aydin Dikmen through a chain of intermediaries who had contracted to buy them for 350,000.

finds.n: Autocephalous Church of Cyprus v. Goldberg
finds.t: Judge Noland of the Southern District of Indiana awarded the mosaics to the Church of Cyprus in 1989, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed on 24 October 1990, holding that a buyer who asked so few questions in such suspicious circumstances could not take good title. The opinion's advice to dealers, to run a full background check on the seller and his claim, is now the standard citation for due diligence in the antiquities trade.
One more roundel from the frieze of apostles was traced and handed back in 2018 through private intermediaries. Several other pieces of the mosaic have never been found.

The wooden-roofed basilica was rebuilt as a three-aisled church with apsidal east ends, vaults and a dome, keeping the old apse. The narthex on the west followed in the twelfth century and the little bell tower in the late nineteenth.

The best-preserved of the church's many layers of painting, with clear Italian influence. The Stylianous, who catalogued the island's painted churches, wrote off the rest as of interest only to specialists because of their condition.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Monastery of Ayios Varnavas
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Near Enkomi (Tuzla), 2 km west of Salamis
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The shrine that made the Church of Cyprus independent. In about 477 Archbishop Anthemios announced that a vision had led him to the tomb of Barnabas, the apostle who was a Cypriot and who had preached on the island with Paul, with a copy of Matthew's gospel lying on his chest. The find let the archbishop appeal over the head of the patriarch of Antioch directly to the emperor. Zeno paid for a basilica on the spot and confirmed the Cypriot bishops' right to consecrate their own. The church standing today was built around 900 over the east end of the old one.

finds.t: A rock-cut tomb reached by a stair under a small domed mausoleum a few hundred metres east of the monastery. The sixth-century Laudatio Barnabae describes the new tomb as faced with silver and marble.
finds.w: In situ, east of the monastery

finds.t: A timber-roofed church with stoas, gardens, aqueducts and hostels, paid for by the emperor and by local notables and built to catch pilgrims breaking their journey to Jerusalem. A monastic community lived beside it from the start.
finds.w: Foundations in situ, built into the later church

finds.t: In return for the discovery Zeno confirmed the church's autocephaly and gave its archbishop an imperial sceptre in place of a crosier, a Tyrian purple mantle under his vestments, and the right to sign in ink reddened with cinnabar. All three are still in use.
finds.w: Practice of the Church of Cyprus

finds.t: A short text recording two buildings that Anthemios's successor added to the complex, one of the few dated inscriptions from the site.

A vaulted cross-in-square church with three aisles and two flat domes on tall drums, raised after the basilica was wrecked in the late seventh-century raids. It may have housed the archbishops for a while after Constantia was given up. Archbishop Philotheos gave the buildings their present shape in 1756.
The Russian pilgrim Vasil Grigorovich-Barsky sketched the cloisters, courtyards and outbuildings, the earliest reliable picture of the monastery.
The church is now a museum of icons and the old cells hold antiquities from the Neolithic onwards. The last three monks, who lived by selling honey and painting icons, left in 1974.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Panagia Phorbiotissa (Asinou)
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A single-aisled barrel-vaulted church five kilometres south of Nikitari, all that survives of the monastery of Phorbia founded in 1099 and abandoned in the eighteenth century. A dedicatory inscription dates the paintings to 1105/06 and names the donor, a court official, in the reign of Alexios I Komnenos. This is the earliest and the finest Komnenian fresco cycle on the island, and the church UNESCO put first when it listed the ten painted churches of the Troodos in 1985.

finds.t: A panel on the south wall records that the church of the Holy Mother of God was painted at the urgent request and expense of a court official in the reign of the emperor Alexios Komnenos. The official's name is read as Nikephoros in most of the English literature and as Nikolaos in some Greek accounts, and the surname Ischyrios is not universally accepted.
In the eastern apse Christ hands John a gold vessel of wine while Judas turns his head away to go and betray him, a piece of narrative timing rare in Byzantine apses.
Forty soldiers freezing to death on a lake, painted at the western end of the north wall, one of the most complete Komnenian versions of the subject anywhere.

The vaulted narthex, added at the end of the twelfth century with apses north and south, is painted with the punishments of the damned, labelled with the wailing and gnashing of teeth. Beside it Saint Anastasia the Poison-Curer holds her phial of medicine.
The founder kneels in the Byzantine court dress of his day, offering a model of the church, one of the earliest such portraits on Cyprus and a rare picture of provincial officialdom.
Like the other Troodos churches, Asinou shelters under a steep timber roof that hides the vault and throws off snow. The present one dates from 1959 but the arrangement is original.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayios Nikolaos tis Steyis
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The only Middle Byzantine monastery church still standing in Cyprus, a domed cross-in-square building of the eleventh century a few kilometres south of Kakopetria. Its name, Saint Nicholas of the Roof, comes from the second steep-pitched timber roof thrown over dome and narthex alike against the Troodos snow, which hides an entirely conventional Byzantine church underneath. Six hundred years of wall painting survive inside. No surviving text mentions the place before the thirteenth century.

finds.t: Scenes from the life of Christ including the Raising of Lazarus and the Dormition of the Virgin, with the deep-set staring eyes that fresco painters of the day took from the manuscript illuminators of the Macedonian revival. Megaw called it a reflection, if a remote one, of Constantinople.

finds.n: The double roof and the narthex
finds.t: The narthex, vaulted with a calotte and two transverse arches, was added at the start of the twelfth century and the great pitched roof thrown over the whole. Megaw argued the steep roof was the local building tradition of these valleys reasserting itself over the imported dome.

The apse wall carries the usual row of Fathers, including Epiphanios of Salamis, who turns up constantly in Cypriot apses because the island claimed him. The Komnenian style here points to painters trained abroad, some perhaps in Constantinople.
Christ in the crown of the dome with prophets on the drum and the four evangelists in the pendentives, the most visible of the church's later campaigns.
Two life-size warrior saints on the north-west pier, part of a group of standing figures in the nave and narthex of the same date.
A pair of large narrative panels added while the island was under Frankish rule, when the church had come down from monastery to village church and pilgrimage stop.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Panagia tou Araka
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A small church on the north-east slopes of Madari, named after the vetch that grows around it, holding the most complete late Komnenian painted programme in Cyprus. An inscription on the north lintel says the paintings were finished in December 1192 by a monk called Theodore Apseudis, trained in Constantinople, the same painter who had decorated the hermitage of Neophytos above Paphos nine years earlier. The patron names himself Leon, son of Authentes, a Byzantine aristocrat who had taken refuge nearby. It is the last great work of Byzantine Cyprus, finished a year after the island changed hands.

finds.t: On the inner face of the north lintel, naming the month, the year and the painter, one of the very few signed and dated Byzantine fresco cycles anywhere.

On the south-eastern wall, the earliest known version of the subject: the Virgin stands full length before her throne holding the Child while two angels, painted as large as he is, carry the spear and the cross of his coming death. The scale given to the angels turns the image into an offering of the child to his fate.

A long inscription beside the Virgin in which the donor calls himself her poor and worthless servant, names his father Authentes, and asks with countless tears for a happy end to his life and his wife's. It is the fullest surviving voice of a Cypriot patron of the period.

finds.n: Saint Simeon with the Christ Child
finds.t: Facing the Virgin of the Passion, the aged Simeon holds the child with John the Baptist beside him carrying a scroll that reads 'Behold the Lamb of God'. Together the two walls stage the Presentation in the Temple across the width of the church.
Water damage forced a restoration in the fourteenth century, signed by a deacon called Leontios; the Winfields could tell his brushwork and palette from Apseudis's.

Dumbarton Oaks paid for David and June Winfield to clean and record the entire cycle over five seasons. Their reports identify ultramarine, vermilion, gold leaf and silver, some of the pigments sourced locally in the valley, and their 2003 book remains the standard study.
finds.w: Dumbarton Oaks, Washington; the paintings in situ

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayios Ioannis Lampadistis monastery
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A monastery on the bank of the Setrachos, three churches and a narthex huddled under one great tiled roof. The oldest part is the katholikon of Ayios Herakleidios, an eleventh-century four-columned cross-in-square church dedicated to the first bishop of Tamassos, whom tradition has Paul and Barnabas ordaining on this river in 45 CE. Beside it stands the chapel of the local saint John Lampadistis, and beyond that a chapel painted around 1500 in a frankly Italian manner. The monastery is no longer active but stays open, and it is one of the ten UNESCO painted churches.

finds.t: The oldest building on the site, with a thirteenth-century Pantokrator in the dome flanked by prophets and evangelists, and beside it the Sacrifice of Abraham, the Crucifixion, the Ascension and a Deesis.

In the Way to the Cross the soldiers leading Christ are painted as Western knights in the armour of the day, one of the sharpest images of Frankish rule made by an Orthodox painter. Nearby in the apse are Barlaam, the ancient Greek sages and the Virgin Blachernitissa.
The chapel on the north side, added for the local saint's cult and largely rebuilt in the early eighteenth century, which is why only two thin layers of older painting survive.

finds.n: The Latin Chapel and its Akathist cycle
finds.t: A chapel painted around 1500 with the hymns of the Akathist. In the scene of the Magi leaving the East an angel points out the star, and two bold figures in Phrygian caps walk in opposite directions to balance the composition. It is a masterpiece of post-Byzantine painting worked with Italian modelling and perspective.
The Second Coming, Christ and the Samaritan woman and the miraculous draught of fishes, painted across the shared narthex that ties the three churches together.
A silver-gilt casket holding the head of John Lampadistis, kept between the two chapels; it was the gift of Archbishop Nikephoros and is still the focus of the local feast.

finds.n: The iconostases and their old icons
finds.t: The katholikon's screen is of the fourteenth or fifteenth century and was altered in the sixteenth; the Lampadistis chapel's is seventeenth or eighteenth century with nineteenth-century sanctuary doors. Icons as old as the thirteenth century are set into both.
finds.w: In situ, Kalopanayiotis; further icons in the monastery collection

SETTLEMENTS.name: Christ Antiphonitis
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A twelfth-century church at the head of a wooded valley on the north slope of the Kyrenia range, built over a natural spring. Its wide dome rests on eight pillars, the only complete church of that type left in Cyprus. The name means Christ who answers, and probably comes from a miracle-working icon of which no account survives. Its wall paintings were hacked off after 1975 and sold on the international market; some icons have since been recovered through the courts, but the Tree of Jesse is gone.

finds.t: A single space covered by a spacious dome carried on eight pillars, a plan otherwise known only from a ruin inside St Hilarion Castle and from the church of St John Chrysostom at Koutsovendis before it was rebuilt. The dome is slightly out of true, perhaps damage from the earthquake of 1222.

The oldest layer, taken as a local reading of the late Komnenian manner of Lagoudera, included the Virgin and prelates in the apse, deacons, martyrs and stylites, and a Baptism on a nave pillar. The heads of the twelfth-century angels in the apse were damaged and partly cut away by the thieves.

An elaborate Judgement covered the north wall in a post-Byzantine local revival style. It is now badly damaged; the Tree of Jesse that faced it on the south wall was removed entirely and has not been recovered.
finds.w: Partly in situ; the rest missing

finds.t: Rupert Gunnis saw the screen painted blue and gold in the 1930s, with most of its icons of the seventeenth century and an Archangel Michael dated 1659. It was taken after 1975; four panels were traced to a private collector in the Netherlands and repatriated in September 2013, and a fifteenth-century Virgin from the church was found in Athens and returned on 14 September 1998.

Names and dates scratched into the lower paintings by ordinary Cypriots who came up the valley, mostly in Greek and a few in the Ottoman Turkish alphabet. They are among the few documents of popular devotion at the site.

Added while the church was under Latin control, and painted with a notably large Saint George now faded by sunlight. Stefano Lusignan wrote in 1580 that Antifoniti had been his family's fief, that his maternal grandmother founded the monastery, and that his brother died there as a monk.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Panagia Apsinthiotissa
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Below Sychari and Vouno (Taşkent), Kyrenia range
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A ruined monastery at the southern foot of the Pentadaktylos, probably an imperial foundation of the eleventh or twelfth century. Its name comes from the wormwood on the hillside, and a local story says a monk hid an icon of the Virgin in a cave behind a wormwood bush during Iconoclasm; centuries later a strange light on the mountain led the villagers to it. Western documents call it the abbey of Abscithi or Apinthi. It was already a ruin when George Jeffery described it in 1918.

finds.t: A cross-in-square church of the standard Byzantine type under a high dome, standing roofless for most of the last century.

A narthex on the west with plain rib vaulting, the clearest sign that the house had passed under the Roman church. Boustronios notes that the Queen of Cyprus worshipped here in 1486, and that on 15 August the whole population of Kyrenia went on pilgrimage to Apinthi and to Antiphonitis.
The monks' dining hall, recorded in three dimensions by the EpHEMERA project, is among the better-preserved parts of the complex.

Leontios, abbot here, was one of the delegates sent to Patriarch Germanos II in the Empire of Nicaea to report what Latin jurisdiction was doing to the Orthodox church. The archbishop of Cyprus, Neophytos, was in Nicaea at the same time, banished for refusing an oath of obedience to the pope.
finds.w: Recorded in the correspondence of the Patriarchate of Nicaea

finds.n: Transfer to the Patriarch of Jerusalem
finds.t: Under Ottoman rule the monastery became the property of the Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem and a dependency of St John Chrysostom at Koutsovendis, a few kilometres to the east.

After the crossings opened, Greek and Turkish Cypriot architects working through their two professional chambers listed and documented the abandoned religious buildings of the island. Apsinthiotissa was among the first they recorded.
finds.w: Records of the technical committee on cultural heritage

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayios Neophytos monastery and the Enkleistra
SETTLEMENTS.desc: In June 1159 the monk Neophytos, twice thwarted in his attempts to get away to a hermitage abroad and robbed of his travel money by his own gaolers, cut himself a cave in the cliff above the Paphos valley: a cell, a chapel and his own grave. Disciples came anyway, and in 1170 the bishop of Paphos ordained him priest and made him take a pupil. He wrote a great deal, including in 1196 an account of Richard I's conquest that is one of the very few Greek eyewitness sources for the Third Crusade in Cyprus, and he was scathing about the Franks.

finds.t: Three chambers cut by hand into the rock face behind a large trapezoidal narthex: the church of the Holy Cross, Neophytos's cell to the south and the refectory to the north. Neophytos enlarged an older hermit's cave to make them.

The nave and sanctuary of the cave church were painted in 1183 by Theodore Apseudis, named in an inscription in the cell; the same painter signed the cycle at Lagoudera nine years later. Deeper parts of the complex were painted after 1197 by other hands with a noticeably different style.

Two portraits of the living founder: one at the crown of the vault flanked by Michael and Gabriel, the other showing him attending a divine service inside the mandorla of Christ. Even sympathetic scholars have called the second close to blasphemy, and read both as symptoms of Neophytos's vanity.

finds.n: The niche for the True Cross
finds.t: A cross-shaped recess in the east wall of the cave church, cut to hold a wooden cross containing a fragment of the True Cross that Neophytos had obtained.
He hewed his own tomb in the Enkleistra and left detailed instructions for his burial in it. His relics were found again in 1756 and moved into the main church.

finds.n: On the calamities against the country of Cyprus
finds.t: A short, furious chronicle of Isaac Komnenos's fall and Richard's conquest, written by an eyewitness who hated both sides. It survives because Konstantinos Sathas printed it in Venice in 1873.
finds.w: Manuscript tradition; printed in Sathas, Mesaioniki Bibliothiki II

finds.t: A large basilica in Venetian taste outside the caves, once painted throughout though little survives. The monastery beside it, made first among Cypriot houses by the Patriarch of Constantinople in 1631, is still inhabited and runs a museum of icons and manuscripts.

A non-invasive survey found at least five painting phases in the Enkleistra, with lapis lazuli, gold and silver among the pigments and unusually high lead content, which suggests painters trained on wooden panels rather than plaster.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Stavrovouni Monastery
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A monastery on a bare limestone peak about 690 m above the Kornos plain, by tradition founded by Saint Helena around 327 to 329 CE and named for the relic of the True Cross she is said to have left there. It was one of the great pilgrimage stops of the crusader centuries and appears in the accounts of nearly every western traveller to Cyprus, who called it Santa Croce or the Mountain of the Holy Cross. Sacked in the medieval and early Ottoman centuries and gutted by fire in 1888, the present buildings are late, but the site itself and its relic are the oldest continuous Christian tradition on the island. Since 1889 it has kept Athonite rule, and women may not enter.

finds.p: Relic by tradition 4th century; present reliquary modern
finds.t: A large silver cross-shaped reliquary holding a small piece of wood, the only major relic to survive the fire of 1888. Whatever the monastery held before that had already gone: the Bohemian traveller Krystof Harant wrote in 1598 that nobody knew what the Turks had done with the True Cross.

The Rus' pilgrim Daniel, who stayed on Cyprus in 1106, wrote that the cross on Mount Olympus was not supported in the ground at all but held in empty space by the Holy Ghost, and that it warded off evil spirits and cured illness. His is the earliest firm outside notice of the monastery.

finds.n: The Cross of the Good Thief
finds.t: One of several relics ascribed to Helena's visit, along with a Holy Nail and a piece of the rope that bound Christ. Willibrand of Oldenburg saw the Good Thief's cross here in 1211 and reported, wrongly, that Stavrovouni was the highest mountain in Cyprus.
The German pilgrim compared the peak to Mount Tabor and claimed that from the top one could see Lebanon. On a clear enough day this is true.
finds.w: Ludolph's Description of the Holy Land

finds.t: The best known of the monastery's metochia, at the foot of the hill. Most of the monks lived down there until water and electricity reached the summit a few decades ago.

Stavrovouni has painted icons since it was refounded from Mount Athos in 1889; work by its monks, above all Father Kallinikos, hangs in churches all over Cyprus, and the small church at the summit was repainted with the Helena legend in his hand.
finds.w: Stavrovouni Monastery and churches across Cyprus

finds.t: A fragment of wood in a silver-gilt cross, with which the monastery has been identified since at least the crusader period; the monks also show the cross of the Good Thief, a nail and a length of rope. The relics are objects of devotion rather than of dated evidence.
The church on the very top of the peak, rebuilt after the fire of 1888; the one part of the monastery women are permitted to visit.

Ludolf von Suchen, Nicolas le Huen, Felix Fabri and others describe the climb, the relic and the story that the cross hung in the air unsupported; Cyprus was a scheduled stop on the Jaffa pilgrim route and Santa Croce was its inland attraction.
The dependency at the foot of the hill where the monks farm and paint icons, and the only part of the community women may visit, on Sundays.
Stavrovouni is the leading icon-painting house in Cyprus, working in a deliberately archaising Byzantine manner; its panels hang in churches across the island.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayia Paraskevi, Geroskipou
SETTLEMENTS.desc: A three-aisled church of the ninth century in the middle of Geroskipou, with three domes over the nave and one over each aisle, the same rare five-domed plan as Peristerona. Its walls are very thick and carry paintings in three layers, the oldest of them purely ornamental, painted while the empire was still forbidding images. The village name comes from Hieros Kepos, the sacred garden on the road to the sanctuary of Aphrodite, and the church may well stand on the older shrine.

finds.n: Aniconic decoration of the Iconoclast period
finds.t: The earliest surviving paint is not figural at all: crosses and pure ornament of the kind the imperial government allowed while images were banned. Cyprus, half outside the empire under the condominium, was little touched by Iconoclasm, which makes these few square metres unusually interesting.
The best-preserved piece of the second layer, on the north wall of the nave, painted over the aniconic ornament three centuries later.
Most of the paintings now visible are of the fifteenth century and take their subjects from the New Testament.

finds.n: Double-sided icon of the Panagia Geroskipiotissa
finds.t: The church's most important portable object, painted with the Virgin on one face and the Crucifixion on the other so that it could be carried in procession and read from either side.
A small chapel attached to the east end of the south aisle, most likely built over the relics or the burial place of a saint or martyr, which would explain why so grand a church went up in a village.
The bell tower on the south-east corner was put up in 1886 and the narthex-like western part built in the nineteenth century as a women's gallery, then extended in 1931.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayia Trias basilica
SETTLEMENTS.modern: Sipahi (Ayia Trias), 2 km east of Yialousa, Karpas
SETTLEMENTS.desc: One of the best-preserved early Christian church floors on the island, dug between 1935 and 1938 and dated to the fifth or sixth century. The basilica was destroyed in the middle of the seventh century, in the years of the Arab raids, and never rebuilt, which is why its mosaics survived where those of busier sites were replaced. They were conserved again in 2018 and 2019 under the bi-communal technical committee on cultural heritage.

finds.t: Geometric carpets of interlace, guilloche and knot patterns in white, ochre, red and slate, laid the length of a three-aisled church. Figural work is almost absent, which is normal in Cypriot church floors of the period.

A small panel near the west end shows a pair of sandals set side by side beside a dedicatory text, usually read as a sign to the worshipper to leave his shoes and go in barefoot. It is the detail visitors remember, though the reading rests on the excavators' interpretation rather than on any inscription that says so.
Greek texts worked into the paving asking for the salvation of the people who paid for each stretch, the ordinary way an early Cypriot congregation financed its church one panel at a time.
A separate baptistery with a cross-shaped font and its own mosaic floor, built when adults were still being baptised by immersion.
The site was uncovered in four seasons under the colonial Department of Antiquities, one of the campaigns that established how many early basilicas the island had held.
finds.w: Records of the Department of Antiquities, Nicosia

finds.t: Greek and Turkish Cypriot conservators relaid and consolidated the pavements together, one of the larger jobs done by the bi-communal committee that works on monuments on both sides of the line.

SETTLEMENTS.name: Ayios Mamas, Morphou
SETTLEMENTS.desc: The church over the tomb of St Mamas, reckoned by Greek Cypriots the third great pilgrimage of the island after the tomb of Barnabas and the monastery of Apostolos Andreas. Mamas was a third-century child martyr of Caesarea, but the Cypriots made him their own: their story has him a hermit near Morphou who dodged the tax collector, and who, when soldiers marched him to town, jumped on a lion that was mauling a lamb, saved the lamb and rode the lion into the governor's presence, and was let off his taxes for it. He is the patron saint of people who do not want to pay tax.
